Interface tour#

What's where in the editor, and how to rearrange it.

When to use it#

When finding your way around, or making the layout suit your screen.

How to use it#

This page follows what you see, in the order you meet it: the launcher Solis starts in, then the editor from its tab bar down to its status line. All of it is drawn in one look: dark neutral greys, lighter the nearer a surface is to you, with one accent colour for what's chosen. The accent, and how large the editor is drawn, are yours to choose in File › Preferences (Settings).

The launcher is what Solis always starts on: a small window of its own. Your projects are cards, each with its kind (2D, 3D or 2D + 3D), with Search projects, a filter by kind, Sort by, Open folder… and New project; down its left side, Projects, Learn and Updates, with Preferences and the User guide at the foot. Double-click a card and the window becomes the editor, with that project open, at the editor's own size and place. Why start there? Solis doesn't open the last project by itself, so you always choose what to work on. File › Close project brings the launcher back.

The tab bar is the dark strip along the very top. From left to right:

  • The logo, in a small light tile.
  • The tabs: File, Home, Library, Shading, Animate, UI, VFX, Audio, Debug and Build. Each is one kind of work, and a click on one changes the ribbon under it and what the editor shows (see The tabs below). The tab in front is lit, with a line of the accent colour under it. Shading and VFX are grey with a small hollow square after their names: those screens aren't built yet (Unfinished parts).
  • A tab that comes with a file (a contextual tab): while a tileset, a picture's crops or a selected tile map is open, a tab such as LIBRARY TOOLS · Tileset stands right after the tab it belongs to, with a ribbon of that file's own tools. Click it to bring that file to the front; it goes when the file closes. A tileset and a picture's crops fill their tab (with ‹ Back to Library at the right of the document's tab); a tile map's tab is Home with the Map tab in front in the bottom panel.
  • Search or run a command, in the middle: one search for everything (see below). Its right end shows its key, Space.
  • The project and the level, as in Harbour / docks, with an amber dot after the level's name while it has unsaved changes.
  • Documentation opens the user guide, this manual as one page in your browser, with a search. It is there on every tab, the File pages too, project or not.
  • The chevron at the far right collapses the ribbon (see below).

The ribbon is the band under the tab bar: the things you do on the tab in front, as buttons you can see instead of menus you have to open. Why a ribbon? Everything for the job at hand is on screen at once, each with its name under it, and nothing is hidden two menus deep. It is made of groups, each with its name underneath:

  • A large button is an icon over a word. Point at one and it says what it does, its shortcut if it has one, and, when it is greyed, why it can't be used right now.
  • A small row is a line of words: a switch has a box that is filled while it is on (Grid · 1 in Snapping), and a row with a small arrow opens a list (More).
  • A button that makes one of several kinds has a small arrow at the end of its name: click the button for the usual kind (Light makes a point light), or click the arrow, or right-click the button, for the list (a spotlight).
  • Grey controls with a small hollow square aren't built yet: they show where things will be (Unfinished parts), and one setting hides them all.

The Play group is at the ribbon's right end on every tab: Play is the one light button on screen. While the game runs it becomes Stop, with Pause and Step beside it; nothing else in the editor changes colour. See Play mode.

When the window is narrow the ribbon doesn't wrap: it scrolls sideways. Turn the mouse wheel while pointing at it.

To give the ribbon's room to the editor, click the chevron at the tab bar's right end, or double-click a tab: only the tabs stay. Click a tab then and the ribbon drops down over the editor until you choose something on it or move the pointer below it. The chevron, or another double-click, brings the ribbon back for good.

The tabs, one per job:

  • Home is for building levels: the level big in the centre with the tool bar floating at its foot (Select, Move, Rotate, Scale and Transform, and while a brush is edited, Points, Edges and Faces; see Selecting and moving), its entities in the Level panel at the left, the picked one's Properties at the right, and your files in the Library under the level. Its ribbon, each group named underneath: Edit (Undo and Redo, each named for the step it acts on when you point at it; see Undo and redo), Create (Entity, Model, Light, Camera, Shape (the brush list; its key, B, is written beside it), and More for a sprite, a tile map, a reverb zone, a trigger zone or a prefab from the selection), the snaps (Grid, Angle and Scale; click the value after "·" for the steps, see Selecting and moving) and Lighting (not built yet). Save and Build aren't on it: save with Ctrl+S, File › Save all, a right-click on the level's tab, or a click on Saved or Not saved yet in the status line; build on the Build tab. With the Library's Place switch on, the ribbon takes its build form for placing.
  • Library is the project's files (Projects and the Library): the same browser as Home's bottom panel, filling the centre, with the file picked in Details at the right. Its ribbon: Add (Import, Create, Folder), View (List, Show folders), Filter (Type) and Use (Place).
  • Animate is for animating sprites: a clips file's frames and clips, or an animator's graph and preview, each with a ribbon of its own (Animating sprites, Animators). With neither open it shows the Sequencer's page, not built yet.
  • UI draws game screens on the Canvas, with the drawing tools down its left edge; double-click a screen's file in the Library and Solis switches to UI with it open (The UI editor).
  • Audio is the mixer: a strip per bus with Master last in the centre, the project's sound events at the left, the bus you pick at the right with its ducking, and the Library under the mixer. Its ribbon: Bus (a new bus), Add rule, Remove, Clear solo, Mute the game and Heard at once.
  • Debug is for testing the game: the Profiler in the centre (the frames as bars, the frame you click as a timeline, and Statistics), with the Game as a tab beside it, and the Console in front under it. Its left slot, Running, isn't built yet; the Profiler holds its own Statistics. Its ribbon has CPU and GPU for the Profiler and the Session group: Load save (Save games), Play and record inputs and Replay a recording… (Input).
  • Build is Export for playtesting as a page: the game's name, the level it starts in, the folder and the window, with Export, and the Console under it. Its ribbon has Export and Open folder (the last export's folder); the full export beside them isn't built yet.
  • Shading and VFX, and the model viewer (a model's right-click in the Library, Open in the model viewer), are screens that aren't built yet: their ribbon and bottom tabs are shown greyed, round one page saying what will be there and when (Unfinished parts).

In a 2D or a 3D project the editor shows only what that kind of game uses (project kind). A 2D project has no Shading tab and no Lighting group, and Home's ribbon is laid out for 2D: Create has Entity, Sprite, Tile map, Camera, Trigger zone (a zone that tells game code when something walks in or out) and More (a point light, a reverb zone, Make prefab…); Paint tiles has the tile painter's Brush, Fill and Eyedropper, which paint the tile map picked; and the snaps are Grid · 16 px (the project's tile size), Snap to tiles and Pixel perfect (moves land on whole tiles, or on the game's whole pixels). The view is the 2D one, its pill saying its zoom (2D · 200%). A 3D project hides the tile painter, tile maps and the 2D view instead. The first few times a project opens as, or is switched to, 2D or 3D, a note on Home's ribbon says what's hidden; its × puts it away. Why hide anything? Each kind of game uses only part of the editor, and the rest is in the way. Nothing is deleted: set Project settings › General › Kind to Both to see everything (What each kind hides).

Each tab remembers its own bottom tab, whether its bottom panel is folded, which panels you hid, the split between its groups and every edge you dragged.

File is different: it is a page in place of the ribbon and the editor, with a column of items down its left side. Back to editor (or Esc) returns to the tab you came from. It holds what belongs to the open project and the editor; your projects, Learn and Updates are the launcher's, which Close project goes back to.

ItemWhat it does
Save allSaves the open level. Every other file saves as you change it.
Project settingsThis project's settings: General, 2D, Input (the game's actions and their keys, see Input) and Build (Settings).
PreferencesThe editor's own settings, such as its accent colour (Settings).
PluginsNot built yet.
AboutThe program's name, version and build, its licences, Check for updates and the user guide.
Close projectCloses the project, asking about unsaved work first, and goes back to the launcher. Closing the editor's window does the same.
ExitCloses Solis, asking about unsaved work first.

One search for everything: press Space (with nothing being typed) or click Search or run a command in the tab bar. Type part of a name and the list finds:

  • everything the editor can do (Save level, Add point light, Play…), each with where it lives and its shortcut beside it when it has one, so you pick up the keys as you go. Going to a tab, collapsing the ribbon, folding the bottom panel, Show hidden panels, Start placing and hiding unfinished parts are there too;
  • every file in the project, which opens it as a double-click in the Library would. A file you place rather than open (a model, a prefab, a sprite sheet, a tile map or a picture) is picked in the Library instead, with its folder open, ready to drag in;
  • every entity in the level, which selects it and points the camera at it;
  • a panel by its name, which comes to the front.

Up and Down choose, Enter does it, Esc closes. Why? You don't have to remember which tab something is on: type what you want. Things without a button on the ribbon are found here too, wherever else they are: New level and Open level… (the + after the level's tab), Save level as… (a right-click on the level's tab), Duplicate, Delete, Rename, Select all and Select nothing (a right-click in the Level list), Reset layout (File › Preferences), Documentation ↗ (the tab bar), Add the sample level, Check for updates (File › About), Close project (File), and showing or hiding the viewport's corner controls (its Show ▾ pill). Things that can't be done right now (Pause while editing, Delete with nothing selected) aren't listed. In the Frames tab, Space still plays and stops the clip, so point somewhere else first.

One frame on every tab. Under the ribbon, every tab divides the window the same way: a left slot and a right slot run full height down to the status line, the centre sits between them, and the bottom panel sits under the centre only. Each tab fills those slots with its own panels (the table below says which): on Home, the Level panel, the level, Properties and the Library. Why the same everywhere? A panel is always where you last saw one, whatever the tab, and the lists and settings keep their full height.

Every edge drags. Point at the line between the left slot and the centre, between the centre and the right slot, or along the bottom panel's top, and the line takes the accent colour and the pointer becomes a two-headed arrow: drag to give one side more room. Each of these three edges has a small grip at its middle. The line between two panels stacked in a slot, between two editor groups and beside the placing column drag too. Double-click an edge to put it back to its standard size. Every part keeps a least size and the centre never goes, so nothing can be dragged away. Sizes are shares of the window: make the window larger or smaller and the panels keep their proportions. Each tab keeps its own sizes; turn Each tab keeps its own panel sizes off in File › Preferences › Layout and a size you drag on one tab is used on all of them. When the window is too narrow for everything, the centre gives way first (down to 240 points), then the right slot, then the left (down to 180 each); narrower still, the right slot goes, then the left, until the window is wide enough again.

Hiding a panel. Each slot's header has its title and, at the right, ⋯: its panel's own menu (the Level panel's folding and showing), then Hide. A hidden panel gives its room to the centre. To bring it back, click its small icon at the right of the bottom panel's bar (Show Level, Show Properties), or press Space and choose Show hidden panels, or choose a layout in File › Preferences › Layout.

The bottom panel holds small tabs of one panel: on Home Library, Console and Problems (and Map while a tile map is selected), each with its count: the Console's warnings and errors, how many problems there are. Open, its bar has the tabs at the left and, at the right, the tools of the tab in front (the Console's Info, Warnings and Errors, Search the log, Clear and Copy; the Library's Place switch on Home, then its search, All kinds ▾ and grid or list) and ▾. Drag its top edge to any height. Fold it with ▾, a click on the tab in front, or Ctrl+Space (while typing too): it becomes one thin line over the status line, still naming its tabs with their counts, the newest warning or error faintly beside them, and Click a name to open it. A name opens that tab at the height it had. The Console's command line shows only on the Console tab, so it's never in the way.

Layouts. File › Preferences › Layout shows each layout as a small drawing: point at one to see it large in the Preview box, click it to use it at once (a small note says Layout is now … with Undo). A layout changes where the slots sit, on every tab, never what the panels do:

LayoutWhere things sit
StandardThe left slot at the left, the right slot at the right, the Library under the view.
Wide viewThe left and right slots share the right; the view gets the width.
Two viewsThe standard, with two views side by side in the centre (from above and in perspective). The view's own menu goes back to one.
Library on the leftThe Library under the left slot, in a tall list; the view runs down to the bottom line.
Tall propertiesThe right slot full height and wider; the bottom panel runs under the left slot too.
Just the viewEvery panel hidden and the bottom panel folded; its line stays, with the panels' names to bring them back.
Library on the rightThe Library under the right slot.

Reset sizes puts every edge you dragged back where the layout in use starts. Layouts saved by an older build open as the nearest one: the side layouts of before as Library on the left, Library on the right or the standard, and the shelf as the standard.

  • Editor groups hold documents: the level, the running game, an animator, a tileset, the mixer. Each group has a strip of tabs along its top (the one in front is lighter, with a thin accent line on top); click one to bring it to the front. A tab for a file has a × that closes the file; nothing asks whether to save, because those files save as you change them. When a tab shows two groups side by side, drag the thin line between them to give one more room; when the window is too narrow for both, they sit one above the other.
  • Drag a document's tab onto the left or right half of the centre and it gets a group of its own there, the rest beside it; drag it onto another group's tabs and the two groups join. Esc while dragging puts it back. Each tab keeps what you did while Solis runs.
  • The level's tab carries a +: New level and Open level…. Right-click the tab for Save, Save as…, Close others and Show in the Library. (Close is there but greyed: one level is open at a time, so open or make another in its place.)
  • What each tab remembers: its bottom tab, whether its bottom panel is folded, which panels are hidden, and every edge you dragged, separately for each layout, also after closing Solis. Reset layout (the search, or File › Preferences › Appearance) puts the tab you're on back as it started.

What each tab shows:

TabLeft slotCentreRight slotBottom panel
HomeLevel or Folders (the toggle in the slot's title)The level (its viewport, with the tool bar floating at its foot); a Game tab beside it, brought to the front, while the game runsPropertiesLibrary (with Place) · Console · Problems · Map, while an entity with a tile map is selected
Library(empty: the browser has its own folders)The LibraryDetails: Properties, showing the file pickedCode (the game's code files and what uses each) · Console · Problems · Import queue and History (not built yet); folded at first
Library tools · TilesetTerrainsThe tileset open (its picture, the chosen terrain's slots, Try it)Slot: the slot pickedConsole · Problems
Library tools · PictureCropsThe picture with its cropsConsole · Problems
AnimateClips while a clips file is open, Parameters while an animator isThe viewport while a clips file is open; with an animator, the Animator beside it and its Preview as a group of its own; with neither, the Sequencer's page (not built yet)Properties (the state picked) while an animator is openFrames (the timeline) and Clip while a clips file is open, each with a × that closes it · Animation, Sequencer and Key (not built yet) · Console
UIElementsThe Canvas, with its toolbox down its left edge (a × closes the screen open on it)Properties (the piece picked)Library · Pictures (for the Image tool) · Console · Problems
AudioSound eventsThe mixer (mixer.solmix)Bus: the bus picked, with a switch to its Effects (not built yet)Library · Snapshot (not built yet) · Console
DebugRunning (not built yet)The Profiler (its Statistics at its right), with the Game as a tab beside itConsole · Problems · Hottest functions and Memory snapshot (not built yet)
BuildExport for playtesting, as a pageConsole · Problems · Build log (not built yet)

Where each panel is:

PanelWhereWhat it's for
ViewportThe level's tab on Home and AnimateThe 3D world, in one, two or four views (flat ones too). See Moving around the viewport.
GameBeside the level while playing; beside the Profiler on DebugThe running game, through its camera, when you press Play. See Play mode.
LevelHome's left slot (in Wide view, over Properties at the right)Every entity in the level, as a tree, with its count in the header. The header's magnifier searches by name, the next button folds everything, and ⋯ unfolds everything, shows what's hidden, unlocks what's locked and hides the panel. Point at a row for its eye (hide) and lock; right-click it for Rename, Duplicate, Delete, Add…, Create prefab and Select all or nothing.
PropertiesThe right slot of Home, UI and Animate (with an animator), and the Library tab's (as Details) and a tileset's (as Slot)Along its top the selected entity: its name (click and type to rename it), what it is and what it's under, + Component, and ⋯ for rarer actions. Below, each component is a card with its settings, side by side as many as fit (a game code component's settings can have sliders, tips, headings and pickers its code asks for: see Field hints); a card's ? opens its chapter of the user guide and its ⋯ (or a right-click on the card) copies, pastes, resets or removes it. The last card is Hints: a few plain sentences about what's selected and what you can do with it. Turn hints off on it once you know your way around; File › Preferences turns them back on.
Library (under the view)The Library tab of the bottom panel on Home, UI and Audio; under the left or right slot in Library on the left or on the rightThe same browser as the Library tab's, showing the same folder: its folder tree, back, up and the breadcrumb, the files as tiles or a list. Drag a tile into the viewport to place it, right-click for the Library's menus. While placing, only what can be placed, with chips and a search, and a double-click places.
FoldersHome's left slot, when its title's toggle says FoldersThe project as trees of folders and files, one or several side by side (Open another tree in a tree's ⋯ menu), to move files between folders by dragging.
PlacementBeside the Library while placing (over it, where the Library is a column)How placed things land: on the grid, or where you point.
The Library browserThe Library tab's centreThe open project's folders and files as tiles or a list, with its folder tree, a kind filter and a search: the same browser as the one under the view.
CodeThe Library tab's bottom panelThe project's game code files in Lust, Rust or Lua. See Game code.
ConsoleA tab of the bottom panel on every tabMessages from the editor and the engine, and (on its tab only) a command line. See The Console.
ProblemsA tab of the bottom panel on Home, the Library, UI, Debug, Build and the Library toolsMistakes found in the game's code and in the level, such as a missing model. See Problems.
Mixer and BusAudio's centre and right slotThe project's buses, a strip each, and the bus picked with its ducking. See The Mixer.
Sound eventsAudio's left slotEvery sound event in the project, and the one picked to change and hear. See Sound events.
ProfilerDebug's centreWhere each frame's time goes. See The Profiler.
Export for playtestingBuildA folder with the game in it, to send. See Export for playtesting.
Clips, Frames and Clip, Animator, Parameters and Preview, Map, Tileset and Terrains, Atlas Crop and Crops, Canvas, Elements and PicturesWhile their file is open (the Map while a tile map is selected)See Animating sprites, Animators, Painting tiles, Tilesets and autotiling, Atlas Crop and The UI editor. Opening the file brings its tab to the front, and shows its slots if they were hidden.

Questions that stop your work (unsaved changes, a file changed on disk, keeping what you changed while playing) are a card over the dimmed window: the answer that sets your work aside at the left, the main one in the accent colour at the right.

The status line is one thin line along the bottom that says what's happening, so you don't have to go looking:

  • On the left, a green dot and Ready while the game's code is clean (Solis checks it when the project opens and each time you save a code file; hover to see when it last did), or, in red, how many mistakes it has. Beside it, the branch and its changes (not built yet).
  • Then Saved, Unsaved changes or Not saved yet for the open level: click it to save (Saving levels). Then Playing or Paused while the game runs, and what is selected (Crate 1 selected, 3 selected). While the brush list is open or a brush is being drawn out, what's going on (Choosing a shape brush: Ramp) stands there instead; for three seconds after you click a part that isn't built yet, so does a line saying so (Unfinished parts).
  • On the right: in the 2D view, the tile map's cell under the pointer while a map is picked (Tile 13, 9); what moves snap to and which way the gizmo points (Snap 0.25 · World, Snap off, or in the 2D view Snap 16 px on tiles and Snap whole pixels); in a 2D or 3D project, the project and its kind (Farm Days · 2D), and in a project of both kinds the level's name, whether the viewport shows it in 2D or 3D, and for 2D the game's size in pixels (farm · 2D · 480 × 270, from File › Project settings); then Solis's version, and Restart to update once an update has downloaded.
  • The problems' counts are on the bottom panel's Problems tab, in its line even while it's folded.

From an older build: panels used to be dragged anywhere and the Library could be a drawer; later the shelf ran along the bottom with its own tabs. An arrangement from the dragging days isn't carried over (the Console says so once); the shelf's tabs and heights are: the tab in front becomes the bottom panel's, and the layout chosen becomes its nearest.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Layout (File › Preferences › Layout)Where the slots sit on every tab, chosen from drawings, with Undo (Settings).
Each tab keeps its own panel sizes (File › Preferences › Layout)On (the standard): each tab remembers its own sizes. Off: a size you drag on one tab is used on all of them.
Reset sizes (File › Preferences › Layout)Puts every edge you dragged, on every tab, back where the layout in use starts.
Reset layout (in the search, and in File › Preferences › Appearance)Puts the tab you're on back as it started: its bottom tab, unfolded, its hidden panels shown, every edge's size in every layout, and how its groups were arranged (Settings).
File › PreferencesThe editor's own settings, such as its accent colour: see Settings.
The viewport's Show ▾ pillSwitches the frame time, the axis locks and camera speed, and the tool bar (Tools) on and off (the search does too).

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Search for anything to do, any file, entity or panel (with nothing being typed)Space
Choose a result in the search listUp, Down
Do what's chosenEnter, or click a result
Close the searchEsc, or click outside it
Leave the File page for the tab you came fromEsc
Collapse the ribbon, or bring it backDouble-click a tab, or the chevron
Scroll a ribbon that doesn't fitThe mouse wheel, over the ribbon
List the other kinds a Create button makesIts small arrow, or a right-click
Fold the bottom panel to one line, or open it again (while typing too)Ctrl+Space, or ▾, or a click on the tab in front
Open a bottom tab (from the folded line too)Click its name
Make the bottom panel taller or shorterDrag its top edge
Make a slot wider or narrowerDrag the line at its edge
Give one of two groups, or two panels in a slot, more roomDrag the line between them
Put an edge back to its standard sizeDouble-click it
Hide a panel⋯ in its header, then Hide
Show a hidden panel againIts icon at the right of the bottom panel's bar, or Space and Show hidden panels
A document in a group of its own, or two groups joinedDrag its tab to a half of the middle, or onto the other group's tabs
Put a dragged tab backEsc, while dragging
New level, Open level…The + after the level's tab
Save, Save as…, Close others, Show in the LibraryRight-click the level's tab

See Keyboard shortcuts for the rest.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a panel has disappeared. Why: it lives on another tab, it was hidden, or the bottom panel is folded. Fix: press Space and type its name: choosing it brings its tab to the front and shows it. Ctrl + Space opens the bottom panel; Show hidden panels brings back what was hidden.
  • Problem: a menu from an older build is gone (File, Edit, Entity, Help). Why: the tabs and the ribbon took the menu bar's place. Fix: press Space and type what you want: the list says where it lives now.
  • Problem: Save and Build aren't on Home's ribbon. Why: Save is Ctrl+S (or a click on Saved in the status line), and Build has a tab of its own. Fix: use either; File › Save all saves too.
  • Problem: the shelf and its Place tab are gone. Why: the shelf became the bottom panel, under the view only, and placing is the Library's Place switch. Fix: see The bottom panel above.
  • Problem: Properties is cramped. Why: its slot is narrow. Fix: drag the edge at its left for more room, it's remembered; or choose Tall properties in File › Preferences › Layout.
  • Problem: a side panel went when the window got narrow. Why: the window is too narrow for both slots and the centre. Fix: widen the window: it comes back by itself.
  • Problem: an edge won't go further. Why: each part keeps a least size, and the centre keeps room. Fix: make the part beside it smaller first, or double-click the edge to start again.
  • Problem: two of a tab's documents are side by side, or one group holds them all. Why: a tab was dragged. Fix: drag it back, or Reset layout.

Related#

  • The launcher: the window Solis starts in, with your projects, New project, Learn and Updates.
  • Projects and the Library: the Library.
  • Play mode: Play, Pause, Step and Stop.
  • Unfinished parts: what is greyed with a hollow square, and the setting that hides it all.

Settings#

Preferences, the editor's own settings, and Project settings, the open project's: two File pages, each with sub-tabs and one search.

When to use it#

When you want to change how the editor itself looks or behaves (its accent colour, how large it's drawn, what the viewport shows, where the panels sit and how they're sized, or hiding the parts that aren't built yet), or a setting that belongs to the whole project, such as its 2D resolution, its game's controls or how it is exported.

  • Preferences are yours, kept on this computer. They aren't saved in the level or the project.
  • Project settings are saved in the open project's folder, in small text files Git can merge, so they travel with it to other computers and other people. They need a project open.

Neither is an undo step. Every change applies at once: there is no Save or Apply button.

How to use it#

  1. Click the File tab, then Preferences or Project settings in its column. Or press Space and type Preferences. Preferences are on the launcher too, at the foot of its column.
  2. Pick a sub-tab under the heading: Preferences has General, Appearance, Layout, Viewport and Shortcuts; Project settings has General, 2D, Input, Tags and Build. The faint sub-tabs with a small square (Source control, Physics, Platforms and others) are unfinished parts.
  3. Each setting is a row, with its name and a line about it on the left and its control on the right: a switch, a row of choices side by side, a drop-down list, colour swatches, a number or a button. They work from the keyboard too: Tab moves from one to the next (a thin ring in the accent colour shows where you are), Space or Enter presses or flips it, and the arrow keys move along the swatches and the choices, or step through a drop-down list without opening it.
  4. Can't find something? Type in the search at the top right: it looks through every sub-tab of the page, at the settings' names and their lines, and shows the matches together.
  5. On Preferences, Reset to defaults (in the column at the right) puts the sub-tab's settings back as they were at first. On Project settings, a setting changed from its standard has a dot before its name and Reset after it; the heading counts them ("2 changed from defaults"), and a card at the right lists each, from what to what.
  6. Back to editor (or Esc) leaves the page.

Preferences#

SettingWhat it does
General › Look for updates when Solis startsAsks GitHub for a newer build at each start, in the background. Off, nothing is asked until you choose Check now on the launcher's Updates.
General › Show hintsThe Hints card, last under Properties, says what's selected and what you can do with it. Its Turn hints off does the same as this switch.
General › Open the guide inWhich program shows the user guide when you click Documentation: Default browser (the standard), a browser Windows lists as installed on this computer, or A program you choose…. A browser that's gone falls back to the default, and the status line says so.
General › Hide unfinished partsSome places in the editor are for features that come in later updates. They are shown faint with a small hollow square, and do nothing yet. Switch this on to hide every one of them, so only what works is on screen. The card beside it shows what one looks like. See Unfinished parts.
Appearance › Accent colourThe colour that marks what's chosen and selected: the chosen tool, the front tab, the selected row. Five colours: Blue (the standard), Grey, Orange, Teal and Purple. Colours that mean something keep their own: Play is the one light button on screen, and warnings and errors are amber and red. The small picture at the right shows the editor in the colour chosen.
Appearance › Interface scaleHow large everything is drawn: 100% to 200%. Raise it when text is too small, common on a laptop or a very sharp (4K) screen. Everything grows together, and thin lines stay crisp. It doesn't change your game.
Appearance › DensityHow tall buttons, fields and drop-down lists are: Compact (22 pixels at 100%), Default (24) or Comfortable (28). Text stays the same size.
Appearance › When something is selectedLeave the panels as they are (the standard) or Show Properties: Properties comes back every time you pick something, even if you hid it.
Appearance › This tab's panelsReset layout puts the tab you came from back as it started: its bottom panel on its first tab, unfolded, its hidden panels shown, and every edge you dragged at its standard size, in every layout. To put back one edge only, double-click it.
Layout › LayoutWhere the panels sit round the view, on every tab (layout), as cards each with a small drawing, its name and what it does: Standard, Wide view, Two views, Library on the left, Tall properties, Just the view and Library on the right. Point at one and the Preview box beside them shows it large, each part named. Click one and it's used at once, on every tab; a small note says Layout is now … with Undo, which puts back the layout before it and every panel you had hidden. In use marks the one in use. A layout changes where panels sit, never what they do. See Interface tour.
Layout › Each tab keeps its own panel sizesOn (the standard): each tab remembers the sizes you drag on it. Off: a size you drag on one tab is used on all of them, so the frame stays the same as you go from tab to tab.
Layout › Panel sizesReset sizes puts every edge you dragged, on every tab, back where the layout in use starts.
Appearance › Code editor splitAn unfinished part: it will show game code next to the viewport. Today, game code opens in your own code editor (Game code).
Viewport › Frame time and frame rateThe pill at the top right of the viewport.
Viewport › Axis locks, axes and camera speedThe pills at the bottom right: Lock X Y Z, World or Object, and the camera's speed.
Viewport › ToolsThe tool bar floating at the foot of the view. Q, W, R, S and T work either way.
Viewport › Preview animationSprites play their clips while you edit. Off (the standard), each shows its clip's frame and the editor rests. The game always animates.
Viewport › Grid step, Angle stepThe steps moves and turns land on while snapping is on (the Home ribbon's Snapping turns it on and off).
Viewport › In the 2D view, moves land onPixels (whole pixels, so pixel art stays crisp), Tiles or Off.
Viewport › Camera speedHow fast the camera flies, 1 to 8. Also changed by holding the right mouse button and turning the wheel.
Viewport › Views, Look, Bands of light, OutlinesThe same as the viewport's own pills: how many views, and how models are shaded while you edit (Looks).
ShortcutsEvery key the editor has, as a table you can filter (All, Keys, Mouse) and search. It is to read: changing a key is an unfinished part. The full list is Keyboard shortcuts.

Project settings#

SettingWhat it does
General › Project nameIts name in the window's title and on the launcher. Type a new one and click elsewhere; the folder keeps its own name.
General › Kind2D, 3D or Both: what the game is made of (project kind). Chosen when the project was made; a click here changes it at once, with no restart, and it's kept in the project's project.solis. The line under it says what the kind hides. 2D hides what only 3D games use: the Shading tab, lighting and baking, models (Create › Model, Import model), shape brushes, the 3D view's cameras (Perspective, Top, Front, Right) and its looks, and their settings. 3D hides what only 2D games use: tile maps and the tile painter, the 2D view, pixel snapping and Project settings › 2D. Both shows everything, and projects made before the kind was asked are Both. Nothing in the project is deleted when the kind changes, and the change isn't an undo step (no project setting is): choose the old kind again to see everything as it was. See What each kind hides.
General › Game starts inThe level the exported game opens in (the same setting as on Build).
General › Engine versionThe build of Solis that last opened the project, with Check now.
General › ScriptingGame code is written in Lust and opens in your code editor.
2D › Base resolutionThe size the project's 2D games are drawn at, in pixels, before they're scaled up: 480 × 270 to start. Pick a common size from the list, or type your own. See 2D.
2D › Pixels per unitHow many pixels make a metre: 16 to start.
2D › Tile sizeThe 2D view's grid, and new tile maps', in pixels: 16 × 16 to start.
2D › Scaling to the screenWhole steps (crisp, with bars if the screen doesn't divide evenly) or Fill the screen. The card beside it says how the base resolution fits 1920 × 1080, 2560 × 1440 and 3840 × 2160 screens.
InputThe game's controls: see Input.
TagsThe project's tags (Enemy, Collectible…), each with what uses it: + New tag, double-click a name to rename it everywhere, ⋯ › Delete. Kept in the project's tags.lst. See Tags.
BuildExport for playtesting: see Export for playtesting.

A number you drag is saved once, when you let go.

What each kind hides#

A 2D game has no use for models or a perspective camera, and a 3D game none for a tile painter, so a project shows only the parts of the editor its kind uses (project kind). It's one list inside Solis, so a part is hidden the same way everywhere: its tab, its ribbon button, its Create item, its component in Add component, its setting and its line in the search all go together, and its keys do nothing.

KindHidesKeeps
2DThe Shading tab; Home's Lighting group (Bake, Quality, Light map view); Create › Model and Shape, and Import model (lamps stay: a light shines on sprites too); the brush list (B paints tiles instead); the Perspective, Top, Front and Right views and the Look pill; the Model, Brush, Collider, Rigid body and Character body components; Preferences › Viewport's grid step, camera speed and looks.Sprites, tile maps and their painter, the 2D view and its camera, lights and the Environment (lamps and day and night), zones, prefabs, animation, screens, sound, the Debug and Build tabs: everything shared.
3DTile maps (Create › Tile map, New tile map, the Map tab and the painter); the 2D view; Pixel perfect and Snap to tiles; the Tile map, 2D collider and Parallax components; Preferences' In the 2D view, moves land on; Project settings › 2D.Models, lights, shape brushes, the 3D views, and everything shared, sprites among them.
BothNothing.Everything, as before projects had a kind.

Something of the hidden kind that's already in a level stays there: the Level panel lists it with a quiet 3D only (or 2D only) after its name, and Properties shows its component with the note 3D only: switch the project to Both to edit it, its values readable but greyed. Switch the kind to Both to change it.

The first few times a project opens as 2D or 3D, or is switched to one, Home's ribbon says what it hides ("No Shading tab and no Lighting group: they are 3D only"), while hints are on. Its × puts it away for good.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: everything in the editor is tiny. Why: on a very sharp screen each pixel is small. Fix: raise Appearance › Interface scale.
  • Problem: a tab, a button or a setting the manual mentions isn't there. Why: the project's kind hides it (a 2D project has no Shading tab, a 3D project no tile painter). Fix: set Project settings › General › Kind to Both, or the kind it belongs to.
  • Problem: a setting is faint, has a small square after its name, and its switch won't move. Why: it's an unfinished part. Fix: rest the pointer on it to read what it will do; switch on General › Hide unfinished parts if you'd rather not see it.
  • Problem: Project settings says Open a project first. Why: its settings belong to a project, and none is open. Fix: open or make one in the launcher (File › Close project goes back to it).
  • Problem: the Console says pixels.solpix had a mistake. Why: the file was edited by hand and can't be read. Fix: the standard 2D settings are used meanwhile; change anything on the 2D tab and the file is written again, with the damaged one kept beside it as pixels.solpix.bak.
  • Problem: the bottom panel is so tall (or folded) that what you want isn't in sight. Why: its height and fold are remembered per tab. Fix: Ctrl + Space opens it; double-click its top edge, or Layout › Reset sizes, puts it back.
  • Problem: after an update, the shelf is gone. Why: every tab has one frame now, and the shelf became the bottom panel under the view; the layout chosen before became its nearest. Fix: see Interface tour; try the layouts in Preferences › Layout.
  • Problem: I chose a layout by mistake. Why: a click applies it at once. Fix: Undo on the note that says Layout is now ….
  • Problem: I can't find the Settings window, or File › Input. Why: they became these pages. Fix: Preferences and Project settings are in the File column; Input is a sub-tab of Project settings.

  • Input: the game's controls, on Project settings › Input.
  • Export for playtesting: on Project settings › Build.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: what the 2D settings do.

Unfinished parts#

Parts of the editor that aren't built yet are shown in grey with a small square mark, and one setting hides them all.

When to use it#

Solis's interface is being rebuilt to one design, and that design is larger than what Solis can do today: it has places for things that come in later updates, such as materials, effects and a built-in code view. Rather than leave holes, the editor shows each of those places where it will be, marked so you can tell it apart from what works. This is called an unfinished part.

Read this page when you see a grey control with a small hollow square beside it and wonder why a click does nothing, or when you'd rather not see any of them.

Why show them at all? So the editor's layout stays the same as it grows: what you learn now is where things will still be, and you can see what's coming and roughly when. If you'd rather work with only what works today, hide them: nothing you can use disappears with them.

They are on the ribbon, the bottom panel and the slots, the File pages (sub-tabs and rows of Preferences and Project settings, Input's Contexts and Fires on), Build's full export, Audio's effects, the Profiler's thread lanes, and whole screens: Shading, VFX and the model viewer (a model's right-click in the Library, Open in the model viewer), each in its own place. File › Preferences › General has a small card showing what one looks like.

How to use it#

  1. Recognise one. An unfinished part has three signs, always together:
    • its words are a quieter grey than a working control's, and its icon fainter still;
    • a small hollow square sits at its top right corner (on a button) or just after its words (on a tab, a row or a setting);
    • it doesn't light up when the pointer is over it.
  2. Find out what it will be. Rest the pointer on it. A note says its name, what it will do in one sentence, and which step of the roadmap↗ builds it, for example: Not built yet: Code editor split. Shows game code next to the viewport when a code file is open. Not planned yet. "Not planned yet" means the design has a place for it but no step of the roadmap builds it so far.
  3. Clicking it does nothing, on purpose. The status line says so for three seconds (Code editor split isn't built yet (not planned yet)), and that's all: no window opens and nothing changes.
  4. Hide them all: open File › Preferences, and on General switch on Hide unfinished parts. Or press Space and type hide unfinished. Every unfinished part goes, and what's left closes up, so there are no gaps where they were.
  5. A whole screen that isn't built (Shading, VFX, the model viewer) is its ribbon and its bottom panel's tabs, all marked, round one card in the middle saying what it will be and when. The card's Hide unfinished parts link hides them all. With them hidden, Shading and VFX leave the tab bar and a model's menu has no way into the viewer.
  6. Show them again: switch it off in the same place, or press Space and type show unfinished.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
General › Hide unfinished partsOff (the standard): unfinished parts are shown, marked. On: none is shown anywhere, and the things around them close up. It's remembered next time you start. Reset to defaults on General turns it off again. See Settings.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Hide or show unfinished partsSpace, then type unfinished and press Enter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I clicked a button and nothing happened. Why: if it's grey with a small hollow square, it's an unfinished part: it marks where a feature will be. Fix: rest the pointer on it to read what it will do and when. For what can be done today, the manual's list of pages covers everything that works.
  • Problem: is a grey control broken, or switched off? Why: neither is the same as unfinished. A control that works but can't be used right now (Add the sample level on Learn with no project open, say) is faded and has no square mark; resting the pointer on it says what to do first. An unfinished part always has the mark. Fix: look for the square.
  • Problem: something I saw before is gone. Why: Hide unfinished parts may be on: it hides only what never worked. Fix: switch it off on File › Preferences to see the marked places again.
  • Problem: I can't find an unfinished part with the search. Why: the search (Space) lists only what can be done. Fix: nothing to do: when a part is built, it joins the search.

Related#

  • Settings: the Appearance page and its other settings.
  • Interface tour: the editor's tabs, frame, bottom panel and lines.
  • Concepts: unfinished part, ribbon, bottom panel, accent colour.

Moving around the viewport#

Fly the camera through the 3D world, split the viewport into several views (flat ones too), and use the tool bar and the pills floating over each view.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to look at the world from somewhere else. Solis has one camera style, the fly camera: you steer it like a drone, as in Unreal Engine.

How to use it#

Looking and flying:

  1. Point at the viewport and hold the right mouse button. The pointer disappears.
  2. Move the mouse to look around.
  3. While still holding the button, use the keys:
    • W forward, S back, A left, D right (forward follows where you look, so looking down and pressing W flies down);
    • E straight up, Q straight down;
    • Shift to go three times faster while held.
  4. Let go of the right button. The pointer comes back where it was.

Without holding the right button:

  • Mouse wheel: moves forward or back in steps.
  • Hold the middle button (the wheel) and drag: slides the view sideways and up or down. The ground under the pointer moves with it.

Several views (the view's pill, Perspective ▾, under Views): One view, Two side by side, Two, one above the other, or Four views. Each view has its own camera and its own look; with four, they start as Perspective, Top, Front and Right, the classic way to line things up exactly.

  • Click in a view (or turn the wheel over it) to use it: it gets a thin coloured outline, the frame time and the axis locks. F, the ribbon's Create buttons, and anything else that goes "where the camera looks" use that view.
  • Selecting, the gizmos, and dragging things in from the Library work in every view.
  • Maximise (in each view's own Perspective ▾ list, while there are several) shows that view alone, filling the viewport; All views brings the others back.
  • Solis remembers the layout and every view's camera next time.

Flat views (concepts): the Perspective ▾ pill at the top left of each view chooses what it shows: Perspective, Top, Front or Right. A flat view shows things at their true size whatever their distance, with the grid standing in the view's own plane, so lining up edges and heights is exact.

  • Hold the right or middle button and drag to slide the view.
  • Turn the wheel to zoom in or out, towards the pointer.
  • Flat views don't fly: switch back to Perspective for that.
  • Flat views have no fog, so faraway parts are as clear as near ones.
  • A camera or spotlight added from a flat view (and Move here) goes just in front of where the view looks from, as if it were a camera above or beside the level looking in.

These are the flat-view controls Unreal Engine uses.

The 2D view (the last in the Perspective ▾ list): a flat view from above like Top, measured in your game's pixels, for 2D games (2D). It slides the same way, but the wheel zooms in whole steps (100%, 200%, 300%…) and every pixel of the game lands on whole screen pixels, so pixel art looks as it will in the game. The grid is the project's tile size, a dashed frame shows what each 2D camera sees, and the pills at the bottom right are Lock X Y, Snap: Whole pixels ▾ (moves land on whole pixels, tiles, or anywhere), the grid and Zoom ▾. Moves go across the ground only (X and Y).

The tool bar floats at the foot of the view in use, in the middle: Select (Q), Move (W), Rotate (R), Scale (S) and Transform (T), each with its key small in its corner, the tool in use filled with the accent colour. While you edit a brush's insides, a short line and Points (1), Edges (2) and Faces (3) follow. See Selecting and moving things. It floats over the picture rather than taking a column beside it, so the view keeps its whole width. It keeps clear of the pills at the bottom right: when the view is too narrow for both on one row, it moves left of them and its buttons get a little smaller; if there's still no room, it goes above them, and in a very narrow view its buttons shrink to fit (point at one to see its name and key). With two or four views it is on the view in use, as the bottom-right pills are. A tile map's painting tools are on their own ribbon instead (Painting tiles); while one is in use, no tool on the bar is lit.

The pills float over each view, so the picture stays as large as it can be:

  • Top left, on every view: the view (Perspective ▾: its kind, and how many views), the look (Standard ▾, how models are shaded; see Looks) and Show ▾: what the viewport shows (the frame time, the axis locks and camera speed, the Tools bar) and Preview animation.
  • Top right, on the view in use: the time each frame takes and the frames per second. Point at it to see how many entities and triangles there are. When nothing moves it says Idle: Solis then draws only when something changes, so your computer isn't kept busy (and a laptop stays cool and quiet). Fly the camera or press Play to see the frame rate.
  • Bottom right, on the view in use: Lock X Y Z (the axis locks), World ▾ or Object ▾ (which way the gizmo points) and the camera's speed. See Selecting and moving things.

Snapping (Grid, Angle, Scale) is on the ribbon, in Home's Snapping group.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Camera speed (1 to 8)How fast W, A, S, D, Q and E move: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 metres a second. Change it by turning the mouse wheel while holding the right button. 4 (8 metres a second) is a good start; use 6 to 8 to cross a big map. Shown in the Camera box.

The camera's position, direction and speed are remembered next time.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Look aroundHold right mouse, move the mouse
FlyHold right mouse + W A S D
Down, upHold right mouse + Q, E
Faster for a momentHold Shift while flying
Change speedHold right mouse + mouse wheel
Forward, back in stepsMouse wheel
SlideHold middle mouse, drag
Slide a flat viewHold right or middle mouse, drag
Zoom a flat viewMouse wheel (towards the pointer)
Use a viewClick in it

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing W picked the Move tool instead of flying. Why: the right mouse button wasn't held. The tool keys work only when it isn't. Fix: hold the right button first, then press W.
  • Problem: you're lost. Fix: fly up with E, look down, and find where the red and green lines cross: that's the origin.
  • Problem: holding the right button doesn't fly. Why: the view is a flat one (Top, Front or Right). Fix: drag to slide it, or switch it to Perspective.
  • Problem: the right button didn't fly while you were drawing a selection box or dragging a gizmo. Why: with the left button held on one of those, a right click cancels it (see Selecting and moving things). Fix: let go of both buttons, then hold the right one.
  • Problem: F or Add entity went to the wrong view. Why: they follow the view in use, the one with the outline. Fix: click in the view you want first.
  • Problem: flying feels too slow or too fast. Fix: change the speed with the wheel while holding the right button.

Related#

  • Keyboard shortcuts

Entities and components#

Everything in a level is an entity, and what it does comes from its components.

When to use it#

Every level in Solis is built the same way, so once you know this you can understand any of them (concepts):

  • An entity is one thing: the sun, a lamp, an imported model, the sky. On its own it is only a name.
  • Components make it something. A Transform gives it a place in the world, a Light makes it shine, a Model draws an imported model, an Environment sets the sky and fog, a Camera is what the game looks through (Play mode), and a RigidBody and a Collider make it take part in physics.

A lamp is just an entity with a Transform and a Light. Give a model a Light (+ Component › Light) and it shines like a lamp too. Your game's own code adds components of its own (Game code), shown the same way.

How to use it#

See what something is made of

  1. Click it in the Level panel, or in the viewport (Selecting and moving things).
  2. Properties shows its Name and each of its components in a card of its own, Transform first, with their settings. Point at a setting's name to see what it does.
  3. Each card's ? opens this manual's page about that component. A component from your game code shows the file it's written in instead, with Open in Ledger ↗ to open that file in the program you write code in. A component written in Lua says Show in folder ↗ and shows its file in its folder for you to open from your editor. Why? Solis only ever opens pictures, text and Lust in another program: a downloaded project's .lua file, opened by a program on your computer that runs Lua, would run outside Solis's sandbox (see Projects and the Library).

What's been changed: a small dot in the accent colour before a setting's name means it isn't the component's standard value (what it starts with). Beside the setting, ↺ and the standard value (↺ 1000) put it back, as one step Ctrl + Z undoes. Why? So you can see at a glance what you've tuned, and undo an experiment without remembering the old number. Places, turns and picked files aren't marked: they start empty and are meant to be set. A light's standard values are its kind's (a sun's, a lamp's, a spotlight's) and the Environment's are a new level's, so a level's own Sun shows no dots until you change it, and ↺ puts back a sun's value, not a lamp's. (These dots are in the accent colour; a prefab's copy marks its own changes with orange dots and ↶ instead.)

Shared files: a file several entities use, such as a model or sprite sheet, says shared by 3 beside it. Changing the file itself (in Aseprite, say) changes all of them, so this tells you before you do.

Add an entity

  • Home › Empty adds an empty one (only a Transform) at the point the camera looks at. Light beside it adds a point light, and its small arrow lists the spotlight (lights); Camera, Sprite and Tile map are there too; importing a model adds an entity for it.

Add or remove a component

  • Click + Component at the top right of Properties, type part of a name to narrow the list, and pick one (or press Enter for the first): a Light turns any entity into a lamp, a Model shows a model, and so on. It starts with its usual settings. The list is in two groups: Built in (Solis's own) and Game code (the ready-made kit's and your own); point at one to see what it does.
  • A setting that points at another entity (a camera's target, say) shows that entity's name. Click it for a list of the level's entities, with a box to find one by name, and None to point at nothing.
  • A card's ⋯ (or a right-click anywhere on the card) has Remove, which takes the component off. Game code's own components appear in the same list.

Select several

  • Click one to select just it. Ctrl + click adds one to the selection, or takes it out. Shift + click selects every row from the one you picked first to this one.
  • With one selected, Properties shows it. With several selected, Properties shows the components they all have. A setting that differs between them shows —; change it and every one of them gets the new value, as one step Ctrl + Z undoes. Change one number of a position or rotation (say Z), and only that number changes on each, so they keep their own X and Y.

Find, fold, hide and lock in the Level column

  • Search (the magnifier in the Level column's header): a field opens under the header; type part of a name to list only the entities called that, with what they belong to. Esc empties and closes it.
  • ▾ / ▸ before an entity with children folds them away or shows them again. The header's fold button folds everything; its ⋯ has Unfold everything, Fold everything, Show everything hidden and Unlock everything. Selecting something in the viewport unfolds the way to it, so you can see it in the list.
  • Point at a row to see its two switches on the right: the eye hides the entity in the editor (it isn't drawn, and nor is anything under it), and the padlock locks it, so clicks in the viewport pass through it to what's behind (handy for a floor you keep clicking by mistake). The switches stay showing while they're on. Show everything hidden and Unlock everything, on the Level column header's ⋯, turn them all off.
  • Hiding and locking are only how you see the level while you work: they aren't saved in the level, aren't undo steps, and don't change the game.

Copy settings from one entity to another

  • A card's ⋯ has Copy values, Paste values and Reset to defaults. Copy a Light from one lamp and paste it onto another to make them match; pasting onto an entity without that component adds it.
  • The ⋯ beside the entity's name has Copy components, which copies all of them at once, and Paste components, which gives them to everything selected.

Rename, move, copy or delete

  • Click its name at the top of Properties and type, press F2, or double-click it in the Level column (or choose Rename in its right-click menu) to rename it (Enter to keep, Esc to cancel).
  • Change Position under Transform, or choose Move here in the ⋯ beside its name to bring it to where the camera looks.
  • Ctrl + D duplicates the selection, with everything under each one, and selects the copies.
  • Unpack (in the ⋯ beside a model's name) splits it into separate entities; Unlink (beside Prefab: … at the top of a placed prefab's Properties) makes a copy plain entities.
  • Delete (the key, the ⋯ beside its name in Properties, or Delete in a row's right-click menu in the Level column) removes the selection and everything under it.
  • Marks at a row's right: a link marks a placed copy of a prefab, and an orange dot one that changes some settings (on a part, that this part does). A plain entity, not from a prefab, has no mark. Pointing at a row shows its hide and lock switches in their place.
  • Right-click a row in the Level column for its menu, close to hand: Rename, Duplicate, Delete; Add entity, point light, spotlight or camera; Make prefab…; Select all and Select nothing. The row right-clicked is selected first, so the menu acts on it. These are the same things the Home tab's ribbon and the search do.
  • F points the camera at the selection.

Parents and children (concepts): drag an entity in the Level panel onto another to put it under that one; it then moves, turns and is deleted with its parent. Drag it onto the empty space below the list to make it stand alone again. It stays exactly where it is in the world either way: only its numbers change, because a child's Position is measured from its parent. Lights brought in with a model start under it. Dragging one of several selected entities moves them all.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Add to or take from the selectionCtrl+click
Select a rangeShift+click
RenameF2, or double-click (Enter keeps the name, Esc leaves it)
Select everythingCtrl+A
Select nothingEsc
DuplicateCtrl+D
DeleteDelete
Point the camera at the selectionF
Put under anotherdrag onto it in the Level panel
Make it stand alonedrag onto empty space in the Level panel

Settings#

The Transform every placed entity has:

SettingWhat it does
PositionWhere it is, in metres along X, Y and Z (Z is up). A child's position is measured from its parent.
RotationHow it's turned, in degrees: X tilts it forward and back, Y tilts it sideways, Z turns it round like a weathervane.
ScaleHow big it is: 1 is its own size, 2 twice as big along that axis.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Properties says Missing component. Why: the level uses a component Solis doesn't know, such as one from game code that isn't there. Fix: nothing is lost: its values are kept as they are. Click Remove if you don't need it.
  • Problem: my entities are gone after closing Solis. Why: the level wasn't saved. Fix: save with Ctrl + S (Saving levels); Solis asks before closing with unsaved changes.
  • Problem: I dragged an entity onto another and nothing happened. Why: an entity can't go under itself or its own children (that would make a loop).
  • Problem: something is missing from the viewport. Why: it (or something it belongs to) is hidden with the eye in the Level panel. Fix: Show everything hidden, in the Level column's ⋯ menu.
  • Problem: clicking something in the viewport selects what's behind it. Why: it's locked (the padlock). Fix: click its padlock, or Unlock everything in the Level column's ⋯ menu.
  • Every change here can be undone with Ctrl + Z (Undo and redo).

Related#

  • Lights and shadows
  • Sky, fog and exposure
  • Importing models
  • Concepts: entity, component, transform, parent
← Previous · Chapter 9Moving around the viewportNext → · Chapter 11Selecting and moving things

Selecting and moving things#

Click things in the viewport to select them, then move, turn and resize them with the gizmos.

When to use it#

Whenever you build a level: picking a model to change it, arranging crates, turning a lamp to face a wall, making a rock bigger. Clicking in the viewport is the quickest way to pick something you can see; the Level panel is better for things you can't see (an entity with no model, or one hidden behind another).

How to use it#

Selecting:

  1. Click a model or a lamp's marker in the viewport. It's outlined in the accent colour, and the Level panel and Properties show it.
  2. Ctrl + click adds another one to the selection, or takes it out if it's already selected.
  3. Drag on empty space to draw a box: everything you can see inside it is selected. Hold Ctrl while dragging to add to what's selected. To give up on a box before letting go, press Esc or click the right mouse button: the selection stays as it was.
  4. Esc selects nothing; Ctrl + A selects everything in the level.

Clicking on empty sky or ground selects nothing.

Copies of prefabs are selected whole the first time: clicking any part of a placed lamp post selects the whole lamp post. Click again on a part to select just that part. This stops you from pulling a copy apart by accident. See Prefabs.

Moving, turning and resizing:

  1. Select something.
  2. Choose a tool with its key or its button on the tool bar, the rounded bar floating at the foot of the viewport: Move (W), Rotate (R), Scale (S), or Transform (T), which shows all three. Select (Q) shows no gizmo, so clicks only select. Each button has its key small in its corner, and the tool in use is filled with the accent colour; point at a button to see its name. The keys and the buttons do the same thing, so use whichever is nearer your hand.
  3. A gizmo appears on the selection. Drag one of its handles:
    • Move: drag an arrow to move along that axis, a square to move in that flat plane (the blue-sided square slides along the ground), or the dot in the middle to move across the screen.
    • Rotate: drag a ring to turn around that axis (the blue ring turns like a record on a turntable), or the outer ring to turn around the line you're looking along.
    • Scale: drag a box at the end of a line to stretch along that axis, a square to grow two axes together, or the dot in the middle to grow evenly (right or up grows, left or down shrinks).
  4. While you drag, a note by the mouse says how far or how much ("X +1.50 m", "+15.0°", "× 1.30").
  5. Let go. The whole drag is one undo step: Ctrl + Z puts it back.

To give up on a drag before letting go, press Esc or click the right mouse button: everything goes back to where it was, and nothing is added to undo.

While the left button is held on a box or a gizmo, the right button only cancels: it doesn't start flying the camera, in any kind of view. Let go of both, and it flies again.

When several things are selected, the gizmo sits in the middle of them and they move together. Something inside another selected entity (a lamp inside a selected room) moves with it, not twice.

Settings#

The axis locks and the axes are the pills at the viewport's bottom right; snapping is the ribbon's Snapping group on the Home tab. Solis remembers them on this computer, and the status line says what moves snap to ("Snap 0.25 · World").

SettingWhat it does
Lock X Y ZLock an axis: drags leave it alone, and its handles disappear. The letter is lit in the accent colour while locked; click it or press its key again to free it. Example: lock Z, then drag the middle dot to slide something around without lifting it off the floor.
World ▾ / Object ▾Which way the gizmo's arrows point: along the world's axes (X, Y and Z of the whole level), or along the selected entity's own axes (useful for a turned object, to slide it along its own length).
Grid · 1Snapping for moving: ticked, moves land on the grid lines, so things line up. Click the number (or right-click the row) to choose the step: 1, 0.5, 0.25 or 0.1 m. With object axes, moves go in steps of that size instead.
Angle · 15°Snapping for turning: ticked, turns go in steps. Click the number (or right-click) to choose 5°, 15°, 45° or 90°.
Scale · 10%Snapping for resizing: ticked, sizes change in steps of 10%.
The camera pillThe camera's speed step (see Moving around the viewport).

Hold Ctrl while dragging to flip snapping for that one drag: on if it's off, off if it's on. Hold Shift to drag ten times more finely, for small adjustments.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
SelectClick
Add to or take from the selectionCtrl + click
Select with a boxDrag on empty space (Ctrl + drag adds)
Select nothingEsc
Select everythingCtrl + A
Select, Move, Rotate, Scale, TransformQ, W, R, S, T
Snapping on or off for one dragHold Ctrl while dragging
Ten times finerHold Shift while dragging
Cancel a box or a gizmo dragEsc, or right click
Lock or free an axisX, Y, Z
World or object axesL

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: no gizmo appears. Why: the Select tool (Q) is chosen, nothing is selected, or what's selected has no position (the level's Environment, for example). Fix: press W, R, S or T, and select something with a Transform.
  • Problem: an arrow or ring is missing. Why: its axis is locked (its letter is lit in the Lock pill), or the arrow points almost straight at you, so it's too short to grab. Fix: free the axis, or move the camera a little.
  • Problem: clicking a part of a placed prefab selects the whole thing. Why: copies are selected whole first. Fix: click the part again.
  • Problem: a turned box stretches oddly when scaled. Why: stretching a turned object along the world's axes would skew it, which a Transform can't hold, so Solis keeps the nearest shape without a skew. Fix: press L for object axes, so it stretches along its own sides.
  • Tip: you can't select something hidden behind another model by clicking; select it in the Level panel instead.

Related#

  • Entities and components: the Level panel and Properties
  • Undo and redo
  • Moving around the viewport
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Concepts: gizmo, snapping, selection
