Undo and redo#

Take back any change to the level, and bring it back again.

When to use it#

Whenever a change didn't turn out as you hoped: a light dragged too bright, an entity deleted by mistake, a model imported into the wrong level. Every change to the level can be undone, so it's safe to experiment.

How to use it#

  1. Press Ctrl + Z (or choose Home › Undo) to take back the last change. Point at the button and it names the step, such as Undo Change Light.strength.
  2. Press again to go further back.
  3. Press Ctrl + Y or Ctrl + Shift + Z (or Home › Redo) to bring a change back.

Undo also selects what the change was about, so you can see what came back.

What counts as one step:

  • A whole drag of a number is one step, however long you drag. Dragging back to where you started leaves no step at all.
  • Typing a name is one step until you click somewhere else.
  • An import is one step, with the lights that came with the model.

Tabs with their own undo: the Clips and Frames tabs, the Animator, the Tileset tab and the Map tab each keep their own steps: Ctrl + Z with the pointer over the tab undoes there. A tileset's steps belong to its file, not to the tab: they are kept while the project is open, whether the change was made in the Tileset tab, in the tileset's Properties (clicked in the Library) or by ticking Solid in the Map tab, and Ctrl + Z over the Tileset tab, or over Properties while it shows the tileset, undoes the last of them. While a tile painting tool is in use, Ctrl + Z undoes the last stroke (each stroke, from pressing the button to letting go, is one step). In these tabs, and in the Atlas Crop tab, a whole drag of a number or of a colour in its picker is one step too: the field shows the value as you drag, and the change is made, and the file saved, once, when you let go. A typed number counts when you press Enter or click somewhere else.

What isn't undone: selecting things, moving the camera, and the editor's own settings (panels, look, accent colour). They aren't part of the level.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
UndoCtrl+Z
RedoCtrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Ctrl + Z changed the text I was typing instead of the level. Why: while you type in a field, Ctrl + Z undoes the typing first. Fix: click outside the field, then press Ctrl + Z.
  • Problem: I undid something, made a new change, and now Redo is greyed out. Why: a new change starts a new path; what you undid can't come back after that, as in most programs.
  • Problem: a change I made in a tab was taken back, and the Console says Couldn't save … It's shown as the file has it, without your change. Why: tile maps, tilesets, clips files, animators and atlases are saved the moment you change them, and this time the file couldn't be written (the disk is full, another program has the file open, or its folder is gone). Solis never shows as saved a change that isn't in the file, so it shows the file as it is, and keeps your change as an undo step. Fix: put right what the Console says went wrong, then press Ctrl + Z with the pointer over the tab the message names: your change comes back and is saved again.
  • Solis keeps the most recent changes, up to about 64 MB of them; the oldest are forgotten first. That's thousands of ordinary changes.

Related#

  • Entities and components
  • Keyboard shortcuts
← Previous · Chapter 11Selecting and moving thingsNext → · Chapter 13Saving levels

Saving levels#

Save a level as a file, open it again, and share it through Git without merge trouble.

When to use it#

Save whenever you've built something you want to keep. A level (a level, a menu, a room) is one file ending in .sollevel, kept in your project (Solis suggests its levels folder if it has one, or else the project's own folder).

The file is plain text, written so that two people changing different things in the same level can merge their work in Git without conflicts. It's also safe to read and edit by hand.

How to use it#

  1. Save: press Ctrl + S (or click Not saved yet or Saved in the status line, File › Save all, or Save on the level's tab's right-click). The first time, choose a name and a folder.
  2. Save as: Ctrl + Shift + S saves a copy under a new name and carries on with that one.
  3. Open: Ctrl + O (or Open level… (press Space and type it, or Ctrl + O)). The models it uses are read from the project, from the cache, so it opens quickly.
  4. New: Ctrl + N starts a fresh level with a sun and an environment.

The tab bar at the top shows the project and the level's name, with an amber dot after it while it has changes that aren't saved (the window's title shows a • too). Solis asks before anything would lose them: a new or another level, closing the project (File › Close project, or closing the editor's window), or quitting. Save, Don't save or Cancel.

Changed on disk: if the file changes while it's open (a Git pull, or an edit in a text editor), Solis loads the new version as one step you can undo with Ctrl + Z. If you have unsaved changes too, it asks: Keep mine or Load the file.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
New levelCtrl+N
Open levelCtrl+O
Save levelCtrl+S
Save level asCtrl+Shift+S

What the file looks like#

-- A level. Safe to edit by hand: one block per entity, one line per field.
level version 3;

entity 2B8D4NE6TV0HC {
    name = "Sun";
    order = "a0";
    Light.kind = "Sun";
    Light.strength = 3.0;
    Transform.rotation = [0.25881904, 0.0, 0.0, 0.9659258];
}
  • One block per entity, sorted by its ID (13 letters and digits that never change), never by the tree or by when it was made, so renaming or moving an entity never moves its block.
  • One line per setting: Component.setting = value;. Text is in quotes, lists in [ ], and -- starts a comment.
  • A child names its parent with parent = "…";.
  • A copy of an prefab is one block naming its prefab. Each part you changed in that copy has a short block of its own, named after the copy and the part (copy/part), holding only what you changed. If you moved the part, its parent line names what it's under now, or is parent = ""; when you moved it out to the top level.
  • Models are named by their asset ID, with the file's path in a comment for people to read; the comment is rewritten on every save and never read.
  • Components Solis doesn't know (from game code that isn't there) are kept exactly as written.
  • A brush's shape is three long lists of numbers, written twelve to a line so no line grows too long: Brush.points (x, y and z of each point, in metres), Brush.faces (for each face, how many corners it has, then which points, counting from 0) and Brush.materials (each face's material, 0 for the plain one). Each brush may hold at most 65,536 points and 65,536 faces, and a face at most 256 corners.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: "line 12: …" when opening. Why: the file has a mistake, perhaps from a hand edit or a bad merge. Fix: the message says the line and what's wrong; fix it in a text editor. Solis never opens half a file.
  • Problem: "it was saved by a newer version". Why: someone saved it with a newer Solis, which may write things this one can't read. Fix: update Solis.
  • Problem: the Console says a level "was saved by an older version". Why: the file's first line says which version of the layout it's in, and this Solis writes a newer one (version 3; version 2 can say that a part of a copy was moved out to the top level, and version 3 holds brushes). Nothing is lost: it opens as it always did. Fix: nothing. When you save, the old file is first copied into the project's .solis/backups folder.
  • Problem: Git reports a conflict in a level file. Why: two people added entities in the same spot, or changed lines right next to each other in the same component (both rare). Fix: open the file in a text editor and keep both blocks, or the line you want; Solis's own merge tool, which isn't built yet, will do this for you.
  • Problem: "Not saved: … already exists". Why: the name typed in the Save window had no .sollevel, and a file with that name and .sollevel is already there; the window only asked about replacing the name as typed. Fix: choose Save as again and pick the existing file to replace it, or type another name.
  • Problem: "Stop playing first" when saving. Why: the game is running, and saving now would save its changes, which Stop undoes. Fix: press Stop, then save. A Save window opened before Play finishes after Stop.
  • Renaming or moving the open level in the Library is safe: Solis saves to its new name from then on. If it's deleted, the next save asks where to put it.
  • Saves are written to the disk in full before they replace the old file, so a crash or power cut leaves either the old file or the new one, never half of one.
  • Numbers are written as briefly as possible but always read back exactly, so saving without changes doesn't change the file.

Related#

  • Projects and the Library
  • Undo and redo
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: level, entity, component
← Previous · Chapter 12Undo and redoNext → · Chapter 14Prefabs

Prefabs#

Build something once (a chicken, a lamp post, a whole market stall) and place copies of it everywhere. Change the prefab and every copy follows.

When to use it#

Use a prefab for anything that appears more than once: props, buildings, animals, groups of enemies, even whole districts (prefabs can hold other prefabs). Every thing in a level is an entity; a prefab is an entity, with its parts and settings, saved to be placed many times, and each placed copy is an entity linked to it.

A copy follows its prefab unless the copy changes a setting: then that one setting is the copy's own. One chicken can walk faster than the rest; one lamp can be brighter. A copy keeps only what it changed, so when you change the prefab, every copy follows in everything it didn't change itself.

An imported model works much the same way: placing it makes one entity, and Unpack splits it into its parts when you need them.

How to use it#

Make one

  1. In the Level panel, pick the entities that make up the thing (a click, Ctrl+click or Shift+click).
  2. Right-click one of them and choose Make prefab… (also on Home's ribbon, under Create › More).
  3. In the dialog, give it a Name, and choose where to Save in (it starts in the folder the Library shows; Browse… picks another folder of the project).
  4. Leave Swap these for a linked copy on to turn what you picked into the prefab's first copy. Turn it off to keep the entities as they are.
  5. Click Make prefab. The dialog says how many entities become one.

The prefab is saved as a file, chicken.prefab.lst, and shows in the Library with its picture, a blue prefab mark, and a New badge. The swap is one undo step: Ctrl+Z puts your entities back (the file stays; delete it in the Library if you don't want it).

One picked entity becomes the prefab's top, with everything under it. Several become the parts of a new top entity named as you named the prefab, each keeping its place in the world.

Make an empty one: right-click in the Library and choose New prefab. It opens on its own page, ready to build.

In the Library: pick a prefab to see it in Details: its picture, its folder, how many times it's placed and in how many levels ("Placed 6 times, in 2 levels"), and its parts. Open opens its page; Place puts a copy where the camera looks. Or drag it into the view.

Place copies: drag the prefab from the Library into the view, as often as you like. Each copy shows a link mark in the Level panel, and its parts are listed inside it.

Change one copy: pick a copy (or one of its parts) and change it in Properties as usual. At the top, Prefab: Chicken says which prefab it follows. Values in white come from the prefab; a setting this copy changes has an orange dot beside it, and after its field ↶ with the prefab's value faint beside it: click ↶ to put that setting back, so the copy follows the prefab there again. ↑ makes the copy's value the prefab's, for every copy.

Change every copy: click Open (in Properties, or in Details), or double-click the prefab's picture in the Library. The prefab opens on its own page, in a tab beside the level's: its entities in the Level panel, the view and Properties, as a level has them, with a save and undo of its own. Change it, then save it (Ctrl+S). Every copy in the open level follows at once, and each keeps its own changes. Close the page with the × on its tab; Solis asks first if it has changes that aren't saved.

Move a part of one copy: drag it in the Level panel, under another entity or onto empty space to bring it out to the top level. It keeps its place in the world and is still part of its copy: the move is one of that copy's own changes, saved with the level, and the part still follows the prefab in everything else. If you delete the whole copy, a part you moved out of it stays, as an ordinary entity that no longer follows the prefab (undo puts both back).

Unlink: click Unlink beside Prefab: Chicken in Properties. The copy becomes ordinary entities that no longer follow the prefab, as one undo step. For a model, Unpack (Properties' ⋯) splits it into one entity per part of the file, so each part can be moved, hidden or given components on its own.

Settings#

What you seeWhat it means
A blue mark on a Library tileThe file is a prefab. New marks one made since the project opened.
A link mark in the Level panelThis entity is a placed copy, linked to its prefab.
An orange dot in the Level panelThis copy changes some settings (on a part: this part does).
No markA plain entity, not from a prefab.
Prefab: Chicken · Open · UnlinkProperties of a copy: which prefab it follows, its page, and making it plain. Part of Chicken on one of its parts.
An orange dot and ↶ 0.8 after a settingThis copy's own value; the prefab's is 0.8. ↶ puts it back.
This part is gone from …The prefab no longer has this part, but this copy had changes to it. They're kept in case it comes back; Remove if you don't need them.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Save the prefab's page (while it's in front)Ctrl+S
Rename, duplicate or delete a copy, as any entityF2, Ctrl+D, Delete
Open a prefab's pageDouble-click its picture in the Library
Place a copyDrag it from the Library into the view

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: "prefabs place each other in a loop". Why: prefab A contains B, which contains A. Fix: remove one of the copies from the other.
  • Problem: "placed more than 16 deep". Why: prefabs inside prefabs, 17 levels down. Fix: unlink some of the middle levels.
  • Problem: I undid Make prefab and the file is still in the Library. Why: undo changes the level, not files. Fix: delete the prefab in the Library if you don't want it.
  • Problem: copies in another level didn't change. Why: saving a prefab updates the copies in the open level at once; other levels show the change when they're opened. Nothing to fix: their copies follow the prefab as soon as they're read.
  • A level file stores each copy as one block naming its prefab, plus only the settings that differ, so copies keep files small and Git merges them easily. The prefab's own file is a Lust data file you can read: a part per entity, a line per setting.
  • Assemblies: Solis called prefabs assemblies until this version. Opening an older project renames each .solassembly file a .prefab.lst beside it, keeping its ID, so every copy and every spawn in game code still finds it; the older file is kept in the backups (Backups and upgrades). In game code, Assembly.Ships.Fighter is now Prefab.Ships.Fighter (Game code).
  • A model's parts keep their links through a new export from Blender, as long as the parts keep their names.

Related#

  • Entities and components
  • Saving levels
  • Projects and the Library
  • Game code: making and removing entities
  • Concepts: prefab, copy, assembly
← Previous · Chapter 13Saving levelsNext → · Chapter 15Brushes

Brushes#

Shapes made in the editor itself: a box, a ramp, stairs, drawn out on the ground, reshaped point by point, edge by edge and face by face, extruded, inset, split and merged, saved in the level and solid in the game.

When to use it#

For blocking out a level: the floors, walls, ramps, steps and platforms you walk on while you work out how a place plays. A brush is a shape made of flat faces, kept in the level itself, so there's no model to make in another program first: you can try a layout, play it, change it and play it again in minutes. Once the layout is right, brushes can stay (simple, clean shapes suit many art styles) or be replaced by models made elsewhere.

Use an imported model instead for anything detailed or curved, such as a character, a tree or a statue: a brush is made of flat faces.

How to use it#

A brush is made in two parts: you choose its shape from the brush list, then draw it out in the view: first its footprint on the ground, then its height.

Choosing a shape

  1. Rest the pointer over the 3D view (or the 2D view) and press B. The brush list opens beside the pointer: Box, Ramp, Cylinder, Stairs, Arch, Sphere and Wedge, each with a small picture.
  2. Press B again to move the highlight down the list, as many times as you need: after Wedge it comes back to Box. The status line says which one is highlighted ("Choosing a shape brush: Ramp").
  3. Press Space to take the highlighted shape, or click any row. Esc, or a click anywhere else, closes the list without taking one.

The Shape button on Home, in the Create group (its key, B, is written small beside it), opens the same list. It stays lit while the list is open and while you draw.

Drawing it out

  1. Press the left mouse button on the ground where one corner of the brush should be, and drag to the opposite corner. This is the brush's footprint: its size shows in metres beside two of its edges, and in the steps at the top of the view ("1 Footprint · 4 × 3 m").
  2. Let go. Now move the mouse up (without pressing anything): the brush rises from the footprint, and an arrow shows its height in metres.
  3. Click to keep it. The brush is added to the Level list, named after its shape (Box_01, then Box_02; Ramp_01 for the first ramp) with its shape's picture and name beside it, and picked, so its gizmo and Properties are ready.

Corners and heights land on the grid, in the step set in the ribbon's Grid (Grid · 0.5: half a metre), so brushes line up with each other; drawing out snaps whether or not Grid is ticked. Hold Ctrl while dragging or pulling up to draw freely, off the grid. Esc or a right-click gives the brush up at any point, leaving nothing behind. Ctrl+Z takes a brush you kept away again in one step, like any change (Undo).

A drag that starts on top of a brush draws the new one on top of it, at that height: that's how you stack a platform on a block, or a step on a floor. Anywhere else it starts on the ground grid.

The Ramp and the Stairs climb along the longer side of the footprint, starting low where your drag started. Stairs get a step for every 25 cm of height; a Cylinder and a Sphere have 16 sides, and an Arch's curve 12 pieces.

In the 2D view (and the flat Front and Right views), the footprint is drawn flat in the view itself and there is no height step: letting go makes the brush, one grid step deep. The status line and Hints say so.

What you see while drawing: the steps along the top of the view (the shape, 1 Footprint, 2 Height, the one in hand outlined), the keys for that step along the bottom, the sizes beside the brush, and what's happening in the status line ("Drawing a Box: height 1.75 m · Click to keep · Esc to give up"). The Hints card in Properties (Interface tour) says how it works too.

Once made, a brush moves, turns and resizes with the gizmos like any entity (Selecting and moving), and its Transform's scale stretches it. Press Play: characters stand on it and bump into it, because it is Solid.

A brush is drawn flat: every face is one shade, so its edges look crisp, as a block-out should. Picked, a brush is outlined along its own edges.

Editing its insides

A brush is made of points, edges and faces. Editing its insides lets you move those parts, not just the whole brush: pull one face of a box out to make it longer, lift one corner of a floor into a slope, turn the top of a pillar.

  1. Pick one brush (click it, or click it in the Level list) and press Tab. The ribbon becomes Home tools · Brush, the other entities fade so the brush stands out, its edges are drawn in white, and the top of the view and the status line say "Editing Box_03 · Faces · nothing picked".
  2. Choose what clicks pick: 1 points (corners), 2 edges (where two faces meet) or 3 faces (the flat sides). The same three are the first buttons on the ribbon, and they also join the tool bar at the foot of the view, after a short line beside Select, Move, Rotate, Scale and Transform, with their keys small in a corner; the mode in use is lit. They show there only while you edit a brush. Editing starts in faces mode; points show as dots, and each face as a dot at its middle. Switching keeps what you picked: the points of a picked face, or the edges and faces made wholly of picked points.
  3. Pick parts as you pick entities: a click picks the part under the pointer (it lights up before you click), Ctrl + click adds a part or takes it away, a drag on empty space picks everything inside the box (through the brush, its far side too), and a click on empty space picks nothing. Clicks reach only this brush: the others can't be picked while you edit.
  4. Use the Move, Rotate or Scale tool (W, R, S, or their buttons on the tool bar) as for entities. The gizmo sits in the middle of what's picked; drag it. Snapping follows Grid and Angle on the ribbon, and Ctrl turns it off for one drag. World or Local (the pill at the bottom right, or L) chooses the world's axes or the brush's own.
  5. Press Tab again, or Done, to stop. The ribbon goes back to Home.

Each drag is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). Parts shared by what you picked move together, so the brush never comes apart at a seam: moving a face moves its edges and corners, and the faces beside it stretch to follow.

A change that would break the brush is refused. If a move, turn or stretch would fold a face over itself (turn it inside out), flatten a face to nothing (two corners on one spot), or push the brush through itself, the brush snaps back when you let go and the status line says why ("Put back: it would fold a face over itself"). A face that ends up bent (its corners no longer on one flat plane, after lifting one corner) is fine: it is cut into triangles to draw and to be solid.

Undo while editing steps back through the brush's changes as usual; undoing past the moment you pressed Tab (the brush's own making, say) ends editing. Picking something else in the Level list ends editing too and picks that instead. Delete and Backspace delete the picked parts while you edit (below), never the whole brush.

Shaping: Extrude, Inset, Split and Delete

Moving parts only reshapes what's there. To add to a brush or take from it, use the Shape group on Home tools · Brush. Each of the four is greyed while it can't be used, and resting the pointer on it says why ("Pick faces to extrude first").

  • Extrude (E): pulls the picked faces out into a new part of the brush, joined to it by new side faces (walls). Pick one or more faces (3), press E (or click Extrude), then move the mouse: the new part follows, straight out from the faces, and the distance shows in metres beside it, at the top of the view ("Extruding 1 face · 2.00 m") and in the status line. Click to keep it. Moving the mouse the other way pushes the faces in, making a dent. The distance snaps to the grid's step (Grid · 0.5: half a metre at a time); hold Ctrl to pull freely. Esc or a right-click gives it up, leaving the brush as it was. Faces that touch go out together as one block (pick the top and a side of a box, and they come out as one L-shaped part); faces that don't touch each go out their own way. The faces you extruded stay picked, so E again pulls out another step.
  • Shift + drag on the Move tool's gizmo does the same in one go: hold Shift, then drag an arrow, a square or the middle of the gizmo, and the picked faces are extruded as they move, any way you drag them.
  • Inset: makes a smaller face inside each picked face, with a border of new faces round it, all still flat: a window frame, or the rim of a well before you extrude its middle down. Click Inset, move the mouse away from where it was to widen the border (it snaps to the grid; Ctrl for no snapping), and click to keep it. Esc or a right-click gives it up. Inset has no key. The inner faces stay picked, ready to extrude.
  • Split cuts what's picked, as the mode says. Points: pick two points on the same face, and that face is cut in two along a new edge between them. Edges: each picked edge gets a new point at its middle (and so does every face along it). Faces: each picked face is cut in two across its middle, so its longer sides are halved (a 4 × 2 m face becomes two 2 × 2 m faces). If the pick doesn't allow it, nothing happens and the status line says why ("Pick two points on the same face").
  • Delete (Delete or Backspace while editing): takes the picked parts out and closes the gap. Points and edges: they go, and the faces around them merge into one (delete the edge between two halves of a split face, and it's one face again). Faces: picked faces that touch merge into one face. A point left in the middle of a straight side goes with them.

Each of these is one undo step (Ctrl+Z).

A brush is never left broken. After every extrude, inset, split and delete it is checked: it must stay closed (no holes), facing outwards, with room inside it, with at least four faces, and not passing through itself. Anything that fails is refused before it's kept: the brush stays as it was, and the status line says why ("Put back: it would make the brush pass through itself"). That's why deleting one face on its own is refused (it would leave a hole: pick two faces that touch to merge them), and why pushing a face in further than the brush is deep is refused too.

A brush read from a file that has a hole, or faces facing the wrong way (written by hand, say, or by another tool), is mended as it's read when that's simple and safe: faces facing the wrong way are turned round, and a hole whose edge is one flat loop is filled with one face. Anything else (a hole whose edge bends round a corner, say) is left as it is: the brush is drawn as read, the Problems list names it and says why, and extruding, insetting, splitting and deleting its parts are refused until it's whole. The file's own text changes only when you change the brush.

In the 2D view you edit the same way, moving parts across the view's plane.

Settings#

The Brush card in Properties:

SettingWhat it does
Made asThe shape the brush was made from. Choosing another makes the brush again as that shape, filling the same box it filled (a 4 × 2 × 1 m box becomes a 4 × 2 × 1 m cylinder), in one undo step. If you had edited its insides, those edits are replaced by the fresh shape, and the status line says so: Ctrl+Z brings them back.
SizeThe brush's box, in metres (X across, Y deep, Z up), in its own space. Typing a size stretches the brush about its middle, as one undo step; a stretch that would break the brush is refused. Each side is kept between 1 cm and 10 km.
MaterialNot finished yet: giving faces materials comes with Materials and shaders, once Solis has materials of its own to give them. Every face is drawn in the plain material.
SolidOn: the game's characters and bodies collide with it, as with a floor or a wall. Off: it's only drawn, and things pass through it (a light shaft, a hint of where something goes). A brush never falls: it stays where it's placed. Also on the ribbon while editing.
Points, Edges, FacesHow many the brush has, in three boxes; while its insides are edited, the box of the mode in use is outlined, and the line under them says what's picked ("Picked: 1 face · Faces mode").

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Open the brush list (pointer over the 3D or 2D view)B
Move down the list (it wraps round)B
Take the highlighted shapeSpace, or click its row
Close the listEsc, or click elsewhere
Draw the footprintDrag on the ground
Draw freely, off the gridHold Ctrl while dragging or pulling up
Keep the brushMove the mouse up, then click
Give it upEsc, or right-click
Start or stop editing the picked brush's insidesTab
Pick points, edges or faces (while editing)1, 2, 3
Pick a part; add or take one away; pick with a boxClick; Ctrl + click; drag on empty space
Pick every part of the mode; pick nothing (while editing)Ctrl+A; Esc
Extrude the picked faces (while editing)E, move the mouse, click to keep
Extrude as you moveHold Shift and drag the Move tool's gizmo
Extrude or inset freely, off the gridHold Ctrl while moving the mouse
Give an extrude or inset upEsc, or right-click
Delete the picked parts, closing the gap (while editing)Delete, or Backspace

With a tile map picked, B is the tile map's Brush instead (Painting tiles); the Shape button still opens the list.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Tab does nothing. Why: editing needs exactly one brush picked, and the game stopped. Fix: click one brush (not a lamp or a model), or stop the game.
  • Problem: a drag snapped back when let go. Why: it would have broken the brush; the status line said how. Fix: move less far, or move the faces beside it too (pick them with Ctrl + click), so nothing folds over.
  • Problem: clicking another entity while editing doesn't pick it. Why: while editing, clicks reach only the brush being edited. Fix: press Tab to stop, or pick the other entity in the Level list.
  • Problem: Delete doesn't delete the brush. Why: while editing, Delete deletes the picked parts of the brush, never the brush. Fix: press Tab to stop editing, then Delete.
  • Problem: deleting a face says it would leave a hole. Why: a face on its own can't go without leaving the brush open. Fix: pick it and a face beside it (Ctrl + click) to merge the two into one, or delete an edge or a point instead.
  • Problem: an extrude or inset was put back when clicked. Why: it would have broken the brush (pushed through its far side, or an inset wider than the face); the status line said how. Fix: pull less far, or make the inset narrower.
  • Problem: E says only an edge on an open side can be extruded. Why: edges extrude only where a brush is open, and brushes are closed. Fix: press 3 and pick faces to extrude instead.
  • Problem: Extrude, Inset, Split or Delete is greyed. Why: the mode or the pick doesn't allow it (Inset needs faces, Split in points mode needs two points on one face). Fix: rest the pointer on the button: it says what to pick.
  • Problem: pressing B paints tiles instead of opening the list. Why: a tile map is picked, and B is its Brush. Fix: pick something else (or nothing, Esc), or use the Shape button.
  • Problem: "Nothing made: the footprint had no size". Why: you clicked without dragging. Fix: press and drag to the opposite corner before letting go.
  • Problem: "Nothing made: the brush had no height". Why: you clicked before moving the mouse up. Fix: after letting go of the footprint, move the mouse up until the height shows, then click.
  • Problem: a brush stands in mid-air. Why: the drag started on top of another brush, so it was drawn at that height. Fix: move it down with the gizmo, or undo and start the drag on the ground.
  • Problem: a character falls through a brush. Why: its Solid is off. Fix: tick Solid.
  • Problem: a brush gives a body or a collider of its own as well. Why: a Collider component on the same entity is used instead of the brush's shape. Fix: take the Collider off to collide with the brush's own faces.
  • Problem: a brush from a damaged file shows nothing, and the Problems list names it. Why: its points or faces couldn't be read (the problem says which: a face naming a point that isn't there, say, or more than a brush may hold, 65,536 points or faces). Fix: the file's text is kept as it was, so it can be put right by hand; or choose its Made as again, which makes it again as that shape at its standard size; or delete it and draw it again.

Related#

  • Entities and components: a brush is an entity with a Brush component.
  • Physics: colliders and bodies, which a Solid brush works with.
  • Saving levels: how a brush is written in the level's file.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: every key in one place.
  • Selecting and moving things: the gizmos, snapping and world or local axes, which editing a brush's insides uses too.
  • Concepts: brush, footprint, mesh, point, edge, face, extrude, inset.
← Previous · Chapter 14PrefabsNext → · Chapter 16Play mode

Play mode#

Run the level as a game inside the editor, try things, and press Stop: keep what you changed, or get everything back exactly as it was.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to see the level the way a player will: through the game's camera, with no grid, gizmos or markers. The game's own code runs too: every component written in Lust runs its update 60 times a second. You can move things, delete things and experiment freely while playing: when you press Stop, Solis lists what you changed and asks whether to Keep it or Undo all, so nothing is lost by accident and nothing sticks that you didn't mean.

How to use it#

Add a camera first (once per level)

  1. Move the viewport to look the way the game should look.
  2. On the Home tab, click Camera in the ribbon's Create group. A camera appears exactly where you're looking from, facing the same way, and is selected. In the viewport it's drawn as a small wire pyramid pointing the way it looks; click it to select it.
  3. Move and turn it like anything else (W, R). Its Field of view in Properties sets how wide it sees.

The game looks through the first camera in the Level panel's list. With no camera, the Game panel shows the editor's own view and says so.

Play, pause and stop (the Play group, at the right end of the ribbon on every tab)

  1. Press Play (▶), the one light button in the editor. A Game tab appears beside the level's tab on Home and comes to the front, showing the game (on the Debug tab the Game is a tab beside the Profiler, which stays in front: click the Game's tab to watch it there). Play itself becomes Stop (■), still the one light button, and Pause and Step appear beside it. Nothing else changes colour: the editor is the same editor while the game runs, and the button that would start the game is the button that ends it. (Earlier builds tinted the whole window blue while playing and amber while paused; the design the editor now follows doesn't.)

  2. Work as usual: the Level panel, Properties, the viewport and its gizmos all still work. Changes show in the game straight away. For game code's components, Properties shows their values as they are right now (a counter counting, a camera's yaw turning), and a value you set there reaches the game: the running component takes exactly what you set, whatever the game had made of it. That holds when you set the value it started with, too: a turret that has fired down to 7 has 12 again when you type 12, or click the ↺ 12 beside the field. Its other values stay as the game has them. When you press Stop, every value the game changed goes back as it was before Play; a value you set yourself is one of your changes, which Stop asks about (step 6). Click the level's tab beside Game to move things with the gizmos in the viewport; click Game to go back. On Stop the Game tab goes from Home, and the level's tab is in front again.

  3. Press Pause (❚❚) to stop the game's clock; the button stays lit while the game is paused (game code can pause itself too, for a pause menu: the corner then says Game speed 0, and the game still runs its code, see Game screens); press Pause again to carry on. The Game panel's corner shows Playing or Paused and how long the game has run.

  4. While paused, press Step (▶❙, beside Pause; faint until the game is paused) to run exactly one tick: game code runs once, everything moves on by a sixtieth of a second, and the game stays paused. It's the way to watch something that happens too fast to see, one step at a time.

  5. Press Stop (■). The game is thrown away and the level comes back exactly as it was when you pressed Play: every entity and setting, the undo history (Ctrl + Z carries on from where you were) and the selection.

  6. If you changed the level while playing, a question lists what you did (Add Point light 1, Move Crate…):

    • Keep makes your changes again on the level as it was before Play, and each can still be undone with Ctrl + Z.
    • Undo all leaves the level as it was before Play.

    Why ask? Other engines quietly throw away everything changed while playing, and people lose work that way. Solis asks instead. The question waits for an answer; until then, Play and the editor's keys wait too. So does anything that would leave the level: quitting, closing the window, a new or another level, and another project go ahead only once you've answered, so your changes can't slip away unasked. If you close the project (File › Close project, or the editor's window) while the game plays, the question is asked before the launcher comes back.

Only your own edits are kept, never what the game did. After Keep, the level is exactly the level as it was when you pressed Play, plus the changes in the list. Entities the game spawned are gone, entities it removed are back, and every value and place it changed is as it was. That holds after loading a save game while playing too: your edits are made on your level, not on the save's. Solis can tell the two apart because each edit of yours is an undo step and nothing the game does is one. What that means when the two meet:

  • A value you set that the game also changes (a counter, where a cart stands) is kept as you set it, not as the game left it.
  • A value you set back to what it was before Play (the turret's 12 again) is in the list too, since you did set it. Keep and Undo all then end the same way for it: the level holds that value either way.
  • A change to something the game made (renaming a bullet it spawned) can't be kept, because that entity goes with the game. It's left out of the list, and the Console says which changes those were. When one change touched your entities and the game's together (a crate and a bullet deleted in one go), your entities' share of it is kept.
  • A change to an entity the game removed afterwards is kept: Stop brings the entity back, and Keep makes your change to it.
  • An entity you deleted stays deleted, whatever the game would have done with it.
  • Undoing, while playing, a change made before Play is a change too: the list says Undid a change made before Play, and Keep leaves it undone (Ctrl + Y makes it again).
  • A change you made while playing and undid again with Ctrl + Z is simply gone: after Stop, Ctrl + Y can't bring it back.

An edit while the game runs changes only what you edit. The field you set takes your value at once, even if the game had changed it. Everything else on that entity stays as the game has it: the screen it shows, a sound game code switched off, the clip its sprite plays and which way it's flipped, its animator, its tile map, where it stands and how it moves. So you can tune a lamp on the entity that shows the health bar without the health bar vanishing, and adding or deleting another entity doesn't put anything back either.

You can also type play, pause, step and stop in the Console.

Playing with the keys, mouse and gamepad: click the Game panel to give the game the mouse and keys (the pointer disappears, and the editor's own keys are off); press Esc to give them back. A gamepad works whenever the game plays. The Debug tab's Session group also records a play's input and plays it back exactly (Play and record inputs and Replay a recording…, see Input), and its Load save plays from a save game.

Smooth on any screen: the game itself always runs 60 ticks a second, so it plays the same on every computer. A screen can show more frames than that (120 or 144 a second): between two ticks, the Game panel draws everything part way from where it was at the last tick to where it is now, so movement looks smooth instead of stepping. What you see is up to a sixtieth of a second behind the game, which no one can notice. While paused, it shows exactly where things are.

What waits until you stop: saving, opening another level or project, new levels, and making or changing prefabs. If you try, the Console says Stop playing first: saving now would save the game's changes, which Stop is about to undo. Quitting or closing Solis while playing stops the game first. If you changed the level while it played, Keep or Undo all is asked before anything closes; then Solis asks about unsaved changes as usual (after Keep, the changes you kept are unsaved, so it asks about them).

Changes from outside while playing: if a prefab's file changes (a Git pull, or Notepad), the game shows it at once, and its copies are updated again after Stop. That isn't one of your changes, so Stop doesn't ask about it, and the level you Keep has the updated copies too. If the level's own file changes on disk, Solis waits until Stop, and until you've answered Keep or Undo all, to offer it.

Renaming, moving or deleting the level's file while playing (in the Library) holds after Stop: the level keeps its new name and place, whether you Keep your changes or not, and Ctrl + S saves it there. If you deleted the file, the level counts as unsaved after Stop, and saving asks where to put it. That's the one thing Stop doesn't put back, because the file really did move.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Camera > ViewPerspective, as the eye sees, or 2D: flat, straight down, drawn pixel-perfect at the project's base resolution (2D).
Camera > Field of viewHow wide the camera sees, top to bottom, in degrees. 50° looks like a normal photo; 90° sees much more but stretches the edges. A 2D camera doesn't use it.
Camera > NearThe nearest it sees. Raise it if far surfaces flicker.
Camera > FarThe farthest it sees; anything beyond isn't drawn.

Shortcuts#

Play, Pause, Step and Stop are buttons only, so a stray key never starts or stops the game. They are in the search too (press Space and type the name), and in the Console: play, pause, step, stop.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I changed something while playing and it went back when I pressed Stop. Why: you chose Undo all when Stop asked. Fix: Undo all can't be taken back; next time choose Keep. A value the game changed (not you) always goes back: copy the component's values with ⋯ > Copy values before Stop, and paste them after.
  • Problem: I chose Keep, but one change I made while playing isn't there. Why: it was a change to something the game made (an entity it spawned, or one a loaded save held), and those go with the game; the Console named it when you pressed Stop. Fix: make the change where the entity comes from: the prefab game code spawns, or an entity of the level itself.
  • Problem: the Game panel shows the editor's view. Why: the level has no camera. Fix: on the Home tab, Create › Camera.
  • Problem: new entities appear in the Level panel while playing. Why: game code made them (World:spawn, see Game code). Fix: nothing: they go when you press Stop.
  • Problem: pressing keys while playing changes the level (W picks the move tool). Why: the editor has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel to give them to the game; Esc gives them back.
  • Problem: I can't tell whether the game is running. Why: the window no longer changes colour while it plays. Fix: look at the ribbon's right end: Stop is there instead of Play while the game runs, and Pause is lit while it is paused. The status line says Playing or Paused too, and the Game tab is in front.
  • Problem: Step is greyed out. Why: it runs one tick of a paused game. Fix: press Pause first.
  • Problem: the game shows the wrong camera. Why: it uses the first one in the Level panel's list. Fix: delete the cameras you don't need, or take their Camera component off (Remove Camera, in the ⋯ on its card in Properties).
  • Problem: the picture in the Game panel looks different from the viewport. Why: the game always uses the standard look; the viewport's look is only for editing. Hidden entities (the eye in the Level panel) show in the game, because hiding is only for the editor.

Related#

  • Interface tour
  • The Console
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: play mode, game, camera

The launcher#

The small window Solis starts in: every project you've worked on as a card, New project, and beside them Learn and Updates. Opening a project turns it into the editor; File › Close project brings it back.

When to use it#

Solis always starts on the launcher, a window of its own (about 1100 × 700). You pick the project to work on, and the window becomes the editor, at the editor's own size and place. Solis never reopens the last project by itself, so you always choose; the projects you opened most recently come first, so it's one double-click.

Why a window of its own? The launcher only has to show and organise projects, so it stays small and calm; the editor gets the whole screen for your game. Each remembers its own size and place on your computer: move the launcher to one corner and it opens there next time, and the editor still opens where you left it.

When you've finished with a project, File › Close project (or closing the editor's window) asks about unsaved work, closes the project and comes back to the launcher. Closing the launcher's window quits Solis.

Use it to:

  • open a project you've worked on before, without hunting for its folder;
  • see at a glance which projects are 2D, 3D or both, and show only one kind;
  • make a new project: Solis makes its folder from the name you type (New project);
  • tidy the list: a project you've finished with, or one whose folder has gone, can be removed from it (its files stay), and one you moved can be found again;
  • rename a project, make a copy of it to try something risky, or open its folder in Explorer;
  • learn with the examples (Learn), and update Solis (Updates).

How to use it#

  1. Each project is a card: a picture of its kind (a field of tiles for 2D, a block for 3D, both for both), its kind in the picture's corner (2D, 3D or 2D + 3D), its name, its folder, and when you last opened it. A project can't keep a picture of its own yet: its kind's picture stands in. Pinned projects come first.
  2. Double-click a card to open it, or click Open on it (shown on the card under the pointer or picked). Clicking a card once picks it; Enter then opens it, and the arrow keys walk from card to card.
  3. ⋯ at the right of a card's name (or a right-click on the card) opens its menu:
    • Open.
    • Show in Explorer: opens the project's folder.
    • Remove from list: only forgets the project here. Its folder and files stay exactly where they are, and Open folder… brings it back.
    • Pin to the top (or Unpin): keeps it first, whatever the order.
    • Rename…: changes the project's name (in the title bar and on its card). Its folder keeps its name, so nothing that points at the folder breaks. Type the new name and press Enter; Esc leaves it as it was.
    • Make a copy…: choose an empty folder, and the whole project is copied there, named "… copy". The import cache is left out (the copy makes its own), and so are links to elsewhere on the computer. A note under the heading says when it's done, and the copy joins the list.
  4. Search projects narrows the cards as you type, by name or folder. Every word you type must appear somewhere, in any order.
  5. The filter beside it shows All projects, or only 2D, 3D or 2D + 3D ones.
  6. Sort by orders the cards by when each was last opened, or by name.
  7. Open folder… opens a project that isn't in the list yet: choose its folder. Choose a folder that isn't a project (such as Documents) and Solis looks through it, and the folders inside it (four levels down), for projects, and adds every one it finds without opening them.
  8. New project opens New project.
  9. Preferences, at the foot of the column, are the editor's own settings, the same as File › Preferences in the editor (Settings). User guide opens this guide in your browser.

New project#

Type a name, and Solis makes the project's folder for you.

  1. Name: what the project is called. The line under it shows the folder it makes, Create in followed by the name (C:\Users\Sam\Documents\Solis projects\Farm Days\). If that folder already exists and isn't empty, or the name can't be a folder's name on Windows, the line says why instead, and Create waits.
  2. Create in: the folder new projects go in. The first time it's a Solis projects folder in your Documents; Browse… chooses another. The folder you make a project in is remembered for the next one.
  3. Kind: 2D (sprites and tile maps), 3D (models, lights and cameras) or Both (2D and 3D). It's kept in the project and can be changed later in Project settings › General › Kind (Settings). The kind decides what the editor shows: a 2D project hides the parts only 3D games use (the Shading tab, lighting, models), a 3D project those only 2D games use (tile maps and their painter), and Both shows everything (What each kind hides). Pick Both if you're unsure: nothing is lost either way, and the kind can be changed whenever you like.
  4. Start from: Empty (only what a project needs to open), or one of Solis's examples (Playground, Turret sample, UI sample, Benchmark), made as your project, under your name. Each example is marked with the kind it was made for: they are all 3D, so they're greyed while 2D is chosen.
  5. Create makes the folder, writes the project and opens it in the editor. Cancel (or Esc) closes the dialog and makes nothing.

A new project gets only what it needs to open: its project.solis, Solis's .solis folder, and Git's .gitignore and .gitattributes. Your files go in the project's folder, in folders you make yourself; Solis makes no folder for them.

A name is refused, with the reason, when it's empty, longer than 100 letters, holds a character Windows doesn't allow in a folder's name (< > : " / \ | ? *) or a line break, starts with a dot (a hidden folder) or ends with one, or is a name Windows keeps for itself (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 to COM9, LPT1 to LPT9). A folder too deep for Windows (its whole path near 260 characters) is refused too.

Learn and Updates#

The column has two more pages:

  • Learn: the four examples, each with a sentence about it and Make it in a folder… (choose an empty folder; it opens in the editor); Your first hour, five steps for someone new; and Open the user guide. The sample level, which goes into an open project, is in the editor's search: press Space and type sample level.
  • Updates: when a newer build of Solis is out, Updates has a 1 new mark in the column, and a card across the top of the page says what it is, with Not now and Download (it downloads while you work), then Restart to update (Solis closes, installs it and opens again). In a copy you didn't install with the setup file, the step is Open the releases page instead. Under the card: the build you have, the newest build with Check now, the Look for updates when Solis starts switch, the releases page and the list of every change. Beside them, what the new build brings. See Installing and updating.

Opening a project from the command line#

A project's folder named after the program opens it in the editor straight away, without the launcher: solis "C:\Games\Farm Days". The four examples can be made the same way, for a script: solis --sample playground "C:\Games\Try" makes the playground in that empty folder and opens it (the others are game, ui and benchmark).

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
FilterAll, or only 2D, 3D or 2D + 3D projects.
Sort byLast opened (the most recent first; projects whose time isn't known come last) or Name (A to Z). Pinned projects always come first.
Create in (New project)Where new projects' folders are made. Remembered: the folder of the last project you made.
Look for updates when Solis starts (Updates)Asks GitHub for a newer build at each start, in the background. Off, nothing is asked until you press Check now. The same switch is on Preferences › General.

The build each project was last opened with#

When a project opens, Solis writes its build number into the project's project.solis file. Rest the pointer on a card to see which build last opened it: the one you're using, an older one (it opens as usual, and its files are upgraded when saved, with a backup first: Backups and upgrades), or a newer one (update Solis first: parts made with the newer build may not open in yours).

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Open the project pickedEnter, or double-click its card
Walk the cards← → ↑ ↓
A card's menuRight-click it, or its ⋯
In New project or Rename…: make it, or close itEnter, Esc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a card says Folder not found. Why: the folder was moved, renamed or deleted, or it's on a drive that isn't plugged in. Fix: plug the drive in and come back to Projects (it looks each time). If you moved the folder, click Locate… on the card and choose where it is now. Otherwise click Remove.
  • Problem: a card says project.solis is gone from its folder. Why: the folder is there, but the file that makes it a project isn't. Fix: if the project is in Git, get the file back from there; otherwise Remove it.
  • Problem: New project says the folder already exists and isn't empty. Why: Solis never makes a project over other files. Fix: choose another name, or another Create in.
  • Problem: project.solis shows as changed in Git after opening a project. Why: Solis noted its build number in it (saved_by), and a kind changed in Project settings is kept there too (kind). Fix: commit it with your other changes.
  • Problem: a project made with an earlier Solis shows 2D + 3D. Why: projects from before the kind was asked are both, so nothing they use is ever hidden. Fix: choose its kind in Project settings › General › Kind.
  • Problem: Open folder… on a big folder says it stopped early. Why: it looks through at most 20,000 folders, so choosing a whole drive can't keep it busy for long. Fix: choose the folder your projects are in, such as Documents.

Related#

  • Projects and the Library: what a project is and what's in it.
  • Settings: Preferences, and Project settings with the kind.
  • Installing and updating: getting a newer build.
  • Backups and upgrades: what happens to a project made with an older build.
  • Concepts: launcher, project, project kind and build.
← Previous · Chapter 16Play modeNext → · Chapter 18Projects and the Library

Projects and the Library#

A project is a folder holding your game's files: models, pictures, levels and code. The Library shows what's in it, with pictures of each model, and is where you place things from.

When to use it#

Make a project as soon as you start something you want to keep. Without one, Solis works as a viewer: models you import are shown but not kept. With one:

  • models you import are copied into the project's folder, so the project has everything it needs, on any computer;
  • each asset gets an ID that never changes, so renaming or moving a file (in Solis, in Explorer, or through Git) breaks nothing;
  • when you save a model again in Blender or Aventail, Solis notices and shows the new version straight away;
  • the Library shows every file, folder by folder, with a thumbnail of each model and picture and the waveform of each sound, ready to drag into the level (or, for a sound, to listen to: see Sounds).

How to use it#

Make a project

  1. On the launcher, click New project, type its name and choose its kind (2D, 3D or Both). Solis makes a folder of that name in Create in (a Solis projects folder in your Documents, the first time).
  2. Solis makes only what the project needs to open: project.solis, a hidden .solis folder for its cache, and .gitignore and .gitattributes files set up for games, for Git. Everything else is yours to arrange: your files go in the project's own folder, in whatever folders you make (levels, pictures, farm…). Solis never makes a folder for them.

Open a project: pick it on the launcher, where Solis always starts, or use its Open folder… and choose the project's folder. Solis doesn't open the last project again when it starts, so you choose what to work on, and the projects you opened most recently are at the top of its list (after any you pinned), one double-click away. File › Close project goes back to the launcher.

Opening another project starts afresh. Everything of the project you leave goes with it: its level, the files open in tabs (Clips, Frames, Animator, Map, Tileset, Atlas Crop, the UI canvas) and their undo steps, components' values you copied, and a seed chosen in the Console. Nothing of one project can then be saved into another by mistake, which matters most with a copy of a project, whose files have the same names. What's yours stays as it is: the layout, the cameras, the theme and the Console's messages.

Add models: Library › Import, or drop a .glb or .gltf file onto the window: it's copied into the project and placed in the level. You can also put files straight into the project's folder (or a folder inside it) from Explorer: they appear in the Library within a moment.

A project made by an older Solis keeps its files in an assets folder. It's left exactly as it was, and the Library shows what's in it, because your game code names files by where they are in it: there, assets is the Library's top, and wherever this guide says the project's folder for your files, read assets. Solis's own folders (the hidden .solis and .git, builds, saves and recordings) and the project's settings files (project.solis, the input actions, the mixer, the 2D settings) never show in the Library, and nothing can be moved or saved into them from it.

The Library is one browser, in two places. On Home (and the UI and Audio tabs) it's the first tab of the bottom panel under the view; on the Library tab it fills the centre, with the file picked shown in Details at the right and the code files on the Code tab of the bottom panel. Both are the same browser, showing the same folder, the same search, kind filter, view and picked files: change one and the other follows, and opening or closing other panels never changes what it does. (The layouts Library on the left and Library on the right put Home's under the Level panel or under Properties instead.)

Find your way around the Library

  • The folder tree on the left starts at the project's own folder, named after the project. Click a folder to open it; click a folder's arrow to fold or unfold what's inside. Show folders on the Library ribbon puts the tree away.
  • Over the files, ‹ goes back to the folder you were in before, ˄ goes up one folder, and the breadcrumb (Farm Days › farm) shows where you are: click a part to go there. At the right, 14 items · 1 selected counts what's shown and what's picked.
  • The folder's folders come first, then its files, as tiles that fill the width: each a square for its picture, then its name, and a coloured dot and word saying what kind of file it is. Pictures, models and sprites show what's in them, a sound its waveform; the other kinds draw their kind in their colour. The colours are the design's: folders yellow, models cyan, prefabs blue, pictures and sprite sheets coral, clips and animators purple, sounds amber, tilesets and tile maps green, levels green, code orange, sound events teal, text light blue. The grid and list buttons at the top switch to a list, one row each with the kind's word.
  • Search (Search Farm Days) finds files and folders by name in the whole project.
  • All kinds ▾ shows one kind of file at a time (Models, Sprites, Maps, Sounds or Code), so a busy folder is easy to scan. Folders still show, so you can go through them.
  • Pick several with Ctrl and a click (another one, or one again to take it out) or Shift and a click (everything between). A click on empty space lets go of them all.
  • Point at a file to see its full path and what you can do with it.

Make new things: right-click empty space in the Library. The menu says where they'll be made (New in "farm"), the folder you're in:

  • New folder, New level, New code file and New sound event…: each is made with a free name (New folder, level, component, New sound event) and starts with its name picked out, ready to type over: type the name and press Enter. New prefab makes an empty prefab there and opens it on its own page, ready to build. New table makes a data table (table), with a Name column and one row, and opens it in the Table tab. More has New tile map, New tileset and New animator (see Tile maps, Tilesets and autotiling and Animators).
  • The first code file is main.lst, at the top of the project, because game code starts there: it keeps its name and opens in the program your computer uses for .lst files (Ledger, once it's installed). Later ones are components, ready to fetch from main.lst; double-click one's picture to open it. See Game code.
  • A new level is an empty level, saved there; double-click its picture to open it (Saving levels).
  • Import… brings in a model; Paste is an unfinished part for now. Show in Explorer opens the folder in your system's file browser.

Rename: double-click a file's or folder's name (or pick it and press F2 with the pointer over the Library, or right-click it and choose Rename). The name turns into a box with it picked out. Enter keeps the new name, Esc puts the old one back, and clicking somewhere else keeps it too. A file keeps its ending (grass.png renamed meadow is meadow.png), so it stays the same kind. A name has to work on every computer: not empty, at most 100 characters, none of < > : " / \ | ? *, not ending in a dot, not a name Windows keeps for a device (CON, NUL, COM1 …), and not one already in that folder. While you type one that won't do, a red note under the box says why; keep it anyway and the old name stays, and the Console says why. Renaming the open level is fine: Solis saves to the new name.

A double-click on a tile's picture opens it (a folder opens, a level opens, a picture opens in its program), and a double-click on its name renames it. In the list, the name is the words; double-click anywhere else on the row to open it.

Move: drag files (or folders) onto a folder tile, a folder in the tree, or a part of the breadcrumb. Picked several? Drag one of them and they all go. The file's ID file goes with it, so everything that uses it (levels, prefabs, tile maps, sound events) still finds it. Moving can't be undone with Ctrl + Z: drag it back instead. Dragging a file into the viewport still places it.

Right-click a file or folder for: Open or Place (a sprite's clips file and a picture offer both; Place is greyed on a file Solis hasn't given its ID yet, such as one copied in a moment ago), what its kind can do (Atlas Crop… for a picture, Play for a sound), Rename, Duplicate (a copy beside it, hay copy.png, with an ID of its own, ready to rename; a folder can't be duplicated yet), Delete, and Show in Explorer. Right-click one of several picked for what applies to all of them: Duplicate, Delete, and Show in Explorer when they're in one folder.

Delete (or the Delete key, with the pointer over the Library) moves the files (or folders) to the Recycle Bin, with their ID files, so you can get them back. Anything in the level still using one keeps showing it until Solis restarts.

Folder trees on Home's left side: the title of Home's left slot reads Level · Folders. Click Folders and the slot shows the project as a tree of folders and files instead of the Level panel; click Level to go back. Click a folder to unfold it, double-click it to make it the tree's folder (˄ goes back up), click a file to pick it, double-click a file to open it, and drag files onto a folder to move them there. To move files between two far-apart folders, choose Open another tree from a tree's ⋯ menu (or the slot's): a second tree opens beside the first, in the same slot, each showing its own folder, and you drag from one to the other. Up to four trees fit side by side; drag the line between two to share the room differently, and Close this tree in its ⋯ menu closes one. The trees keep their folders while Solis runs.

Place a model or prefab

  • Drag it from the Library into the viewport: it goes on whatever surface is under the mouse when you let go (a table, the floor), or on the ground. In a flat Front or Right view, dropped on empty space, it goes exactly where you point, at that height. It's selected, ready to move.
  • Drag it onto an entity in the Level panel: it goes under that entity, at its place.
  • Or pick it and press Place on the Library ribbon to put it where the camera looks. A double-click on its picture only picks a file that would be placed (so a stray double-click never drops something in the level), on either tab; while placing (below), a double-click places it.
  • A prefab shows a blue prefab mark on its tile (and New just after it's made). Pick it to see it in Details: its parts, its folder and how many times it's placed, in how many levels, with Open and Place. A double-click on its picture opens it on its own page (Prefabs).

Placing, with the Library's Place switch Click Place at the right of Home's Library bar (or in its header, where a layout puts the Library beside the view; or press Space and choose Start placing) and you're placing: the ribbon shows its building form (Place, Snapping, Paint and Transform, which holds the five tools while the tool bar is put away), Placement (how placed things land) shows beside the files (over them, where the Library is a tall list), and the Library shows only the files that can be placed (Favourites and Recent are unfinished; All, Models, Sprites, Maps, and Find something to place, which looks in every folder). While you drag a file over the viewport, a square in the accent shows where it will land, a label says what it is and where ("crate", "x 2.75 y -13.25 · grid"), and a strip at the bottom says how. With the ribbon's Grid on and Align to: Grid, it lands on the grid's step; Free never snaps, and holding Ctrl as you drop doesn't snap that once. Clicking Place again, or another tab of the bottom panel (the Console, say), leaves placing.

Open things: double-click a level's picture to open it (Solis asks first if yours has unsaved changes). Double-click a picture to open it in its own program (your picture editor, say); to put it in the world as a sprite, drag it into the viewport instead. Any other file, one Solis doesn't know, opens its folder instead of the file itself, and its name is shown in full with its ending: a file called brick.png.exe is a program pretending to be a picture, and opening it would run it. Projects you download or are sent can hold anything, so Solis never runs what's in them.

Text files (.md and .txt notes, and data in .json, .csv, .toml and .ron) show in the Library in one light blue. Click one and Properties shows it, read only: a Markdown file's headings, lists, quotes, code and bold as they read, the others as plain text (up to 512 KB and the first 3,000 lines). Open in its program (or a double-click) opens it in the program your computer uses for that kind of file, such as Ledger for Markdown, to edit it there; Properties shows the change as soon as you save. They're under the Code chip too.

Import on the Library ribbon brings in a model. It's greyed until a project is open, since the model is copied into it.

A .gltf model reads the files beside it, so it can't be moved to another folder on its own: move its whole folder instead. Renaming it in place is fine.

The Code tab beside the Library lists the project's code files (Lust .lst, Lua and Rust), with a search box. Double-click a Lust file to open it in the program Windows has for .lst files: make that a text or code editor (right-click a .lst file in Explorer > Open with > Choose another app), never a program that runs Lust, since a downloaded project's code should only run inside Solis's sandbox. A Lua file shows its folder instead (some computers have a program that runs .lua files rather than editing them), so open it from there in your editor. Solis checks your Lust whenever you save; see Game code. The solis folder holds files Solis writes, describing the engine to your code; it's Solis's to change, so the Library doesn't show it (it's there in Explorer).

Change a model: export it again over the same file in Blender. Everything using it shows the new version a moment later. If the new file is broken, the old version stays, and the Console says why.

Settings#

File or folderWhat it is
project.solisMarks the folder as a project and holds its name.
Your folders and filesEverything you made or brought in, beside project.solis, in folders of your own. Watched for changes. (A project from an older Solis keeps them in assets/.)
solis/Files Solis writes describing the engine to your game code. Not shown in the Library.
<file>.solmetaA small text file beside each asset holding its ID. Commit it with the asset, and move or rename them together (Solis copes if you forget, as long as the content didn't change).
.solis/Solis's own folder. cache/ holds models it has already read, so they open quickly; it keeps within 4 GB, deleting the models used least lately, and is safe to delete (it's rebuilt). backups/ holds copies of files saved by an older Solis, kept before they were upgraded (Backups and upgrades). Never committed.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the Console says a sidecar couldn't be read. Why: the .solmeta file was damaged, perhaps by a bad Git merge. Fix: fix it in a text editor, or delete it to give the model a new ID (anything using the old ID will then say the model is missing).
  • Problem: the Console says a model "is a copy, so it got a new ID". Why: a file was copied together with its .solmeta; two files can't share an ID. The original (whose .solmeta is older) keeps its ID, so nothing using it changes. Nothing is wrong.
  • Problem: a model I saved into the project from Blender takes a couple of seconds to show in the Library. Why: Solis waits two seconds before giving a new file its ID, because Git writes a file and its .solmeta one after the other: a look in between would give the file a new ID and lose the one it has on other computers. Fix: nothing; models brought in with Import model show at once.
  • Problem: I renamed a model in Explorer and changed it before Solis was open, and it lost its ID. Why: Solis finds a renamed file by its content; with the content changed too, it can't tell. Fix: rename and change in separate steps, or rename the .solmeta along with it.
  • Problem: models placed before opening a project disappeared. Why: opening a project starts a new level. Fix: Solis asks to save first; save the level inside the project to keep it.
  • Imported models open much faster the second time: the cache remembers them, even after a rename.
  • Problem: a file shows an icon instead of a thumbnail. Why: thumbnails are made for models and pictures only, a few at a time on other threads, and a damaged file gets none; levels draw their kind for now. Fix: wait a moment; for a damaged file, the Console says what's wrong when you place it.
  • Problem: a new file's name box opened when I came back to the Library. Why: something just made starts with its name picked out, wherever the Library is. Fix: type a name and press Enter, or press Esc to keep the one it has.
  • Problem: Solis says there's already a file with that name. Why: renaming and moving never replace another file. Fix: choose another name, or delete the other file first.

Related#

  • Importing models
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: project, asset, sidecar, cache

Backups and upgrades#

Files saved by an older Solis keep opening, and a copy of each is kept before Solis changes it.

When to use it#

You don't need to do anything: it works by itself. This page explains what happens when you open a project after updating Solis, so the messages in the Console make sense.

Each kind of file Solis saves (levels, prefabs, sound events, the Mixer's buses, input actions, recordings, save games, the project file and sidecars) has a format version: a number at its top saying how it's laid out. When an update changes how a kind of file is laid out, its number goes up, and the update brings an upgrader that turns the old layout into the new one.

How it works#

  1. Opening an older file: Solis upgrades it as it reads it, in memory. The file itself isn't changed. For a level, a prefab you open, the input actions and the Mixer, the Console says so: "input.solinput was saved by an older version (format 1), so it's been upgraded to format 2 as it was read…".

  2. Saving it: before the file is written in the new layout, Solis:

    1. checks that the new file reads back exactly as what's being saved;
    2. copies the old file to the project's .solis/backups/ folder, into a folder named by the date and time (such as .solis/backups/2026-10-28 09-15-02/input.solinput), keeping its place in the project;
    3. writes the new file, and checks it on disk.

    This happens for levels, prefabs, sound events, the input actions and the Mixer, the files you change in the editor, and for save games: a save made by an older Solis is copied before a new save replaces it in its slot (the saves folder isn't in Git, so the copy is the only one). If any step fails, the old file stays exactly as it was and the Console says why. When it works, the Console says where the copy went.

  3. Files moving to Lust (what Solis makes is Lust): the files Solis makes are becoming ordinary Lust files you can read and check in Ledger, each named for what it holds, such as farm.tilemap.lst and ground.tileset.lst. When you open a project, each older one (farm.soltilemap, ground.soltileset) is moved at once: Solis writes the Lust file beside it, checks it reads back the same, moves the small .solmeta file with it (so everything that uses it still finds it), and puts the older file in .solis/backups/. The Console says how many moved. One that can't move (it's damaged, or a file already has the new name) stays as it is and still works, and the Console says why. Why: Lust is the language you write your game in, so every file of your project reads the same way, and Ledger can open them all.

  4. Areas renamed levels: levels were called areas until late 2026, and saved as .solarea files. When you open a project from then, each of its areas is renamed at once: farm.solarea becomes farm.sollevel, beside it, with its first line saying level instead of area and every other line kept as it was (your own comments too). Solis checks the level reads exactly as the area did, moves its .solmeta file with it if it has one, and puts the area in .solis/backups/. The Console says how many were renamed. Everything that named an area finds the level: a recording, the level your game starts in when you export it, a save game. The project file is copied to the backups too and then says it's a project with levels, so a Solis from before the rename won't open it: it says the project was made by a newer version, rather than opening it with no levels. An area that can't be renamed (it's damaged, or a level already has its name) stays as it is, still opens as a level, and the Console says why. Why: "level" is the word game makers use for a place in a game you build and play, and every name in Solis (the Level panel, New level, the file ending) says the same thing.

  5. Assemblies renamed prefabs: prefabs were called assemblies until late 2026, and saved as .solassembly files. When you open a project from then, each is renamed at once: chicken.solassembly becomes chicken.prefab.lst, beside it, a Lust data file you can read (a part per entity, a line per setting). Solis checks it reads as exactly the same prefab, moves its .solmeta file with it (so its ID stays, and every copy placed in a level still finds it), and puts the older file in .solis/backups/. Game code names it as before, by its folders and name (Prefab.Animals.Chicken); only the word changed, from Assembly to Prefab. The Console says how many were renamed. The project file then says it's a project with prefabs, so a Solis from before won't open it. An assembly that can't be renamed stays as it is, still opens as a prefab, and the Console says why.

  6. After that the file is in the new layout, so later saves don't make more copies. Your project's Git history is the undo for ordinary changes.

A file saved by a newer Solis than yours isn't opened at all: the Console says to update. Solis never changes a file it doesn't fully understand: input actions or a Mixer from a newer Solis aren't saved over (the Console says to update), and a save game from a newer Solis is copied to the backups before a new save replaces it in its slot.

Settings#

There are none. Old backups are tidied away by themselves:

RuleWhat it means
Older than 90 daysRemoved the next time a backup is made.
More than 1 GB in allThe oldest are removed until they fit, but never one less than a week old (a save game's backup may be its only copy).
The newest, and the one just madeAlways kept, however old or big.

Tips and common problems#

  • A file you save from inside .solis/backups/ (to look at an old one) is saved as it is, with no backup of its own: Solis never tidies away a backup you're working in.
  • Problem: you want the old file back. Why: an upgrade changed something you didn't expect. Fix: copy the file from .solis/backups/<date and time>/ back over the new one, or use Git to go back. To open it in its old layout, use the Solis build that saved it (the last ten are kept on the Releases page; see Installing and updating).
  • Problem: the backups are gone. Why: .solis/ is also Solis's cache; deleting the whole folder deletes the backups with it. Fix: nothing is lost while the project is in Git: its history has every committed version. Deleting .solis/cache alone keeps them.
  • Problem: the Console says "this … file was saved by a newer version". Why: someone saved it with a newer Solis. Fix: update Solis (the launcher's Updates › Check now).
  • The backups folder isn't committed to Git (new projects' .gitignore leaves out .solis/), so each computer keeps its own.

Related#

  • Saving levels: how levels are saved, and why they merge in Git.
  • Installing and updating: how updates arrive.
  • Concepts: format version, cache, sidecar.
← Previous · Chapter 18Projects and the LibraryNext → · Chapter 20Checking a project before updating

Checking a project before updating#

Opens a project without the editor, reads every file, checks the game's code and plays back recordings, and says whether anything changed.

When to use it#

Before you update Solis on a project that matters (your own game), or in a workflow that tries each new build on it before you do. It answers one question: does this build still open my project and play my game the same? If the answer is no, don't update yet: the report says what changed.

The samples Solis makes (the turret sample, the benchmark and the playground) are checked this way by Solis's own tests on every change, so a build that breaks them never ships.

How to use it#
