local Turret = component("Turret", {
    { "cooldown", "int", 0 },
})

function Turret:update(dt)
    self.cooldown = self.cooldown - 1
    if self.cooldown <= 0 then
        local from = solis.entity.position(self.me)
        solis.World:fire(from, vec3(0, 1, 0), 60, 2, vec3(4, 0.3, 0.2))
        self.cooldown = 30
    end
end

fire takes where it starts, which way it flies (any length), its speed in metres a second, how long it lives in seconds, and its colour as red, green and blue. Above 1 glows brighter: [4, 0.3, 0.2] is a hot red laser.

  • It flies in a straight line and disappears when its time is up. It doesn't hit anything: lasers are kept out of physics so a million can fly. To see what a shot would hit, look along its line with castRay.
  • It's drawn in the Game panel as a glowing streak, as long as it flies in two frames. Streaks add their light where they cross.
  • Up to 1,000,000 can fly at once. Past that, new shots aren't fired until some run out, and the Console says so once.
  • Like a move, a shot lands after every update in the tick is done (what game code sees), so it starts flying next tick.

Making and removing entities#

Game code can make copies of prefabs while it plays, and take entities away:

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Prefab;

component Hangar {
    has {
        int made = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        is made < 10? then {
            entity ship = World:spawn(Prefab.Ships.Fighter, [made * 5, 0, 10]);
            made = made + 1;
        }
    }
}

pass Hangar;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hangar {
    made: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Hangar {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        if self.made < 10 {
            // The prefab by its file in the project, without .prefab.lst.
            let place = Vec3::new(self.made as f32 * 5.0, 0.0, 10.0);
            let _ship = cx.host().spawn("ships/fighter", place);
            self.made += 1;
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Hangar = component("Hangar", {
    { "made", "int", 0 },
})

function Hangar:update(dt)
    if self.made < 10 then
        -- The prefab's name as text: Prefab.Ships.Fighter is "Ships.Fighter".
        local ship = solis.World:spawn("Ships.Fighter", vec3(self.made * 5, 0, 10))
        self.made = self.made + 1
    end
end
  • Which prefab: one of the project's, named from its file with folders as options inside options: ships/fighter.prefab.lst is Prefab.Ships.Fighter (each part's first letter a capital). Solis writes the names into solis/project.lst whenever you add, rename or remove a prefab, so a misspelt or deleted one is a mistake before the game runs, listing the real ones. A file whose name can't be a Lust name (it starts with a digit, has a dash or space, is all capitals, or is one of Lust's own objects like time) is left out, and the Console says which. Prefab.None is there when the project has none, and makes nothing.
  • When: like a move, it happens after every update in the tick (what game code sees). World:spawn gives back the new entity at once, so you can keep it. It joins the game at the end of the tick, after the tick's moves: its components start then and run from the next tick, even when a slow frame runs several ticks at once. A despawn lands at the same moment, in the order they were asked for, so spawning something and taking it out in one tick leaves nothing behind. New copies go at the end of the level's tree, in the order they were spawned.
  • Where it shows: copies game code makes appear in the Level panel while playing, and are gone when you press Stop, like everything else the game did. They aren't undo steps, which is how Solis tells them from your own edits: Stop offers to keep only yours (Play mode), so a change you make to one of these copies goes with it.
  • At most 10,000 copies are made in one tick, and a level holds at most a million entities; past that, the Console says so and the rest aren't made.
  • When a copy can't be made: World:spawn still gives back an entity, but nothing appears, and the Console says why in a warning: Game code spawned "squad", but it places a prefab (…) that isn't in the project, so nothing was made. The reasons are those of prefabs themselves: the prefab places another whose file is missing or can't be read, prefabs place each other in a loop (the message names them in order), they're placed more than 16 deep, or a copy would be more than a million entities. Each prefab's reason is said once each time you press Play, however many times the code asks, so a spawn in update doesn't fill the Console. Fix the prefab and press Play again.
  • despawn() is how a component takes its own entity away, and target:despawn() takes another. It ends at the end of the tick.

Random numbers#

Dice, loot, where an enemy wanders next: random() gives a number from 0 up to 1, randomRange(low, high) one between two numbers, and randomInt(low, high) a whole number, both ends included.

fetch "solis/world":World;

component Die {
    method update(float dt) {
        World:say("rolled " + World:randomInt(1, 6).text());
    }
}

pass Die;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Die;

impl RustComponent for Die {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        // random() is from 0 up to 1: six sides make 1 to 6.
        let roll = (cx.host().random() * 6.0).floor() as i64 + 1;
        cx.host().say(&format!("rolled {roll}"));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Die = component("Die", {})

function Die:update(dt)
    solis.World:say("rolled " .. solis.World:randomInt(1, 6))
end

Solis makes them from the game's seed (random numbers), so the same seed gives the same numbers, on any computer and any number of cores. Each Play has a new seed; type seed in the Console to see it, and seed 42 to start every Play from 42, so you can watch the same game again. setSeed(n) starts the numbers again from n at the end of the tick. Lua's own math.random and math.randomseed follow the same seed. Lust's own Random (Random[1, 6], Random:chance, an array's pick and shuffle) doesn't yet: its first roll starts it from the computer's clock, and with it the game's seed, so the same game can't be played again. Use World:random and the rest above. The numbers carry on while the game is paused with World:setGameSpeed(0): every tick still rolls new ones, so a pause menu can shuffle or roll like any other code.

Tweens#

A door that swings open over half a second, a health bar that slides down, a light that fades: a tween glides a field to a new value over time, so you don't write the in-between steps yourself.

fetch "solis/world":World;

component Door {
    has {
        float open = 0;
    }

    on Opened() {
        tween open to 1 over 0.5 [ease OutCubic] {
            World:say("the door is open");
        }
    }
}

event Opened();
pass Door;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// Tweens are Lust's own. In Rust, move the field a step in update:
// here a steady glide from 0 to 1 over half a second.
pub struct Door {
    open: f64,
    opening: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for Door {
    fn handle(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Opened" {
            return false;
        }
        self.opening = true;
        true
    }

    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        if self.opening {
            self.open = (self.open + dt / 0.5).min(1.0);
            if self.open >= 1.0 {
                self.opening = false;
                cx.host().say("the door is open");
            }
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
-- Tweens are Lust's own. In Lua, move the field a step in update:
-- here a steady glide from 0 to 1 over half a second.
local Door = component("Door", {
    { "open", "float", 0 },
    { "opening", "bool", false },
})

function Door:on_Opened()
    self.opening = true
end

function Door:update(dt)
    if self.opening then
        self.open = math.min(1, self.open + dt / 0.5)
        if self.open >= 1 then
            self.opening = false
            solis.World:say("the door is open")
        end
    end
end
  • What it moves: a field of the component (or a variable at the top of the file) that's an int, float, vec2, vec3, colour or rotation. [ease OutCubic] picks how it speeds up and slows down (any of the Ease curves; leave it out for a steady glide), and the { } after it, if any, runs once when it gets there.
  • When: each tick, tweens move after the game-wide objects and before any component's update. So an update sees this tick's value, and what a done block changes is there for the same tick's updates. A tween started in an update first moves on the next tick. Starting another tween on the same field replaces the first, whose { } never runs.
  • New code while playing stops the tweens the old code started, where they are, without their { }.
  • A game-wide object's fields can't be tweened: an object changes only in its own update (below), so the tween stops with a message saying so. Glide the field in the object's update instead, with Maths:moveTowards(hour, 18, dt) or lerp.
  • When a tween fails (its { } divides by zero, say), the Console says where, once, until the code changes. Tweens started after it wait until it has run its time, so fix it first.

Tweens are Lust's own. In Lua or Rust, move the field a step in update, as the switch above shows; for an ease, bend the step with a curve of your own.

Game-wide objects#

Some things belong to the whole game, not to any one entity: the time of day, the player's money, the weather. Write one as a Lust object and pass it, and Solis runs it for you (game-wide object):

object Clock {
    has {
        int day = 1;
        float hour = 6;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        hour += dt / 60;
        is hour >= 24? then {
            hour -= 24;
            day += 1;
        }
    }

    method bool isNight() {
        return hour < 6 || hour >= 20;
    }
}

component StreetLamp {
    has {
        bool lit = false;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        lit = Clock:isNight();
    }
}

pass Clock, StreetLamp;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// Game-wide objects are Lust's own: Rust and Lua components can't read
// them yet. Keep the clock in Lust, as in the Lust example, and have a
// Lust component tell the lamps with an event when night falls.
pub struct StreetLamp {
    lit: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for StreetLamp {
    fn handle(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        match event.name.as_str() {
            "NightFell" => self.lit = true,
            "DayBroke" => self.lit = false,
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
-- Game-wide objects are Lust's own: Lua and Rust components can't read
-- them yet. Keep the clock in Lust, as in the Lust example, and have a
-- Lust component tell the lamps with an event when night falls.
local StreetLamp = component("StreetLamp", {
    { "lit", "bool", false },
})

function StreetLamp:on_NightFell()
    self.lit = true
end

function StreetLamp:on_DayBroke()
    self.lit = false
end
  • Ticked first: each passed object's update(float dt) runs once a tick, objects in order of their names, before any entity's components. So every lamp sees the same hour, the one the clock has just moved to.
  • Read anywhere, changed only in its own update. Components read an object's fields and call its methods (Clock.hour, Clock:isNight()). Changing one of its fields anywhere else (Clock.hour = 12; in a component) stops that component, with a message pointing at the line: "Clock.hour can't be changed here: an object changes only in its own update". An object's update may change other objects too. Why: Solis runs game code on every core of the computer at once, each core with its own copy of the code. Objects run on the first, and their fields are copied to the others before the components run; if a component on one core could change the clock, the others would never know.
  • Kept in save games: a save keeps every object's fields, and loading gives them back (Save games). New code while the game runs keeps them too, field by field, by name, like a component's.
  • Which fields: the kinds a component's fields can be (bool, int, float, string, a state, vec3, vec2, rotation, colour, entity) are copied and kept. A list, a map or a thing in an object isn't saved yet, and each core keeps its own copy, so the Console says so when you press Play. Keep what every part of the game must see in plain fields.
  • An object that fails in its update stops, and the Console says where, like a component; it runs again when the code changes. Components can still read it.
  • Lust only: objects are written in Lust. Lua and Rust components can't read them yet.
  • An object that isn't passed is its file's own helper, and Solis leaves it alone.

Saving and loading#

Saves:saveTo("quick") saves the whole game and Saves:loadFrom("quick") puts it back exactly as it was: see Save games. (save and load on their own are Lust's own words, for its files.)

Sounds#

Game code plays sound events by the project's names for them: Solis writes each event into solis/project.lst as state Sound, folders as options inside options, so sfx/footstep.solsound is Sound.Sfx.Footstep. A misspelt or deleted event is a mistake before the game runs. Fetch Audio from solis/sound and Sound from solis/project:

fetch "solis/sound":Audio;
fetch "solis/project":Sound;

component Walker {
    has {
        int steps = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        steps = steps + 1;
        is steps % 30 == 0? then {
            Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.Footstep, position());
        }
    }
}

pass Walker;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent, SoundAt};

pub struct Walker {
    steps: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Walker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        self.steps += 1;
        if self.steps % 30 == 0 {
            // The sound event by its place in the Library, without .solsound.
            let me = cx.me();
            let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().play_sound("sfx/footstep", SoundAt::Place(here));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Walker = component("Walker", {
    { "steps", "int", 0 },
})

function Walker:update(dt)
    self.steps = self.steps + 1
    if self.steps % 30 == 0 then
        -- The sound event's name as text: Sound.Sfx.Footstep is "Sfx.Footstep".
        solis.Audio:playAt("Sfx.Footstep", solis.entity.position(self.me))
    end
end
  • Audio:play(Sound.Music.Theme) plays it the same everywhere: music, the interface.
  • Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.Footstep, place) plays it at a place in the world: quieter far from the camera, and from its direction (for an event whose Placement is In the world).
  • playSound(Sound.Sfx.Engine) plays it on the component's entity and follows it as it moves: an engine, a voice (target:playSound(…) on another). stopSounds() stops them, with a short fade, even ones asked for earlier in the same tick; it doesn't stop the entity's AudioSource (use setSoundPlaying for that).
  • setSoundPlaying(playing) turns the entity's AudioSource (a sound that keeps playing: an engine, a campfire) on or off.
  • Audio:setVolume(Bus.Music, volume) sets a bus for the rest of the play (the buses are the Mixer's, as state Bus in solis/project.lst; the UI bus is Bus.Ui, since Lust names aren't all capitals), from 0 (silent) to 1 (as set in the Mixer): what an options menu's volume sliders call. Stop puts the Mixer's back.

In Lua they're solis.Audio:playAt("Sfx.Footstep", solis.entity.position(self.me)) and so on (the option's name as text; "sfx/footstep" works too). In Rust, through the component's host: cx.host().play_sound("sfx/footstep", SoundAt::Place(place)), and cx.host().set_bus_volume("Music", 0.5).

Sound never changes the game. None of these gives anything back, so code can't ask "is it still playing?": a game plays exactly the same with sound on, off, or with no sound card, and a recording replays the same. Each play picks its take from the game's seed and the tick, so the same game even sounds the same each time. Like a move, a sound lands at the end of the tick.

  • The camera is what hears (or a Listener), and the entity whose code plays a sound is who caused it, for a sound event heard by Only who caused it: a sound to its right comes from the right. Pausing the game pauses its sounds, Play carries them on, and Stop fades them out. A Step plays that tick's sounds.
  • A sound placed past its event's Silent past distance isn't started at all.
  • Up to 256 sounds can be asked for in one tick (more are left out, and the Console says so once), and up to 256 play at once.
  • If the computer stalls for a moment, only the last few ticks' sounds play, so a hitch doesn't play a pile of footsteps at once.

Input#

Game code reads the player's controls as named actions, never keys: Input:axis(Action.Move), Input:pressed(Action.Jump), Input:held(Action.Sprint), with Input from solis/input and Action from solis/project. See Input, which also covers gamepads, rebinding and recording a play.

Physics#

Things that fall, collide and get pushed have a RigidBody and a Collider: see Physics. Game code pushes them (push), reads and sets how fast they move (velocity, setVelocity), and looks along lines with Physics:castRay, which gives back a RayHit. Characters with a CharacterBody are moved with walk and asked grounded: see Characters and cameras, which also has the ready-made character controller and cameras in solis/kit/.

What the engine offers#

InMethodWhat it does

solis/worldfloat World:time()How long the game has been running, in seconds.
solis/worldentity World:find(string name)The first entity with this name, in the Level panel's order, or nothing.

solis/screensScreens:setUiSize(float size), Screens:uiSize()The player's UI size: every screen bigger or smaller, 0.5 to 2.

solis/windowWindow:setResolution(int width, int height), Window:resolution(), Window:useNextResolution()The window's size in pixels, and the next usual one, for a menu.
solis/windowWindow:quit()Closes the game at the end of the tick, for a menu's Quit button. While playing in the editor, play stops (Exporting for playtesting). In Lua solis.Window:quit(); in Rust quit.
solis/worldfloat World:timeOfDay(), World:setTimeOfDay(float hour)The game's hour, 0 up to 24, from the Environment's Day and night; setting it moves the day on from there, at the end of the tick (Sky, fog and exposure). In Lua solis.World:timeOfDay(); in Rust time_of_day.

solis/soundAudio:setVolume(Bus bus, float volume)Sets a bus's volume for the rest of the play, 0 to 1.

An entity's abilities are called bare for the component's own entity (moveTo(place)) and with : on any other (target:moveTo(place)). In Lua they're solis.entity.moveTo(target, place), and the objects' solis.World:say(words).

Calls that changed. Solis's calls now follow one shape (methods on things, the project's names as states), so some older ones are written differently. Old code is a mistake that says the new way: "positionOf is now written target:position() (inside a component, position() for its own entity)".

BeforeNow

rotationOf(e), turnTo(e, r), nameOf(e), despawn(e)e:rotation(), e:turnTo(r), e:name(), e:despawn()
turnTo(this, facingAlong(d))face(d)
say, time, frameTime, find, fire, random, randomRange, randomInt, setSeedthe same names on World: World:say(words)
spawn("ships/fighter", p)World:spawn(Prefab.Ships.Fighter, p)
Assembly.Ships.Fighter, fetch "solis/project":Assembly; (assemblies are called prefabs, decision 0118↗)Prefab.Ships.Fighter, fetch "solis/project":Prefab;. The old name is a mistake that says the new one. Rust and Lua name a prefab by its path as text, which didn't change.
saveGame(slot), loadGame(slot)Saves:saveTo(slot), Saves:loadFrom(slot)
held("Jump"), pressed, released, axis("Move")Input:held(Action.Jump) and so on, with fetch "solis/input":Input; and fetch "solis/project":Action;
bindingOf("Jump"), rebind("Jump", key)Input:binding(Action.Jump), Input:rebind(Action.Jump, key)
push(e, f), velocityOf(e), setVelocity(e, v)e:push(f), e:velocity(), e:setVelocity(v)
moveCharacter(e, w), onGround(e)e:walk(w), e:grounded()
playSound("sfx/x"), playSoundAt("sfx/x", p)Audio:play(Sound.Sfx.X), Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.X, p)
playSoundOn("sfx/x", e), stopSoundsOn(e), setSoundPlaying(e, b)e:playSound(Sound.Sfx.X), e:stopSounds(), e:setSoundPlaying(b)

playClip(e, "walk"), replayClip, stopClip(e)e:animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk), e:animateFromStart(…), e:stopAnimation()
on AnimationCue(string name), on ClipFinished(string clip)on CueReached(Cue cue), on ClipFinished(Clip clip)
castRay(…), castRayHit(…), castRayNormal(…)one call: RayHit hit = Physics:castRay(…); then hit.distance, hit.entity, hit.normal
Lua solis.positionOf(e), solis.say(w), solis.held("Jump")solis.entity.position(e), solis.World:say(w), solis.Input:held("Jump")

When an update renames something. What game code can call doesn't change by accident: Solis's own checks stop any update that changes it without saying so. When a name does change on purpose, the old name keeps working for a few phases, so your game still runs the day you update. Each place your code uses the old name shows in the Problems panel as a warning, with its file and line, the new name, and when the old one stops working. Change the call to the new name before then.

Safe to open#

Game code runs inside a sandbox: it can reach the game through the engine's methods, and nothing else. It can't read or write files, start programs or reach the network, it has 64 MB of memory, and code that runs too long is stopped. Lua's require isn't there either (it would read files from anywhere on the computer). So a project you download or are sent can't harm your computer through its code, and Solis never runs the other files in it (see Projects and the Library).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says "there's already something called Health". Why: two components, classes, objects, nodes or schemas have the same name (often a copied one not yet renamed), perhaps in two files; the message says where the other is. Fix: rename one.
  • Problem: Problems says checking the code took more than 30 seconds and was given up on. Why: something in the code is more than the checker can handle; it shouldn't happen. A check can't be stopped once it has started, so that one keeps running in the background (and keeps one processor core busy) until it ends by itself, which it may never do. Fix: undo your last change, then restart Solis so the code can be checked again, and please report it with the code that caused it.
  • Problem: Problems says "the code wasn't checked: the check that started … never finished, and is still running". Why: an earlier check was given up on (the problem above) and is still running. Solis doesn't start another beside it, or every save would leave one more running and slow the computer down further. The message says what that check was checking: the same code as now, or the code before the files it names changed (the trouble is in that older code). Fix: restart Solis to check the code straight away. If you'd rather wait, the code is checked by itself as soon as the old check ends.
  • Problem: Problems says the game's code starts at main.lst and there isn't one. Why: there are .lst files of your own, but none is called main.lst at the top of the project's folder (the Library's top). (The files Solis writes into its own folder don't count: a game written only in Lua needs no main.lst.) Fix: make main.lst there, and fetch your other files from it.
  • Problem: changes I made to solis/world.lst (or solis/kit/…) disappeared. Why: Solis writes the solis files again when the project opens, so they always match the engine. Fix: put your own code in your own files, outside solis/: anything in that folder counts as the engine's, never as your game's code. To change a ready-made component, copy its file outside solis/ and rename the component.
  • Problem: my component isn't in + Component. Why: the code has a mistake (see Problems), or its Lust file isn't fetched from main.lst (directly, or through a file main.lst fetches). Lua files are all read, wherever they are in the project. Fix: fix the mistake, or fetch the file.
  • Problem: "solis.entity.moveTo isn't something the engine offers" in Lua. Why: the name is misspelt, or the method was used outside update or an on_ function, when the game isn't running. Fix: check the name against the table above.
  • Problem: the Console says a call "wants text for words, and was given nothing (nil)" in Lua. Why: one of the values given to the call isn't the kind it takes. Nothing (nil) usually means a value is missing, a variable's name is misspelt (a name Lua doesn't know is nil), or the call is written with a dot where it needs a colon: solis.World.say("hello") for solis.World:say("hello"). Fix: the message names the call, the value and the line; check that value there.
  • Problem: the Console says "this calls something of Solis's that was kept from earlier" in Lua. Why: a call was put in a variable, as local say = solis.World.say at the top of a file does. Solis lends its calls to game code only while that code runs, so the one kept stops working as soon as the file has loaded. Fix: write the call out where it's used (solis.World:say("hello")), or keep the object and call through it: local World = solis.World, then World:say("hello").
  • Problem: a component is called the same as one of Solis's (Light) or a Rust one, or a Lust and a Lua component share a name. Why: two components can't share a name. The one in your code doesn't run (Solis's own, or the Rust one, does). Fix: rename yours; Problems says where it is.
  • Problem: I saved new code while playing, and the Console says the running game couldn't take it. Why: the code's start failed with the game's world (it ran fine with no world while checking). Fix: fix the line it points at; the game keeps the last code meanwhile.
  • Problem: Problems says "a state is set with =, so write mode = Mode.Burst;". Why: Lust sets a state with =, like any other value, and keeps is for questions. Code written for an older Solis set one with is (mode is Mode.Burst;, or state is Mood.Calm; in a has). Fix: change that is to =, as the message shows. Questions (is mode == Mode.Burst? then) stay as they are.
  • Problem: Problems says something is nested too deeply. Why: more than 150 levels of brackets, blocks or operators inside each other (a + b + c … counts each +) is more than Lust takes. Fix: split it up with variables or methods.
  • Problem: Problems says the code stopped while starting. Why: Solis runs the code's own start (the lines outside components, and each field's starting value) to read its components, before anything plays and with no world: World:find finds nothing then. A start that fails or takes more than a second is a mistake. Fix: fix the line Problems points at.
  • Problem: the Console says a code file was left out. Why: each code file can be at most 1 MB, and all of them together 16 MB. Files that aren't text are left out too. Fix: split a huge file into smaller ones.
  • Problem: a component reads another entity's place and gets where it was before this tick's move. Why: during a tick, game code sees the world as it was when the tick started (see Components, above), so every core sees the same world. Fix: usually nothing: it catches up next tick. If it must be at once, do both in one component, or send an event (events see the moves made before them).
  • Commit the solis folder with your game, so lust check works on other computers too.

Which language when#

Lust, Lua and Rust can all write game code, and they work together on one entity. This page says which to use for what, with Solis's own measurements.

When to use it#

When you're starting a component and wondering which language to write it in, or when the Profiler says game code takes much of a frame.

The short answer#

  • Lust for most of your game: it's made for Solis, Problems checks it as you type, and it's fast enough for almost everything. Start here.
  • Lua for logic you already know how to write in Lua, or code copied from elsewhere: deciding things, reacting to events, menus, quests. It's fine anywhere the work is small per tick.
  • Rust for the heaviest per-tick work on many entities (crowds, simulations), once it's clear that's where the time goes. For now, Rust components need a Solis built from source.

All three can sit on the same entity and send each other events (see Game code), so you can start a component in Lust and move just the slow part later.

The numbers#

The same work, written once in each language: 2,000 entities each doing a running sum of 40 sines every tick. Milliseconds for one tick of all 2,000 (a frame at 60 frames a second has about 16 ms in all), from Solis's scale check:

RustLustLua
40 steps of number work each0.362.76.0
400 steps each (ten times as much)4.32736

What that means:

  • Rust is about 7 times quicker than Lust at number work, and Lust about twice as quick as Lua when the work is light.
  • Most of Lua's time is reaching its own fields (self.value), which Solis checks every time. A Lua component that keeps its sums in local variables and writes its fields once at the end runs closer to Lust.
  • All three give exactly the same answer, to the last bit, so a game plays the same whichever you choose, and recordings replay the same.

Solis tried making Lust and Lua faster with Luau's "native code". Lust's heavy work got about a third quicker but Lua's got slower, so it's off for now (the report↗).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: game code takes most of a frame. Why: many entities do a lot each tick. Fix: see which component it is, then: do the work every few ticks instead of every tick; keep sums in local variables; or move that component to Lust (from Lua) or Rust (from Lust).
  • Problem: "is Lua bad, then?" Why: no: 2,000 Lua components doing light work each tick take about 6 ms, which fits easily in a frame. Fix: nothing, unless the Profiler says otherwise.

Related#

  • Game code: writing components in all three languages.
  • The Profiler: where each frame's time goes.
  • Concepts: game code, components.
← Previous · Chapter 31Game codeNext → · Chapter 33Physics

Physics#

Make things fall, collide, stack and get pushed, the same way on every computer.

When to use it#

Whenever something in your game should move like a real object without you writing how: a crate that tips off a ledge, a ball that bounces, a door that swings shut and knocks things out of the way, or a floor and walls that characters and objects can't pass through.

Not everything needs it. Projectiles (lasers, bullets) fly in straight lines without physics, which is why a million of them are cheap. And a unit that only slides across a map is simpler to move yourself with moveTo.

Solis's physics is strict: the same game, with the same inputs, comes out exactly the same on every computer, to the last decimal (determinism). Recordings play back the same anywhere, and online strategy games can keep every player's game in step. It costs physics a little speed, which you won't notice at the sizes Solis aims for.

How to use it#

A floor

  1. Select the entity that should be the floor (an imported model, or an empty one from Home › Empty, placed where the floor goes).
  2. In Properties, choose + Component › Collider. A green outline shows its shape in the viewport while it's selected.
  3. Set its Shape and Size to cover the floor. A box 20 × 20 × 1 m is a good start; its middle sits at the entity, so lower the entity half a metre to put the top at its feet, or set Centre to 0 0 -0.5.

An entity with a collider and nothing else never moves: floors, walls, rocks.

Quicker still: a Solid brush (B over the view, or Create › Shape, then drawn out on the ground) is a floor or wall with no collider to add. Its own faces are what physics bumps into, exactly as drawn, and it never falls, even with a RigidBody (a Kinematic one still moves it as game code says, as a platform). A Collider on the same entity is used instead of its faces.

A crate that falls

  1. Select the crate and add a Collider sized like it (a 1 m crate: Box, size 1 1 1).
  2. Add a RigidBody too. Its Kind is Dynamic: physics moves it.
  3. Press Play. The crate falls onto the floor and settles. Press Stop and it's back where it was.

Moving things yourself

  • A Kinematic body is moved only by your game code (moveTo, turnTo), and pushes dynamic things out of its way without being pushed back: lifts, moving platforms, doors. A character standing on one is carried along.
  • For 2D games, use a Collider2D instead, with solid terrains for walls: see Walls and walking in 2D.
  • A player's character is better with a CharacterBody, which climbs steps, slides along walls and walks up slopes: see Characters and cameras.
  • A Fixed body never moves, like a collider on its own.
  • You can still moveTo a dynamic body to put it somewhere new (say, back on its shelf); physics carries on from there.

From game code, a body's abilities are on its entity (ball:push(force), or push(force) for the component's own), and rays are asked of Physics (in Lua, solis.entity.push(e, force) and solis.Physics:castRay(from, direction, reach), whose answer is a table with the same four fields; in Rust, cx.host().push(e, force) and cx.host().cast_ray(from, direction, reach), which gives back the hit or nothing):

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/physics":[Physics, RayHit];

component Kicker {
    has {
        int kicked = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        entity ball = World:find("Ball");
        is kicked == 0? then {
            ball:push([5, 0, 2]);
            kicked = 1;
        }
        -- Is anything below, within 2 metres?
        RayHit below = Physics:castRay(position(), [0, 0, -1], 2);
        is below.found? then {
            World:say(below.entity:name() + " is below me");
        }
    }
}

pass Kicker;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Kicker {
    kicked: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Kicker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        if self.kicked == 0 {
            if let Some(ball) = cx.host().find("Ball") {
                cx.host().push(ball, Vec3::new(5.0, 0.0, 2.0));
            }
            self.kicked = 1;
        }
        // Is anything below, within 2 metres?
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        if let Some(below) = cx.host().cast_ray(here, Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, -1.0), 2.0) {
            let name = cx.host().name(below.entity).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().say(&format!("{name} is below me"));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Kicker = component("Kicker", {
    { "kicked", "int", 0 },
})

function Kicker:update(dt)
    local ball = solis.World:find("Ball")
    if self.kicked == 0 then
        solis.entity.push(ball, vec3(5, 0, 2))
        self.kicked = 1
    end
    -- Is anything below, within 2 metres?
    local below = solis.Physics:castRay(solis.entity.position(self.me), vec3(0, 0, -1), 2)
    if below.found then
        solis.World:say(solis.entity.name(below.entity) .. " is below me")
    end
end
MethodWhat it does
push(vec3 impulse)A push, like a kick: a heavy body moves less than a light one. [5, 0, 0] gives a 1 kg crate 5 m/s along X.
vec3 velocity()How fast and which way it's moving, metres a second.
setVelocity(vec3 velocity)Makes it move this fast, this way, whatever its weight.
RayHit Physics:castRay(vec3 from, vec3 direction, float reach)Looks along a line and gives back what it met, all at once: hit.found (whether anything was within reach), hit.distance (how far, or -1), hit.entity (whose collider, or nothing) and hit.normal (which way its surface faces: [0, 0, 1] for a floor).

Why one call for a ray? Each question a ray answers is worked out at once, so asking for the distance, the entity and the surface separately looked three times; RayHit keeps them together.

Like moves, pushes and velocities land when every update in the tick is done, then physics moves everything on once (what game code sees). A ray sees the world as the tick started. A ray that starts inside a collider (your own character's, say) passes out of it and finds what's beyond.

Settings#

RigidBody

SettingWhat it does
KindDynamic: moved by physics. Kinematic: moved by game code, pushing dynamic things. Fixed: never moves.
MassHow heavy, in kilograms. 0 works it out from the collider's size: a kilogram for each cubic metre (a 1 m box weighs 1 kg). Give real things their real weight: a crate 20 kg, a person 75 kg.
DampingHow quickly it slows down by itself, like air resistance. 0 never; 1 or 2 feels like moving through water.
Turn dampingHow quickly it stops spinning by itself.
GravityHow much gravity pulls it: 1 as normal, 0 floats, below 0 rises.
Stays uprightIt never tips over or spins: for characters and things that should stand.
FastChecked between ticks too, so it can't pass through thin walls when it moves fast (thrown things). Costs a little more.

Collider

SettingWhat it does
ShapeBox, Sphere, or Capsule (a cylinder with rounded ends, standing up: the usual shape for a character).
SizeA box's size along X, Y and Z, in metres.
RadiusA sphere's or capsule's radius.
HeightA capsule's height, end to end.
CentreWhere the shape's middle is, from the entity's origin. Raise a character's capsule by half its height so its feet are at the origin.
FrictionHow much it grips: 0 ice, 0.5 most things, 1 rubber.
BouncinessHow much it bounces back: 0 not at all, 1 keeps all its speed.

Shapes grow with the entity's Scale.

CharacterBody is described in Characters and cameras. It takes the place of a RigidBody and Collider on the same entity, and doesn't grow with Scale.

Shortcuts#

Physics adds no keys. In the Console, seed and checksum help check that two plays come out the same.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: my crate falls through the floor. Why: the floor has no Collider, or it's smaller than it looks (check the green outline with the floor selected). Fix: add a Collider to the floor and size it.
  • Problem: something small and fast passes through a thin wall. Why: between two ticks it went from one side to the other. Fix: tick Fast on its RigidBody, or make the wall thicker.
  • Problem: a dynamic body doesn't move when I push it. Why: it's heavy for the push (a push of 5 moves a 1 kg box at 5 m/s, but a 100 kg one at only 0.05 m/s), it's resting on something with high friction, or it's Kinematic or Fixed. Fix: push harder, or make it Dynamic.
  • Problem: my character tips over. Why: physics turns it when it bumps into things. Fix: give it a CharacterBody instead of a RigidBody (Characters and cameras), or tick Stays upright.
  • Problem: a collider under another entity (a lift's floor) and the lift moves. Why: everything with physics under something that game code or an edit moves goes with it, at the next physics step: colliders, kinematic and dynamic bodies, characters (a crate in a group you move comes along). What's under a body physics moves goes too, except dynamic bodies, which physics moves itself. Fix: nothing to do. But don't put a collider under a dynamic body: it follows, but the body bumps into it. Give the body its collider directly.
  • Problem: the Console says the game has the most physics bodies it can. Why: at most 100,000 entities take part in physics at once. Fix: use fewer bodies; things that never move can share one big collider.
  • Problem: the game paused, saying physics took too long. Why: one tick of physics took more than a quarter of a second. Fix: fewer bodies, or simpler shapes.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Play mode
  • Entities and components
  • Characters and cameras
  • Concepts: physics, rigid body, collider, determinism
← Previous · Chapter 32Which language whenNext → · Chapter 34Input

Input#

Your game's controls as named actions: Move, Look, Jump, Sprint, Interact, the cameras' Pan, Turn, Zoom and Drag, the menus' MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack and Pause, and any you add, from the keyboard, mouse or a gamepad, and rebindable.

When to use it#

Whenever the player controls something. Game code never asks "is W down?"; it asks "is the player moving?" (Input:axis(Action.Move)) or "did they press Jump?" (Input:pressed(Action.Jump)). Which keys and buttons mean Jump is set in one place, File › Project settings › Input, so:

  • a gamepad works without extra code (the A button is bound to Jump too);
  • players can change the keys (rebinding) without changing your game;
  • a play's input can be recorded and played back exactly, which is how you check the game always comes out the same.

How to use it#

Playing with the keys and mouse

  1. Press Play.
  2. Click the Game panel. The game now has the mouse and keys: the pointer disappears (moving the mouse turns, instead of moving a pointer), and the editor's own keys (W for the move tool, Delete, Ctrl + Z…) are off, so they can't change your level by accident while you play.
  3. Press Esc to give the mouse and keys back to the editor. Stop does too.

A connected gamepad works whenever the game is playing; it has nothing of the editor's to clash with. Solis uses the first one connected, Xbox layout.

The ready-made actions

ActionKeyboard and mouseGamepadWhat game code gets
MoveW A S D, or the arrow keysleft stickwhich way to go: x across (right +1), y forward (+1)
Lookmouseright stickhow far to turn this tick, in degrees
JumpSpaceAheld, pressed, released
SprintShiftleft stick clickheld, pressed, released
InteractFXheld, pressed, released
Panarrow keysleft stickwhich way to move the RTS camera
TurnAlt + left and right arrowsright stickwhich way to turn the RTS camera
Zoommouse wheel, Page Up and Page Downright and left triggershow far to zoom this tick, in steps (a wheel notch is one)
Dragmiddle mouse buttonheld while dragging the map
MenuMovearrow keysd-pad, left stickmoves the focus between a screen's buttons
MenuChooseEnter, SpaceAchooses the button with the focus
MenuBackBackspaceBheld, pressed, released (your code decides what "back" does)
PausePStartheld, pressed, released (your code opens its pause menu)

While a screen with buttons is shown, only the four menu actions reach game code: Jump on Space doesn't also jump while Space chooses a button. A project whose input actions file is from before them still gets them while playing.

Changing them: File › Project settings › Input

  1. The table lists every action: its name, whether it's a Button or an Axis, its keyboard and mouse inputs as keys, and its gamepad's. All devices, Keyboard & mouse and Gamepad over the table show one kind or both; Find action or key narrows the rows.
  2. Click an action's row to pick it: its card at the right lists its bindings, each with the device it's on. Click a binding to pick it, then Backspace clears it; its × does the same.
  3. + Add binding (on an axis: + Up, + Down, + Left, + Right), then press the key, mouse button or gamepad button to bind. Esc calls it off; while it waits, Backspace is a key you can bind like any other. Hold Ctrl, Alt or Shift while pressing a key to bind the combination, such as Alt+Left; turn the mouse wheel to bind a notch up or down.
  4. An axis (like Move) has Up, Down, Left and Right keys, and whole-axis inputs (a stick, the mouse's movement, or the mouse wheel), ticked under Whole axis. One that goes with the mouse or the wheel has a Mouse speed and a Stick and key speed. Button and Axis at the top of the card change which it is; Remove the action takes it away.
  5. Add action ▾: type a name and choose Add button or Add axis (letters, digits and _, starting with a capital: OpenMap, Fire_2, so game code can name it Action.OpenMap).
  6. Add the ready-made actions it's missing appears in projects made before the cameras: it adds the ones it lacks (Pan, Turn, Zoom and Drag; MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack and Pause) and changes nothing else. Restore the ready-made actions puts all the ready-made ones back as they were, leaving your own.

Clashes. The ready-made actions share some keys on purpose: the arrows are Move, Pan and MenuMove, and Space is Jump and MenuChoose. When an action of your own shares a key with another, both are marked with ⚠ and the key in amber, and a line under the table says which: both fire on one press. Contexts, Fires on, Buffer, the stick's dead zone and Invert look Y are unfinished parts.

Combinations. A key on its own doesn't count while you hold modifiers that some action binds with it. With Turn on Alt+Left and Pan on Left, holding Alt and pressing the left arrow turns, and doesn't pan as well. The up arrow (with no Alt+Up bound) still pans while Alt is held.

Changes are saved straight away, and a game that's playing takes them at once (any rebinding game code did in this play gives way to them). A speed you drag shows its number as you go and counts when you let go of the mouse, and a typed one when you press Enter or click somewhere else: the change is saved, and reaches a playing game, then. They're kept in the project's input.solinput, a small text file beside project.solis that Git can merge.

In game code, the actions are names Lust checks: Solis writes them into solis/project.lst as state Action whenever you change them here, so Action.Jmp is a mistake before the game runs, listing the real actions. Fetch Input and Action, and ask Input. In Lua the action's name is text (solis.Input:held("Jump")), and in Rust the host gives an action's whole state at once (cx.host().action("Jump"), with held, pressed, released and axis):

fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Walker {
    has {
        float speed = 4;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        vec3 way = Input:axis(Action.Move);
        vec3 step = [way.x, way.y, 0];
        moveTo(position() + step * speed * dt);
        is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
            moveTo(position() + [0, 0, 1]);
        }
    }
}

pass Walker;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Walker {
    speed: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Walker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let way = cx.host().action("Move").axis;
        let step = Vec3::new(way.x, way.y, 0.0);
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        cx.host().move_to(me, here + step * self.speed * dt as f32);
        if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
            cx.host().move_to(me, here + Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Walker = component("Walker", {
    { "speed", "float", 4 },
})

function Walker:update(dt)
    local way = solis.Input:axis("Move")
    local step = vec3(way.x, way.y, 0)
    solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, solis.entity.position(self.me) + step * self.speed * dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
        solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, solis.entity.position(self.me) + vec3(0, 0, 1))
    end
end
MethodWhat it gives
bool Input:held(Action action)Whether it's held down this tick (an axis: not at rest).
bool Input:pressed(Action action)True once, the tick it went down. A tap between two ticks still counts.
bool Input:released(Action action)True once, the tick it came up.
vec3 Input:axis(Action action)An axis's two numbers as x and y (z is 0).
string Input:binding(Action action)The key that sets it off, such as F, for showing "Press F" to the player.
Input:rebind(Action action, string input)Binds a new input ("E", "Mouse Right", "Pad Y") in place of its others of the same kind, from the next tick: what a controls menu does. Lasts while the game plays.

Input is read once per tick, so every component, on every core, sees the same input for that tick.

Recording and playing back (the Play menu)

  1. With a project open, choose Debug › Play and record inputs. Play as usual.
  2. Press Stop. The recording is saved in the project's recordings folder (the Console says its name).
  3. Choose Debug › Replay a recording… and pick it. (While it replays, the game's Saves:saveTo makes its save as the recorded play did, but doesn't write over your saves.) Solis plays from the start with the same seed and every tick's recorded input, checking the game is exactly the same tick by tick (checksums). At the end it pauses and says whether it matched, or by which tick it stopped matching (the world is compared every tick, game code's own values once a second).

A replay that stops matching means the game came out differently from the same input: the level or code changed since recording, or something in the game isn't deterministic. That's how you find it the tick it starts.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Mouse speedFor an axis that goes with the mouse: how far a pixel of movement (or a notch of the wheel) goes. For Look, 0.15 degrees suits most mice; raise it for a faster turn. For Zoom it's 1: a notch is one step.
Stick and key speedHow far a stick or key held all the way goes in a second. For Look, 180 is half a turn a second; for Zoom, 8 steps.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Give the game the mouse and keysClick the Game panel while playing
Give them back to the editorEsc
Give up binding an input (after + Add binding)Esc
Clear the picked bindingBackspace
Pick an actionClick its row

While the game has them, every key is the game's: the editor's shortcuts are off.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: my character doesn't move when I press W. Why: the editor has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel first; its corner says when the game has the mouse and keys.
  • Problem: pressing W while playing picked the move tool. Why: the same: the game didn't have the keys. Fix: click the Game panel.
  • Problem: Input:pressed(Action.Jump) is never true. Why: the action has no inputs. Fix: check File › Project settings › Input.
  • Problem: the Console says an input action "can't be named in game code". Why: game code names actions as Lust names, which start with a capital and hold letters, digits and _ (OpenMap, Fire_2), and aren't all capitals. Fix: rename it in File › Project settings › Input.
  • Problem: Esc does nothing in my game. Why: in the editor, Esc gives the mouse and keys back, so a game can't use it there. Fix: give the action another key as well, to try it in the editor (the ready-made Pause is on P). In an exported game every key is the game's, Esc included.
  • Problem: the Console says the input actions couldn't be read. Why: input.solinput was changed by hand and has a mistake. Fix: the Console says what; fix it, or change any action in the window, which writes it again.
  • Problem: the Console says the input actions file had a mistake and was kept as input.solinput.bak. Why: the file couldn't be read, so the ready-made actions were used; changing anything in the window writes the file again, so Solis kept yours first. Fix: copy what you need from the .bak file, then delete it.
  • Problem: recording paused, saying it reached the most Solis keeps. Why: a recording is at most an hour, or 64 MB. Fix: Stop saves what was recorded; record shorter plays.
  • Problem: a replay stops matching at once. Why: the level or the code changed since it was recorded, or it was recorded with an earlier Solis, whose checks were worked out differently. Fix: record again.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Play mode
  • Physics
  • Characters and cameras
  • Concepts: action, binding, recording
← Previous · Chapter 33PhysicsNext → · Chapter 35Game screens: a HUD and menus in Lust

Game screens: a HUD and menus in Lust#

A screen (the HUD, a pause menu, a shop) is a Lust file that says what's on it, drawn over the game while it plays and reading the game's values as it goes.

When to use it#

Use a screen for anything the player reads on top of the game: the day and time, money, an energy or health bar, an ammo count. A screen only shows the game; it can't change it, so it can never make the game play differently on another computer or in a replay.

A screen can also have buttons (a pause menu's Resume, a shop's Buy). A button doesn't change the game either: it sends an event, and game code decides what happens, in the next tick. That keeps a menu as fair as the keys: what was clicked is kept in a recording like a key press, and plays back the same.

A menu can be used with the keys or a controller too: the arrow keys (or the d-pad) move a ring between its buttons, and Enter (or A) chooses.

This page writes screens by hand in Lust. The UI editor draws them on a canvas instead, and edits the same files, so you can go back and forth.

How to use it#

  1. Make the file. In the Library, make a folder called ui at its top, and a Lust file in it named after the screen: ui/hud.lst is the screen Hud. Its name starts with a letter and holds only letters and numbers.

  2. Write the screen. The file holds an assembly with the screen's name and a view, and passes it. The view uses Lust's own pieces (the same ones as Lust's windows):

    fetch "main":Clock;

assembly Hud {
    has {
        int coins = 3;
    }

    view [width 1920, height 1080] {
        stack [width fill, height fill, bottom, left, pad 48] {
            column [gap 8] {
                text "Day " + Clock.day.text() + ", " + Clock.hour.text() + ":00" [size 32, bold, white];
                progress Clock.energy [to 100, width 300, height 20, green];
            }
        }
    }
}

pass Hud;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Hud", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Hud")
    • [width 1920, height 1080] is the size you design at. On other screens everything grows or shrinks with the screen's height, and a wider screen (ultrawide) gets more room at the sides.
    • To pin something to a corner, put it in a stack as big as the screen (width fill, height fill) and say where: bottom, top, left, right, center, middle, with pad for the distance from the edge.

  3. Show it. Add a Screen component to an entity (the player, or a "Game" entity), and pick Hud in its Screen field. Shown turns it on and off; Order decides which of several screens is on top.

  4. Press Play. The screen is drawn over the Game panel, and changes with the game: after every tick it reads the game's values again.

What a screen can read:

  • the game's game-wide objects (Clock.hour, Money.amount);

  • its own fields (coins above): the screen's memory;

  • the entity it's shown for (the one whose Screen component shows it): Ui:entity(), and a copy of any of that entity's Lust components, with a reading method named after the component: Ui:entity():health() gives its Health. Fetch Ui from solis/screen and the component from its file:

    fetch "solis/screen":Ui;
fetch "main":Health;

assembly DroneHealth {
    view {
        Health health = Ui:entity():health();
        text "Drone " + health.hp.text() + " / 20" [size 26, bold, white];
        progress health.hp [to 20, width 360, height 18, red5];
    }
}

pass DroneHealth;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "DroneHealth", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "DroneHealth")

    The copy is the component as the last tick left it: its methods work (health:fraction()), and changing it changes nothing in the game. The turret sample (Turret sample on the launcher's Learn) has this health bar over its drone.

    Lua and Rust components, and Solis's own (Transform, Sprite, Camera, AudioSource and the rest) are read the same way. Solis describes each one to screens as a Lust component of its fields, so fetch it from solis/screen instead of from a file of yours:

    fetch "solis/screen":[Ui, Transform, Sparks];

assembly Where {
    view {
        Transform t = Ui:entity():transform();
        Sparks s = Ui:entity():sparks();
        text "x " + t.position.x.text() + ", sparks " + s.shown.text() [white];
    }
}

pass Where;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Where", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Where")

    Their fields are copies, as Lust components' are; they have no methods. A field Lust can't hold (a model or other asset, or one named like one of Lust's own words) is left out.

Buttons. A button has its words and, in { }, what a click does: usually send an event to the entity the screen is shown for. Declare the event in game code, fetch it in the screen, and handle it in a component on that entity:

-- ui/pauseMenu.lst
fetch "solis/screen":Ui;
fetch "main":[Resumed, Quit];

assembly PauseMenu {
    view {
        stack [width fill, height fill, center, middle] {
            column [gap 12, background gray9, pad 32, round 12] {
                text "Paused" [size 40, bold, white];
                button "Resume" [width 240, blue] { send Resumed() to Ui:entity(); }
                button "Quit" [width 240, hover:[background red7]] { send Quit() to Ui:entity(); }
            }
        }
    }
}

pass PauseMenu;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "PauseMenu", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
-- main.lst
fetch "solis/project":Screen;

event Resumed();
event Quit();

component Pauser {
    on Resumed() {
        hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
    }
}

pass Pauser, Resumed, Quit;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// The events are declared in Lust (main.lst), where the screen fetches
// them from.
pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Resumed" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", false);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The events are declared in Lust (main.lst), where the screen fetches
-- them from.
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:on_Resumed()
    solis.entity.hideScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
end
  • A button is drawn light grey with rounded corners; a colour word (blue, green, red5) colours it, and its words turn white or dark to stay readable. disabled greys it out and stops clicks.
  • Under the pointer it darkens a little, or takes the styles in its hover:[…].
  • The { } may also change the screen's own fields (a tab picked, say). It can't change the game: send an event for that.
  • What a button sends reaches the game at the start of the next tick, before the components' updates.

Showing and hiding screens from game code. Every entity can show one screen at a time. Its calls take the screen by name, from solis/project.lst (fetch Screen from "solis/project"):

CallWhat it does
showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu)Shows that screen on the entity's Screen component, at the end of the tick. An entity without one is given one.
hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu)Hides it, at the end of the tick, if the entity shows that screen.
screenShown(Screen.PauseMenu)Whether the entity shows that screen, as the tick started.

In Lua they're solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu"), solis.entity.hideScreen(…) and solis.entity.screenShown(…) (the screen's name as text), and a button's event arrives in on_Resumed. In Rust, through the component's host: cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "PauseMenu", true) (false hides it) and cx.host().screen_shown(cx.me(), "PauseMenu").

Use another entity (a "Menus" entity) for a second screen shown at the same time. Which screens are open is part of the game: it's in save games and recordings.

The mouse while a screen has buttons. While a screen with buttons is shown, the pointer stays visible over the Game panel, even after you click the game to give it the keys, so you can click the buttons. A click on a button goes to the button, not to the game; a click anywhere else gives the game the mouse and keys as usual. When the last screen with buttons goes, the pointer is held by the game again.

With the keys or a controller. Once the game has the keys, MenuMove (the arrow keys, the d-pad or the left stick) moves the focus to the nearest button that way, shown with a blue ring; held down, it moves on again every tenth of a second. MenuChoose (Enter, Space or A) chooses the button with the focus, just as a click would. A menu's first button has the focus to start with, so Down moves to the second. The focus is on the topmost screen with buttons, and moving the mouse over a button moves the focus there (the ring hides until the keys are used again).

While a screen with buttons is shown, the game's own actions wait: only MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack (Backspace, B) and Pause (P, Start) reach game code, so Space choosing a button doesn't also jump. Use MenuBack and Pause in game code to close a menu or open the pause menu: is Input:pressed(Action.Pause)? then { showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu); }. They're ordinary input actions, rebindable in File › Project settings › Input.

A pause menu. World:setGameSpeed(0) stops the game while game code keeps running: game time, physics, projectiles and sprites stand still and every dt is 0, but components' updates, events and the screens go on, so a menu can be used. World:setGameSpeed(1) carries on (anything between 0 and 4 runs slower or faster). The Game panel's corner says Game speed 0 meanwhile, and the speed is kept in save games. The turret sample has one: press P (or Start) while it plays.

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":[Action, Screen];

event Resumed();

component Pauser {
    method update(float dt) {
        is Input:pressed(Action.Pause)? then {
            showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
            World:setGameSpeed(0);
        }
    }

    on Resumed() {
        hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
        World:setGameSpeed(1);
    }
}

pass Pauser, Resumed;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        if cx.host().action("Pause").pressed {
            let me = cx.me();
            cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", true);
            cx.host().set_game_speed(0.0);
        }
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Resumed" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", false);
        cx.host().set_game_speed(1.0);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:update(dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("Pause") then
        solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
        solis.World:setGameSpeed(0)
    end
end

function Pauser:on_Resumed()
    solis.entity.hideScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
    solis.World:setGameSpeed(1)
end

Text size and UI size for players. Some players need bigger text, and a game played from a sofa needs a bigger HUD. Two player settings grow every screen: text size (Screens:setTextSize(1.5): every text half as big again, from 0.5 to 3; the columns and rows round it make room, and long lines wrap) and UI size (Screens:setUiSize(1.25): the whole screen bigger, from 0.5 to 2). A pause menu usually offers them. They're the player's, not the game's: they're not in save games or recordings, a loaded game keeps the player's, and they're kept from one play to the next. So only let them change what's shown and offered, never the game itself (how hard it is, say): a recording played back with other settings would go differently. Screens read them too (text "Text " + Screens:textSize().text();), but only game code changes them, so a menu's button sends an event and the entity's code does it:

fetch "solis/screens":Screens;
fetch "solis/window":Window;

event BiggerText();
event Fullscreen();
event NextResolution();

component Pauser {
    on BiggerText() {
        float size = Screens:textSize() + 0.25;
        is size > 2? then {
            size = 1;
        }
        Screens:setTextSize(size);
    }
    on Fullscreen() {
        Window:setFullscreen(not Window:fullscreen());
    }
    on NextResolution() {
        Window:useNextResolution();
    }
}

pass Pauser, BiggerText, Fullscreen, NextResolution;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        match event.name.as_str() {
            "BiggerText" => {
                let mut size = cx.host().text_size() + 0.25;
                if size > 2.0 {
                    size = 1.0;
                }
                cx.host().set_text_size(size);
            }
            "Fullscreen" => {
                let on = cx.host().fullscreen();
                cx.host().set_fullscreen(!on);
            }
            "NextResolution" => cx.host().use_next_resolution(),
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:on_BiggerText()
    local size = solis.Screens:textSize() + 0.25
    if size > 2 then
        size = 1
    end
    solis.Screens:setTextSize(size)
end

function Pauser:on_Fullscreen()
    solis.Window:setFullscreen(not solis.Window:fullscreen())
end

function Pauser:on_NextResolution()
    solis.Window:useNextResolution()
end

The window. Window:setFullscreen(true) fills the screen, and Window:setResolution(1920, 1080) (or Window:useNextResolution(), for a menu's Resolution button) sizes the window; Window:fullscreen() and Window:resolution() read them. Alt+Enter switches fullscreen in any game, as players expect. Window:quit() closes the game, for a menu's Quit button. While you play in the editor, the game stays in the Game panel: the Console says what the exported game would do, the settings are kept so the menu shows them, and Quit stops play. In an exported game they're real: the window changes, the game closes, and the settings are kept in the player's own folder.

A screen's look. On the Screen component, Glow puts a soft light round everything on the screen, in each piece's own colour; Outline puts a line just outside everything, in Outline colour; and Pixel size draws the whole screen in blocks that many pixels big, for a pixel-art look that matches a 2D game's. They're on the component, not in the file, so the same screen can glow on one entity and not on another. For a single piece, Lust's own shadow (box [shadow, red]) draws a soft glow in its colour.

Drawing it instead of writing it. Double-click a screen's file in the Library to open it on the UI editor's canvas: pick pieces, drag them, size them and change their look, and Solis writes the Lust for you, changing only what it must.

Pictures. image shows a picture from your project, named by its place in the Library: image "sprites/coin.png";. To show one part of a sprite sheet, cut it out with Atlas Crop and add # and the crop's name: image "sprites/tools.png#Axe";. A crop is better than a picture of its own for icons: the artist keeps drawing on one sheet, and every crop follows.

assembly Hotbar {
    view {
        stack [width fill, height fill, bottom, center, pad 24] {
            row [gap 8, background gray9, pad 8, round 8] {
                image "sprites/tools.png#Axe" [width 64];
                image "sprites/tools.png#Hoe" [width 64];
                image "sprites/tools.png#Can" [width 64, opacity 0.4];
            }
        }
    }
}

pass Hotbar;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Hotbar", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Hotbar")
  • A picture is as big as it is unless you give it a width or a height; give one and the other follows, keeping its shape. Give both and it fits inside that box, in the middle; add cover to fill the box instead, cutting off what reaches past it.
  • round rounds its corners, and opacity fades it.
  • Shown bigger than it is, a picture's pixels stay sharp squares, as pixel art wants; shown smaller, it's smoothed so it doesn't flicker.
  • The name can be worked out as the game runs (image item.icon;): that picture is read the first time it's shown.
  • A name written out in the screen's code that names no picture, or no crop of it, is listed in Problems with its line before you press Play. A missing picture shows as a grey box with its name.

What a screen can use: column, row, stack, space, text, button, image, progress bars, and canvas with box, circle and line placed by x and y (anything reaching past the canvas's edges is cut off there, so a needle or a bar can't spill out of its dial). Styles: pad (and padX, padTop…), gap, width and height (a number, or fill), grow, size, bold, nowrap, font (one of the project's fonts, with fallbacks: Text on screens), the alignment words, colour words (white, red5, gray9, #ff8800), background, round, border, opacity and, for pictures, cover. Other pieces are laid out but not drawn yet.

Settings#

The Screen component:

SettingWhat it does
ScreenWhich screen: a file in the Library's ui folder, by its name (ui/hud.lst is Hud).
ShownWhether it's on screen. Game code shows and hides screens with showScreen and hideScreen.
OrderWhich screen is on top when several are shown: higher is on top.
GlowA soft light round everything on the screen, in each piece's own colour, this many pixels out (on its design size). 0 for none.
OutlineA line just outside everything on the screen, this thick. 0 for none.
Outline colourThe outline's colour.
Pixel sizeDraws the whole screen in blocks this many pixels big (1 is smooth).
Line heightThe room from one line of its text to the next, as a share of the font's own (100%). See Text on screens.
Letter spacingRoom added after every letter of its text, in pixels. See Text on screens.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says "each file in ui/ passes the assembly named after it". Why: Solis finds a screen by its file's name. Fix: the file ui/hud.lst holds assembly Hud { … } and ends with pass Hud;.
  • Problem: the Console says "The screen Hud stopped: … can't be changed here". Why: a screen only reads the game; it tried to change one of the game's objects. Fix: change the game in game code, and let the screen show the result. A screen may change its own fields.
  • Problem: the screen stopped, and the Game panel still shows the last picture. Why: something in its view failed (the Console names the file and line), so its last good picture stays. Fix: fix the line; the screen runs again when the code is saved.
  • Problem: the Console says the screen's view "holds too much text" or "has too many styles". Why: after a view runs, Solis copies its pieces out of your code, and one view may hold 10,000 pieces, 200 thousand styles and 4 MB of text in all (a piece's words, or one style's such as a tip, are cut at 16 KB), so that no screen can slow the game to a crawl or fill the memory. Pieces past the 10,000th are left out; past the other two the view isn't shown, and its last picture stays. Fix: show less at once: a page of a long list rather than all of it, and shorter texts.
  • Problem: the Console says "this entity has no Health, so health() has nothing to give". Why: the entity whose Screen shows the screen has no such component. Fix: put the Screen component on the entity that has it, or add the component.
  • Problem: the Console says "Screens can't read the component Position: entities already have a position()". Why: a reading method is named after its component, and this name is an engine call on entities already. Fix: give the component another name.
  • Problem: game code says there's no file solis/screen.lst. Why: only screens can fetch it: game code reads other entities through its own calls. Fix: fetch it only in files in the ui folder.
  • Problem: clicking a button does nothing in the game. Why: the event goes to the entity the screen is shown for (Ui:entity()), and only its components' on blocks hear it. Fix: put the component that handles it on the entity with the Screen, and check the event's name and values match its on line.
  • Problem: Screen.PauseMenu is "not an option". Why: a screen's name comes from its file, first letter made a capital: ui/pauseMenu.lst is PauseMenu. Names in all capitals (HUD) can't be Lust names. Fix: rename the file, or use the name the Problems panel suggests.
  • Problem: the Console says a screen "sent events the game couldn't take". Why: at most 64 events wait for each tick, and an event from a screen carries plain values (no assets, texts of at most 4,096 letters). Fix: send fewer, smaller events.
  • Problem: Problems says "there's no picture sprites/x.png in the project". Why: image names a picture by its place in the Library, with / between folders and its ending (.png). Fix: check the path in the Library: right-click the picture to see where it is.
  • Problem: Problems says a picture "has no crop called Axe". Why: the part after # is the name of a crop made in Atlas Crop, and capitals don't matter but spelling does. Fix: open the picture's Atlas Crop tab and name a crop that, or use one of the names Problems lists.
  • Problem: a picture "can't be shown on a screen: there's no room left". Why: all the screens' pictures share one sheet of 2048 × 2048 pixels on the graphics card. Fix: use smaller pictures, or crops of one sprite sheet instead of whole big pictures.
  • Problem: the Console says "a screen can't change the player's settings". Why: screens only read the game, settings included. Fix: have the button send an event, and call Screens:setTextSize in the entity's code.
  • Problem: with a big text size, words reach past a box. Why: a piece with a set width or height stays that size, so its text has no room to grow. Fix: leave the size out (it then fits what's in it), or use minWidth; or let it end in "…" (Text on screens); check on the canvas with Text 150% and 200%.
  • Problem: text is dark and hard to read over the game. Why: like Lust's windows, text is dark unless told otherwise. Fix: give it a colour word: white.

Related#

  • Text on screens: wrapping, alignment, "…", the project's own fonts and fallbacks.
  • Game code: game-wide objects, which screens read.
  • Play mode: the Game panel, where screens are drawn, and recordings.
  • The UI sample: a HUD and a pause menu with the player's settings, start to finish.
  • Concepts: game UI, screen.
