Text on screens: wrapping, alignment, fonts and fallback#

Words on a game screen wrap inside their box, are shaped as their font says, line up left, in the middle or right, can be cut short with "…", and can be in your project's own fonts, with fallbacks for letters a font doesn't have.

When to use it#

Every text and button on a screen is laid out this way, with nothing to switch on: a long line of dialogue or an item's description wraps to fit its box by itself. Read this page when you want more than the standard look:

  • Your own font, such as a pixel font for a pixel-art game or a handwritten one for a diary. Any TrueType (.ttf) or OpenType (.otf) file whose licence lets you ship it in a game will do.
  • Other writing systems. Latin, Greek and Cyrillic letters work with the game's own font, Inter. For Chinese, Japanese or Korean, add a font that has those letters (Noto Sans JP, say) as a fallback.
  • Names that might be too long for their box (an item's name in a slot): cut them with "…" rather than letting them spill out.
  • Spacing: wide titles with room between the letters, or lines further apart.

The editor's own menus and panels aren't game screens: their text isn't changed by anything here.

How to use it#

Wrapping. A text wraps when it's wider than the room it's given: put it in a column with a width (or anywhere narrower than it), and its words move onto new lines where Unicode's line-break rules allow: between words, after a hyphen or a slash, between Chinese or Japanese letters. A word too long for a line on its own (a very long name) breaks between its letters. \n in the text always starts a new line, and nowrap keeps a text on one line.

assembly Quest {
    view [width 1920, height 1080] {
        column [width 600, pad 24, gap 8, background "#1e2228", round 8] {
            text "The old well" [size 32, bold, white];
            text "Someone has been dropping coins into the old well at night. Find out who, and why they look so worried." [white];
        }
    }
}

pass Quest;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows it through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Quest", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Quest")

Alignment. left (the standard), center and right on a text place each of its lines: a wrapped paragraph in the middle has every line in the middle, not just the first.

Cutting with "…". A text asks to be cut by having its own size limited:

  • a wrapping text with a height or maxHeight shows the lines that fit, and its last line ends in "…": text item.description [maxHeight 60];
  • a nowrap text with a width or maxWidth is cut on its one line: text item.name [nowrap, maxWidth 180];

A text without those keeps all its words, spilling past its box if it must, so nothing you write is hidden without you asking.

Your project's own fonts.

  1. Put the font file in the Library, in a folder such as fonts. It's listed as a Font, with its own icon.
  2. Name it in the screen with font and its place in the Library: text "Inventory" [font "fonts/Pixel.ttf", size 24];. On the view's own [ ] it's the font of every piece that doesn't name one: view [width 1920, height 1080, font "fonts/Pixel.ttf"] { … }.
  3. Press Play, or look at the screen on the UI editor's canvas: the font is read on its own, without the editor waiting, and the screen is drawn in it.

A font file is one weight: bold doesn't make a font of your own bold (it still makes the game's Inter bold). Use the bold file of your font instead.

Fallback fonts. List more fonts in the same font, between commas, first choice first:

assembly Dialogue {
    view [width 1920, height 1080, font "fonts/Lora.ttf, fonts/NotoSansJP.otf"] {
        column [width 900, pad 24] {
            text "Merchant: いらっしゃいませ! Welcome!" [size 28, white];
        }
    }
}

pass Dialogue;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows it through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Dialogue", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Dialogue")

Each letter comes from the first font in the list that has it: here the English from Lora, the Japanese from Noto Sans JP, which Lora lacks. After the list comes the game's Inter, so a letter none of your fonts has is still drawn if Inter has it; a letter no font has shows as the first font's empty box. Spaces, and accents written as a letter of their own, stay with the letter before them.

A font with Chinese, Japanese or Korean letters is big (often 5 to 20 MB). Only the fonts a screen names are read, so list one only on the screens that need it. A font may be at most 32 MB, and screens can use at most 32 of a project's fonts.

In game code, a field can hold one of the project's fonts, as it can a sound or a picture: its type is Font, and Properties offers a list of the project's fonts to pick from, which follows a font file you rename. The fonts are Font.Fonts.Lora for fonts/Lora.ttf (see Game code).

-- sign.lst: a sign whose words and font are picked in Properties.
fetch "solis/project":[Font];

component Sign {
    has {
        Font font = Font.None;
        string words = "Welcome";
    }
}

pass Sign;
end
use reflect::{ComponentSchema, FieldInfo, FieldKind, Hint, NameKind, Offer, Value};

// A Rust component's field picks one of the project's fonts with an offer
// of Font names; it holds the font's name ("Fonts.Lora"). (Its update,
// values, set and RustKind are as in Game code, so they're left out.)
pub fn sign_schema(fonts: Vec<String>) -> ComponentSchema {
    let font = FieldInfo::new("font", "Font", FieldKind::Choice(fonts), Value::Text("None".into()))
        .hint(Hint {
            offers: Offer::Names(NameKind::Font),
            ..Hint::default()
        });
    ComponentSchema {
        name: "Sign".into(),
        help: "A sign whose words and font are picked in Properties.".into(),
        fields: vec![font],
    }
}
-- sign.lua: a field whose kind is Font picks one of the project's fonts.
local Sign = component("Sign", {
    { "font", "Font", "None" },
    { "words", "string", "Welcome" },
})

Settings#

The Screen component's two settings for its text:

SettingWhat it does
Line heightThe room from one line to the next, as a share of the font's own (100%). 120 to 150% makes long paragraphs easier to read; under 100% packs a list tighter. 50 to 300%.
Letter spacingRoom added after every letter, in pixels of the screen's design size. 2 to 4 suits titles in capitals; a little less than 0 tightens a label. −10 to 50.

The player's text size (Game screens) still grows every text, and wrapping makes room for it.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says "there's no font fonts/Lora.ttf in the project". Why: font names a font by its place in the Library, with / between folders and its ending. Fix: check the path in the Library; capitals don't matter.
  • Problem: Problems says a font "isn't a font" or "can't be used: it isn't a TrueType or OpenType font Solis can read". Why: the file is something else with a font's ending, or damaged. WOFF and WOFF2 web fonts aren't read. Fix: use the .ttf or .otf file from the font's download.
  • Problem: some letters show as empty boxes. Why: none of the fonts listed has them, and neither does Inter. Fix: add a font that has them to the end of the font list.
  • Problem: a line of Arabic or Hebrew reads backwards. Why: right-to-left writing isn't laid out yet; it comes in a later milestone. Fix: for now, keep screens in left-to-right writing systems.
  • Problem: a long name spills out of its slot. Why: text is only cut when it asks to be. Fix: give it nowrap and a maxWidth (or a maxHeight for wrapped text).
  • Problem: a font named on the view isn't used by one piece. Why: a piece that names its own font uses that instead (only that list, then Inter). Fix: list the view's font after the piece's own, between commas.
  • Problem: Lust's own window (lust run) shows a screen with a list of fonts in Inter. Why: Lust's windows take one font file, and read the list as a file they can't find. Fix: nothing to do: the game draws it right. Lust is asked for lists of fonts.

Related#

  • Game screens: writing screens, and the Screen component.
  • The UI editor: the canvas draws text as the game does.
  • Concepts: shaping, line breaking, fallback font.

The UI editor: drawing a screen on the canvas#

Opens a screen on a canvas, so you can pick its pieces, move them, size them and change how they look, while Solis rewrites its Lust file for you.

When to use it#

A screen (a HUD, a pause menu) is a Lust file in your project's ui/ folder. You can always write it by hand, but placing and styling pieces is quicker when you can see them: drag a button above another, stretch a panel, try another colour, and see each change at once.

The canvas never takes your file away from you. It changes only the letters it has to (the gap 14 becomes gap 20, and nothing else moves), so comments, spacing and code you wrote by hand stay exactly as they were. You can keep the file open in a code editor beside Solis: a change saved there shows on the canvas within a second.

How to use it#

  1. In the Library, open the ui folder and double-click a screen's file (pauseMenu). Solis switches to the UI tab and draws the screen on the Canvas.
  2. Pick a piece: click it on the canvas, or its row in Elements, the left slot beside the canvas. Shift-click (Ctrl-click in Elements) picks more; drag a box round pieces on an empty part of the canvas to pick everything inside it.
  3. Change it in Properties, the right slot: its words, its width and height, how what's inside it lines up, its padding, colour, corners and opacity. Every change is saved straight away, and Ctrl+Z over the canvas undoes it.
  4. Move it: drag it on the canvas to another place among its neighbours, or into another column or row; a blue line shows where it will land. A piece inside a canvas goes exactly where you drag it instead: an outline follows the pointer, and the piece is moved there when you let go (one Ctrl+Z puts it back). In Elements, drag its row above or below another row, or onto the middle of a column's row to put it inside.
  5. Size it: pick one piece and drag the small square on its right edge, bottom edge or corner.
  6. Check the screen on other screen sizes with the size list in the UI tab's ribbon (Full HD, 4K, ultrawide, a phone), and with players' bigger text with its Text list (150% and 200%). The dashed line is the safe area: keep text and buttons inside it, since some TVs cut the edges off.
  7. Open as code (the ribbon's Code group) opens the file in your code editor, for anything the canvas doesn't edit.
  8. Close the screen: the × on the Canvas tab closes it. Nothing is lost: every change was saved as you made it. Double-click the file in the Library to open it again.

Drawing new pieces#

The toolbox down the canvas's left edge holds the tools: Select (picking and moving, as above), Box, Ellipse, Line, Pen, Text, Image and Button. Keys 1 to 7 pick them while the pointer is over the canvas, and E opens them all in a ring at the pointer, so your hand never leaves the canvas. The hint along the canvas's foot names these keys.

  • Box, Ellipse, Line: drag where it goes. Inside a canvas piece the shape is placed where you drew it (its x and y); anywhere else it gets a small canvas of its own, just big enough, among the pieces where you started the drag. (Shapes only exist inside a canvas in Lust, so a lone box is a canvas holding one.)
  • Pen: click each corner, then press Enter or double-click to finish. Each corner-to-corner part becomes a line. Curves wait for Lust to have paths.
  • Text, Button: click where it goes. In a column or a row it goes between the pieces where you click (a blue line shows where), so the column stays tidy.
  • Image: choose the picture in the Pictures tab of the bottom panel first (a click there takes the Image tool too), then click.

The new piece is picked at once, so Properties is ready to change it. Esc goes back to Select (or, with the Pen, forgets the corners so far).

Tying a piece to the game#

A screen is only useful when it shows the game: the player's health, the coins. Under Tied to the game in Properties, Tie to… lists the components of the entity the screen is shown for (its own Lust components, and Solis's own such as Transform), and the fields that fit:

  • Words (text and buttons): shows the field as words, health.hp.text().
  • Value (progress bars and sliders): progress health.hp.
  • Fill across, Fill up (anything with a set width or height): a bar that's as wide as it is now when the field is at its most. Pick the field, then what it is out of: another field holding the most, or its starting value (health starts full): width 300 * health.hp / health.maxHp, or / 20.
  • Opacity: fades it with a number field.

Solis writes the Lust for you: it reads the component once at the top of the view (Health health = Ui:entity():health();) and fetches it from its file, then uses it. It's ordinary Lust, so you can change it as code later.

Preview values (top of the canvas) lets you try other numbers for what the screen reads, with a slider each: drag health down to see the bar empty. They're never saved; Back to the starting values forgets them.

What a button does#

A button's When clicked in Properties has a Sends list: the events your game's code declares (event Pause();). Pick one and the button sends it to the screen's entity (Solis fetches it at the top of the screen's file for you), whose code reacts with on Pause() { … }. This is the safe way for a screen to change the game: screens never change it themselves (why). A button whose { } does more than send one event shows its code instead.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
WordsThe text on a text or a button. Text worked out by code ("Score " + score.text()) shows as code and is changed in the file.
Width, Heightset a size in the screen's pixels (on a 1920 × 1080 design), fill the room it has, or auto: as big as what's in it.
AlignWhere what's inside it sits: a 3 × 3 grid, from top left to bottom right. On a column or a row this places its pieces; on text, the words.
PaddingRoom inside its edge, all round.
GapRoom between the pieces inside a column or a row.
X, YWhere a piece sits inside a canvas. Dragging it on the canvas changes these, by as many of the screen's pixels as you dragged it, whatever the zoom.
ColourA button's or shape's colour, text's colour, or a column's background, from Lust's colour words (blue, gray9, red5).
CornersHow round its corners are, in pixels.
Opacity1 is solid, 0 is invisible.
Text size, BoldFor text and buttons.
HoverA look while the pointer is over it. + Add a hover look dims it a little; edit it in All its settings.
DisabledGreyed, and clicks do nothing.
Tie to…Shows a field of one of the entity's components in this piece: its words, its value, how full it is, or its opacity.
SendsFor a button: the event sent to the screen's entity when it's clicked, from the game's events.
When clickedWhat a button does, as written in its { }, when it's more than one event: change it as code.
Preview valuesOther numbers to try on the canvas for what the screen reads. Never saved.
All its settingsEverything in the piece's [ ], as written. Type anything Lust has (nowrap, spread, minWidth 200); press Enter to keep it. If it doesn't read, it isn't changed.
Text 100% / 150% / 200%Previews the screen with players' bigger text (Screens:setTextSize), to check nothing spills out.
Safe areaShows the guide 5% in from each edge.
SnapSizes snap to whole pixels and to other pieces' edges.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Select, Box, Ellipse, Line, Pen, Text, Image1 to 7 (pointer over the canvas)
All the tools in a ring at the pointerE
Back to Select (Pen: forget the corners)Esc
Finish the Pen's lineEnter or double-click
Pick more (canvas)Shift+click
Pick more (Elements)Shift+click or Ctrl+click
Delete what's pickedDelete (over the canvas or Elements), or Backspace (over the canvas)
Copy what's picked, just after itselfCtrl+D
Pick nothingEsc, or click an empty part of the canvas
Undo, redoCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y (over the canvas or Elements)
ZoomMouse wheel
Move the viewMiddle mouse button drag
Fit the canvasDouble-click an empty part, or click the zoom button

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a piece has a yellow code badge and can't be picked. Why: code made it: a loop or an is …? then in the view. The canvas draws it from the screen's starting values, but its letters are code. Fix: Open as code and change it there.
  • Problem: the canvas says it "can't follow" the file. Why: the file has a mistake the canvas can't read past, such as a [ never closed. Fix: Problems says where; fix it as code, and the canvas follows again.
  • Problem: "Updating…" shows after a piece was moved, added or deleted. Why: the canvas waits for the game's code to be checked again, which takes a moment. Fix: nothing: it goes in about a second.
  • Problem: a bar or a number shows as empty. Why: the canvas draws the screen for an entity whose values are all their starting ones (health 0, say). Fix: try other numbers with Preview values, or press Play to see it with the game's real values in the Game panel.
  • Problem: Tie to… says to give the entity a component. Why: the game's code has no components a screen can read yet, or has a mistake. Fix: write a component (component Health { has { float hp = 20; } }), check Problems is empty, and try again.
  • Problem: Sends has nothing to pick. Why: the game's code declares no events yet, so there's nothing a button could send. Fix: declare one in your game code (event Pause();, and pass it), and check Problems is empty.
  • Problem: the canvas says The screen's view stopped: … in place of the screen. Why: the screen's own code stopped with an error as its view ran (the message says what and where), so there's nothing to draw. The canvas tries a screen once each time the game's code changes, not over and over. Fix: put the line right as code and save: the canvas draws the screen again by itself.
  • Problem: dragging a piece doesn't move it where expected. Why: in a column or a row, pieces go one after another: a piece moves between its neighbours, not to any spot. Fix: to place pieces freely, put them in a canvas and drag them there.

Related#

  • Game screens: what a screen's Lust file holds, and how the game shows it.
  • Atlas Crop: pictures cut from a sheet, for image pieces.
  • Concepts: screen, canvas, tie.

The UI sample: a HUD and a pause menu, start to finish#

A small game whose screens show everything game UI can do: a HUD that follows the game, a health bar, and a pause menu offering the player's settings, each drawn on the UI editor's canvas.

When to use it#

Open it when you're about to give your own game a HUD or a menu: it's the shortest working example of each part, and every file is meant to be read and changed. The turret sample is the place to start for game code itself; this one is about screens.

How to use it#

  1. On the launcher's Learn, click Make it in a folder… under UI sample and choose an empty folder (or start a New project from UI sample). The project opens on its level.
  2. Press Play, then click the Game panel so the game has the keys.
    • Space (or a gamepad's A) fires the turret at the drone. The HUD in the bottom left counts the ammo and the hits, with a yellow bar that empties as you fire; the drone's health bar at the top follows its health.
    • P (or Start) pauses: the game stops and the pause menu shows. Move with the arrow keys or the stick, choose with Space, Enter or A, or click.
  3. Try the menu:
    • Text size makes every screen's text a quarter bigger each time (back to 100% after 200%). The menu's buttons grow to fit it (they're at least 360 wide, minWidth 360, rather than exactly).
    • Fullscreen and Resolution say in the Console what the exported game would do; in the editor the game stays in the Game panel.
    • Resume carries on, and Quit closes the game (Window:quit()): while you play in the editor, play stops; in an exported game, the game closes.
  4. Press Stop, open the Library's ui folder and double-click hud: it opens on the canvas. Pick a piece and change it in Properties, or try Preview values to see the ammo bar empty.

How its parts fit together:

FileWhat it does
main.lstThe game code: the Turret (fires on Jump, reloads), the drone's Health, and the Pauser, which opens the menu and changes the player's settings when the menu's buttons say so.
ui/hud.lstThe HUD, shown by the Turret's Screen component. It reads the turret's ammo and hits (Ui:entity():turret()); the bar is a box whose width is 300 * ammo / maxAmmo, and while the turret reloads it stays empty, with shadow for a glow. The Screen component's Glow gives the whole HUD a soft light.
ui/droneHealth.lstThe drone's health bar, shown by the Drone's Screen component, reading its Health.
ui/pauseMenu.lstThe menu. It reads the settings (Screens:textSize(), Window:fullscreen(), Window:resolution()) to show them, and each button sends an event to the Game entity (send BiggerText() to Ui:entity();), since screens never change the game themselves.
ui.sollevelThe level: the camera, the turret, the drone and the Game entity with the Pauser.

Why the buttons send events instead of changing the settings themselves: a screen only reads the game. That keeps every change in game code, where recordings and replays see it, so the sample plays back the same from a recording, menu and all.

Settings#

The sample has no settings of its own. The Screen components on the Turret and the Drone have the screen's look (Game screens): try Pixel size 4 on the Turret's for a pixel-art HUD.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
FireSpace, or the gamepad's A
Pause, and backP or Start (Backspace or B too)
Move in the menu, chooseArrow keys or the stick; Space, Enter or A
Switch fullscreenAlt+Enter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing Space does nothing. Why: the editor still has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel first; Esc gives the keys back.
  • Problem: Fullscreen doesn't fill the screen. Why: while playing in the editor, the game stays in the Game panel. Fix: it's the exported game that changes its window; the Console says what it would do.
  • Problem: after a big text size, the HUD's words reach past its panel. Why: a piece given a fixed width keeps it. Fix: leave sizes out where text grows, and check with Text 150% and 200% on the canvas.

Related#

  • Game screens: what a screen's file holds, the player's settings, and screens' looks.
  • The UI editor: drawing and changing screens on the canvas.
  • Your first game: the turret sample, for game code in all three languages.
  • Concepts: screen, tie, player setting, focus.

2D: the pixel-perfect view#

Make a 2D game whose pixel art stays crisp: the game is drawn small, at its own resolution, and scaled up to the screen in whole steps, and the editor's 2D view shows the world in pixels.

When to use it#

For a 2D game, especially one in pixel art: a farming game, a platformer, a top-down adventure. Pixel art is drawn one pixel at a time, and it only looks right when every one of its pixels becomes the same number of screen pixels. Draw it straight at the screen's size and pixels end up different widths, edges blur when the camera moves by less than a pixel, and sprites shimmer as you walk. Solis avoids all three by drawing the game small, at its base resolution, then scaling the finished picture up.

2D in Solis lives in the same world as 3D: flat things lie on the ground, seen from straight above, so lights, the sun, sound, saving and game code all work on them as they do in 3D. A project can mix both, with a 3D camera in one level and a 2D camera in another.

This page covers the groundwork: setting a project up for 2D, looking at it in pixels and playing it through a 2D camera. What you put in that world has pages of its own: sprites from Aseprite, animating them, tile maps for the ground, and walls and walking.

How to use it#

  1. Set the project's 2D settings: File › Project settings › 2D. The standard ones suit most pixel-art games: 480 × 270, 16 pixels to a metre and 16-pixel tiles. They're saved in the project (pixels.solpix), so everyone working on it shares them.
  2. Look in pixels: in the viewport, the Perspective ▾ pill at the top left, then 2D. The view looks straight down at the ground. The grid is the tile size, and the corner shows the zoom. Beside the pointer, a small readout says where it is in the game's pixels (x 192 · y 64 px, with y counting down the picture as in pixel-art programs) and, with a tile map selected, the cell under it (cell 12, 4), so you can place things exactly without counting grid lines.
    • Hold the right or middle button and drag to slide the view.
    • Turn the wheel to zoom in or out one whole step at a time (100%, 200%, 300%…), towards the pointer. At whole steps every pixel of your game is the same size on screen, so nothing blurs.
  3. Add a 2D camera: with the 2D view in use, Home › Camera. It goes over the middle of the view, on a whole pixel, as a 2D camera. A dashed frame shows what it sees, labelled Game screen for the camera the game looks through (the first camera in the level). To turn an existing camera into one, set its View to 2D in Properties.
  4. Move things on whole pixels: in the 2D view, moves land on whole pixels of your game by themselves, so nothing rests between two pixels and looks smeared. Snap ▾ in the bottom-right corner changes that to whole tiles, or off. Hold Ctrl while dragging to flip it for one move.
  5. Press Play. The Game panel draws the game at its base resolution and scales it up to fill the panel in whole steps, with black bars round the edge if the panel doesn't divide evenly. Move the 2D camera (game code moves it like any entity) and the picture slides smoothly, without shimmering.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Base resolutionThe size the game is drawn at, in pixels, before it's scaled up. 480 × 270 scales to a 1080p screen four times and to 4K eight times exactly; 320 × 180 gives chunkier pixels and shows less of the world; 640 × 360 shows more. The menu offers common sizes, or type your own.
Pixels per unitHow many pixels make one metre of the world. Usually the same as the tile size, so a tile is one metre: physics, sound distances and game code then all count in tiles.
Tile sizeThe 2D view's grid, in pixels, and the size of each cell of a tile map.
Scaling to the screenWhole steps (the standard): every pixel becomes the same whole number of screen pixels, with bars at the edges when the screen doesn't divide evenly: always crisp. Fill the screen: no bars; it scales up as far as whole steps go, then smooths only the last bit at each pixel's edge, so edges stay sharp.
Camera > ViewPerspective (as the eye sees) or 2D (flat, straight down, at the base resolution). A 2D camera follows its entity's place but never turns.
2D view > SnapWhat moves land on: whole pixels, tiles or off.
2D view > ZoomScreen pixels for each pixel of the game, from 25% (to see a big map) to 2400%.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Slide the 2D viewHold right or middle mouse, drag
Zoom the 2D view a stepMouse wheel
Flip snapping for one moveHold Ctrl while dragging

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: black bars round the game. Why: the panel or screen isn't a whole number of times the base resolution, and Whole steps keeps every pixel the same size. Fix: that's expected; choose Fill the screen if you'd rather have no bars, or a base resolution that divides your screen (480 × 270 for 1080p and 4K).
  • Problem: the Game panel looks blurry or the pixels are uneven. Why: the level's first camera is a 3D one. Fix: set its View to 2D, or move the 2D camera first in the Level panel.
  • Problem: something isn't in the game's picture though it's under the camera. Why: a 2D camera sees what's below it, between its Near and Far. Fix: keep the camera above everything (Add camera puts it 100 m up), or raise its Far.
  • The 2D view's frame and the Game panel show the same thing, so you can line up a scene in the editor and know what the player will see.

Related#

  • Settings: Preferences, and Project settings with its 2D tab.
  • Moving around the viewport: the other views.
  • Play mode: cameras and the Game panel.
  • Concepts: base resolution, pixels per unit, pixel-perfect, whole steps.

Sprites from Aseprite#

Draw your pixel art in Aseprite, save it into the project, and place it in the world as sprites: Solis reads the file as it is, packs its frames, and shows every save at once.

When to use it#

For the characters, crops, trees, furniture and anything else in a 2D game that's a picture rather than a tile of the ground. A sprite is one frame of a sprite sheet, lying flat on the ground at its entity, standing on its pivot.

Solis reads Aseprite's own .aseprite files: there's nothing to export. Its tags (runs of frames such as walk or swing) and slices (named rectangles such as feet) come with it, so the picture and how it's used stay in one file. Keep the files in the project's folder, as you'd keep models and sounds.

Plain pictures work too. A .png or .jpg in the project can be a sprite as it is: drag it from the Library into the viewport, or pick it in a Sprite's Sheet (it's listed as name (picture)). It's a sheet of one frame, the whole picture, standing on its bottom middle. That's handy for a background, a hill or a sign drawn in any paint program; for frames, tags and a feet slice, use Aseprite. A picture is read only once a sprite uses it (so the textures of 3D models aren't read twice), and up to 4096 × 4096 pixels. Saving it again in your paint program updates it in Solis.

Sprites are drawn with the colours you painted, never tone mapped. Whether light falls on them is the level's choice: with Light sprites ticked on its Environment (new levels have it ticked), the day's colour and lamps light them (Sky, fog and exposure). With no lamps and day and night off, a sprite looks exactly as drawn.

For the ground itself, use tile maps. To make sprites move, see Animating sprites: a sprite plays its sheet's tags as clips.

How to use it#

  1. Save your Aseprite file into the project's folder, for example in a sprites folder of your own: sprites/farmer.aseprite. It appears in the Library with its first frame and how many frames it has. Saving it again in Aseprite updates it in Solis straight away.
  2. Look it over: click it in the Library. Properties shows the frame big, a strip of every frame (click one to see it), and what Solis read from the file: its size, layers, tags (with their direction and repeats), slices and palette. Anything it couldn't use is listed in yellow.
  3. Give it a pivot: in Aseprite, draw a slice called feet (or pivot) round where the character stands, and set the slice's pivot point on the ground between its feet. Without one, a sprite stands on the bottom middle of its frame.
  4. Place it: drag it from the Library into the viewport, double-click it, or right-click it and choose Place. It lands under the pointer (or in the middle of the view) on a whole pixel, standing on its feet or pivot slice, as drawn. The new entity is named after the file and has a Sprite component.
  5. Choose the frame and the rest in Properties: the Sprite component's Sheet offers every sprite sheet in the project, Pivot offers the sheet's slices, and Frame picks which frame it shows.
  6. Front and behind look after themselves: the lower on the screen a sprite stands, the nearer it's drawn, so a farmer walking down past a tree goes in front of it, and walking up goes behind it. Things a whole metre higher (a roof, a bird) are always on top.

Settings#

The Sprite component, in Properties:

SettingWhat it does
SheetThe sprite sheet (an Aseprite file in the project). Empty draws nothing.
Clip, Playing, Speed, Clip timeThe clip it plays, and how: see Animating sprites.
FrameWhich frame it shows when no clip plays, counting from 1 as Aseprite does. A frame past the end shows the first.
PivotThe slice it stands on, such as feet: the slice's pivot point (or its middle, if it has none) sits on the entity's place. Empty: the bottom middle of the frame.
Flip acrossMirrored left to right, round its pivot: one drawing faces both ways.
Flip upMirrored top to bottom.
TintMultiplied into its colours. White leaves it as drawn; a blue tint for night, red for a hurt enemy.
FlashHow white it flashes, 0 to 1. Turn it up for a moment when something's hit.
OutlineA one-pixel outline round it, to show what's selected or can be picked up.
Outline colourThe outline's colour.
See-throughFor glass, smoke, ghosts and shadows painted half see-through. Otherwise each pixel is drawn or not (half see-through pixels are treated as clear), which needs no sorting and is faster.

What Solis takes from the Aseprite file:

In AsepriteIn Solis
Frames and their durationsThe frames, and how long each shows in a clip.
TagsClips: a run of frames with its direction (forward, reverse, ping-pong) and repeats.
SlicesPivots (where a sprite stands), and later 9-slices, hitboxes and attach points.
User data on a celAn event on that frame, such as footstep: it plays the sound event of that name and tells game code (Animating sprites).
Visible layersFlattened into one picture, with each layer's and cel's opacity. Hidden layers and reference layers are left out. Blend modes other than Normal are drawn as Normal (Properties notes it).
PaletteListed in Properties.

Shortcuts#

Sprites add no keys or mouse actions of their own: placing them uses the Library's, and moving them uses the usual move tools.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a sprite looks slightly smeared, or Problems says it rests between pixels. Why: it was moved or typed in at a place that isn't a whole pixel (perhaps with snapping off, or by game code). The game draws it on the nearest pixel, so it may seem to jump a pixel as it moves. Fix: move it with snapping to pixels on (the 2D view's standard), or type a place that's a whole number of pixels (with 16 pixels a metre, a multiple of 0.0625).
  • Problem: the sprite floats above or sinks below where you put it. Why: it stands on its pivot, and the sheet has none, or the slice's pivot point isn't where the feet are. Fix: add a feet slice in Aseprite with its pivot between the feet, then pick it in Pivot.
  • Problem: Properties says the file couldn't be read. Why: it isn't an Aseprite file, it's damaged, or it's bigger than Solis takes (64 MB, 4096 × 4096 pixels, 2048 frames, 256 layers). Fix: save it again from Aseprite. While you're saving, a half-written file keeps the last good picture, so sprites never vanish.
  • Problem: a picture you dragged into the viewport didn't appear, and the Console says Couldn't place the picture as a sprite. Why: it's damaged, isn't really a PNG or JPEG, or is bigger than 4096 × 4096 pixels. Fix: save it again from your paint program, smaller if need be.
  • Problem: Properties says the frames don't fit in a 4096 × 4096 picture. Why: all the frames of one file, packed together, must fit in a 4096 × 4096 atlas. Fix: split the file into several (one per character, say).
  • Problem: Problems says a Sprite has no sprite sheet, or that its sheet isn't in the project. Why: the Sheet field is empty, or the file was deleted or never committed. Fix: choose a sheet in Sheet, or bring the file back.
  • Tip: identical frames (a held pose repeated to last longer) are packed once, so long animations cost little.

Related#

  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: base resolution, the 2D view, snapping to pixels.
  • Projects and the Library: where asset files live.
  • Entities and components.
  • Concepts: sprite, sprite sheet, tag, slice, pivot, atlas.
← Previous · Chapter 392D: the pixel-perfect viewNext → · Chapter 41Animating sprites

Animating sprites#

Make sprites walk, swing and wave: play the clips you tagged in Aseprite, make clips of your own in Solis, and give frames events that play footsteps and tell your game code.

When to use it#

For anything in a 2D game that moves frame by frame: a farmer walking, a hoe swinging, crops swaying, a door opening. A clip is a run of a sprite sheet's frames, each shown for its own time, played forward, backward or there and back (ping-pong), over and over or a number of times.

The quickest way is Aseprite's own: tag runs of frames there (walk, idle, hoe) and every tag is a clip in Solis, with Aseprite's frame times. To change a clip's speed, give frames events (a footstep on the frame a foot lands), or make clips Aseprite doesn't have, Solis keeps a small clips file (.solframes) beside the Aseprite file. A sprite can play either.

To choose clips by what's happening (walking when moving, idle when not, facing the right way), use an animator.

How to use it#

  1. Tag your frames in Aseprite and save. In Solis, click the file in the Library: Properties lists its tags.

  2. Play a clip on a sprite: select a sprite and pick a Clip in its Sprite component. Press Play: it plays at its frame times. To see it move while you edit, open the viewport's ≡ menu and tick Preview animation.

  3. Open the clips: in the Aseprite file's Properties, press Edit clips…. Solis makes walker.solframes beside walker.aseprite (or opens the one there) and opens two tabs:

    • Frames, the timeline: a tab of the bottom panel on the Animate tab (the clips file opens there; an × after the Frames or Clip tab closes the file). In the left slot, Clips: every clip, with how long it is and where it comes from (Aseprite or made here). Click one to choose it. Beside them, the chosen clip's frames in order along a time ruler, each as wide as it lasts, so you see its timing at a glance. A ping-pong's way back is shown faded after them. The line in the accent colour is where it's playing; the lane below shows its events.
    • Clip, the next tab of the bottom panel: the chosen clip's Speed, Direction, how many times it Plays, and Plays first. A clip's settings have a tab of their own so the frames keep the panel's whole width.

    While a clips file is open, Animate's ribbon is the clips file's: Clip (New, Copy, Delete), Frames (Take out), and how the clip plays (Plays, Speed, and a Direction list for a clip of your own). The design's cutscene controls after them (Keys, Step, Linear, Smooth, Tracks) are unfinished parts.

  4. Watch it: press ▶ (or Space over the Frames tab). ⏮ goes back to the start, ■ stops, ⏭ goes to the last frame. − and + zoom the ruler.

  5. Give a frame an event: click the frame, then type a name in event, or pick a sound event from ◆ ▾. When the clip reaches that frame:

    • a sound event of the same name (footstep, or its path, sfx/footstep) plays on the sprite by itself, with no code;
    • game code on the entity hears CueReached, with the event as one of the project's names (Cue.Footstep). Events typed in Aseprite (a cel's user data) work the same way.

  6. Make a clip of your own: the ribbon's New makes an empty one; Copy copies the chosen clip (a tag's copy can then be changed here). In the Frames tab, ＋ Add frames ▾ shows the sheet's frames: click one to add it after the picked frame. Double-click a clip of your own to rename it.

  7. Change frames of your own clips: click a frame to pick it (Ctrl+click or Shift+click for several), then set its time, drag it to a new place, or press Delete to take it out.

  8. Close the file: the × on either tab closes both.

Every change is saved at once and shows at once on every sprite playing the file. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y over either tab undo and redo changes to the file. If the file changes on disk (edited by hand, or by Git), the tabs show it as it is now, as a step Ctrl+Z undoes; if it's deleted or moved, they close. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

In game code#

Clips and their events are names Lust checks. Solis writes them into solis/project.lst whenever the sheets change: each clip as state Clip, under its sheet's path (sprites/farmer.aseprite's walk is Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk), and each frame event as state Cue (Cue.Footstep). A misspelt clip is a mistake before the game runs. Bring in the names and the events at the top of a file:

fetch "solis/project":[Clip, Cue];
fetch "solis/animation":[CueReached, ClipFinished];

component Farmer {
    has {
        int steps = 0;
    }

    -- Count the footsteps as they land.
    on CueReached(Cue cue) {
        is cue == Cue.Footstep? then {
            steps = steps + 1;
        }
    }

    -- Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
    on ClipFinished(Clip clip) {
        is clip == Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Hoe? then {
            animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Idle);
        }
    }
}

pass Farmer;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Farmer {
    steps: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Farmer {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        // The engine's events carry the project's names as text.
        let named = match event.values.first() {
            Some(Value::Text(name)) => name.as_str(),
            _ => "",
        };
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // Count the footsteps as they land.
            "CueReached" if named == "Footstep" => self.steps += 1,
            // Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
            "ClipFinished" if named == "Sprites.Farmer.Hoe" => {
                let me = cx.me();
                cx.host().play_clip(me, "idle", false);
            }
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Farmer = component("Farmer", {
    { "steps", "int", 0 },
})

-- Count the footsteps as they land.
function Farmer:on_CueReached(cue)
    if cue == "Footstep" then
        self.steps = self.steps + 1
    end
end

-- Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
function Farmer:on_ClipFinished(clip)
    if clip == "Sprites.Farmer.Hoe" then
        solis.entity.animate(self.me, "Sprites.Farmer.Idle")
    end
end

  • animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk) plays a clip on the component's entity (target:animate(…) on another). If it's already playing that clip, or has finished it, it carries on as it is, so it's safe to call every tick; another clip starts from its beginning.

  • animateFromStart(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Hoe) plays a clip from its beginning, whatever it was doing: a swing each time a button is pressed.

  • stopAnimation() stops it where it is; animate with the same clip carries on from there.

  • setFlip(across, down) mirrors the sprite (its Flip across and Flip up settings): setFlip(true, false) faces it the other way. So you draw a run facing right only once, and one Run clip does both ways, instead of a RunLeft as well:

    fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":[Action, Clip];

component Runner {
    method update(float dt) {
        -- Face the way the player pushes.
        bool walkingLeft = Input:axis(Action.Move).x < 0;
        setFlip(walkingLeft, false);
        animate(Clip.Sprites.Hero.Run);
    }
}

pass Runner;
end
    use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Runner;

impl RustComponent for Runner {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        // Face the way the player pushes.
        let walking_left = cx.host().action("Move").axis.x < 0.0;
        cx.host().set_flip(me, walking_left, false);
        cx.host().play_clip(me, "run", false);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
    local Runner = component("Runner", {})

function Runner:update(dt)
    -- Face the way the player pushes.
    local walkingLeft = solis.Input:axis("Move").x < 0
    solis.entity.setFlip(self.me, walkingLeft, false)
    solis.entity.animate(self.me, "Sprites.Hero.Run")
end

    It's safe to call every tick, and like the other calls it lands at the end of the tick.

  • In Lua: solis.entity.animate(e, "Sprites.Farmer.Walk"), solis.entity.animateFromStart(e, …), solis.entity.stopAnimation(e) and solis.entity.setFlip(e, true, false); a function called on_CueReached(cue) or on_ClipFinished(clip) reacts to the events, with the names as text. In Rust: cx.host().play_clip(entity, "walk", false) (true to start it again), stop_clip and set_flip(entity, true, false), and the events arrive in handle named CueReached and ClipFinished.

A clip's place is part of the game: the same inputs give the same frames every time, and a saved game comes back on the same frame.

Settings#

The Sprite component's clip settings:

SettingWhat it does
SheetAn Aseprite file (its tags are its clips) or a clips file (.solframes).
ClipThe clip it plays. Empty: the clips file's clip marked Plays first, or with none, the still Frame.
PlayingWhether the clip moves on while the game runs. Game code's animate and stopAnimation turn it on and off.
Speed1 as drawn, 2 twice as fast, 0 stopped. Multiplies the clip's own speed.
Clip timeHow far into the clip it is, in seconds. Give a crowd of copies different times so they don't all step in step.
FrameThe frame shown when no clip plays.

A clip's settings in the Clip tab:

SettingWhat it does
SpeedHow fast this clip plays for every sprite, 1 as drawn. A tag's speed is kept in the clips file.
DirectionForward, reverse, ping-pong (there and back) or ping-pong reversed. A tag's is Aseprite's.
PlaysOver and over, once, or a number of times; it then stays on its last frame and game code hears ClipFinished. A tag's is Aseprite's (its Repeat field).
Plays firstThe clip a sprite plays when its Clip is empty.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Rename a clip (your own clips)Double-click it in the Frames tab's list of clips (Enter keeps the name, Esc leaves it)
Pick a frameClick it
Pick several framesCtrl + click, or Shift + click for a run
Move picked frames (your own clips)Drag them
Take picked frames out (your own clips)Delete over the Frames tab
Play or stop the clipSpace over the Frames tab
Undo or redo a change to the clips fileCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y over either tab

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: sprites don't move in the viewport. Why: the editor rests unless something changes. Fix: tick Preview animation in the viewport's ≡ menu, or press Play.
  • Problem: a tag's frames can't be moved, timed or taken out. Why: a tag's frames are Aseprite's, so saving there keeps both in step. Fix: change them in Aseprite, or Copy the clip (on the ribbon) to change the copy here.
  • Problem: an event doesn't play a sound. Why: no sound event has its name. Fix: name it after the sound event (footstep or sfx/footstep), or pick one from ◆ ▾.
  • Problem: a whole field of crops sways in step. Fix: give each a slightly different Clip time.
  • Problem: two footsteps in a ping-pong walk. Why: a ping-pong shows its middle frames twice a pass, there and back. Fix: put the event on the first or last frame, or use Forward for walks.

Related#

  • Sprites from Aseprite: sheets, placing sprites, pivots.
  • Sound events: the sounds an event plays.
  • Game code: components and events.
  • Concepts: clip, clips file, frame event.
← Previous · Chapter 40Sprites from AsepriteNext → · Chapter 42Animators

Animators#

Let Solis choose which clip a sprite plays: idle when standing, walking when moving, a swing when a tool is used, each facing the right way.

When to use it#

A farmer has an idle, a walk and a tool swing, each drawn facing up, right, down and left: twelve clips, and rules for when each plays. You could pick every clip yourself (see Animating sprites), but an animator keeps those rules in one place, drawn as a picture you can read at a glance:

  • States are what the sprite can be doing: Idle, Walk, Use tool. Each plays a clip, or a clip for each direction.
  • Transitions are the arrows between them: Idle goes to Walk when moving is on.
  • Parameters are the values transitions look at: moving (a switch), speed (a number), swing (a trigger) and facing (a direction).

Why a picture rather than code? Because animation rules get tangled fast ("swing, unless already swinging, then go back to walking if still moving…"), and a graph shows every way in and out of each state. The animator also runs inside the game's ticks, so the same inputs always give the same animation, on every computer and in every replay and save.

For one-off sprites (a door, a crop swaying) a plain clip on the Sprite is simpler: no animator needed.

How to use it#

  1. Make one: in the Library, open the folder you want it in, then New › Animator (right-click in the Library, or + New). Solis makes animator.solanim with one state, Idle, and opens it. (Rename the file in the Library, as any other.)
  2. The animator opens on the Animate tab of the tab bar, as a document beside the viewport's (a × on its tab closes it), with its Preview as a group of its own on the right. What you pick in its graph shows in Properties, the right slot; its parameters are in the left slot, Parameters. While it is open, Animate's ribbon is the animator's: State (Add state, Start here, Delete) and Preview (Start again), then the design's cutscene controls as unfinished parts.
  3. Choose its clips: click empty space in the graph. Properties shows the animator: pick Clips from, the sprite sheet (or clips file) whose clips its states play.
  4. Add states: the ribbon's Add state, or right-click empty space › Add state. Click a state to change it in Properties:
    • Name: what it's called.
    • Plays: one clip, or a clip by facing. With a clip by facing, pick a clip for each direction (↑ up, → right, ↓ down, ← left); + Direction adds the next one, up to eight with the diagonals. Solis makes a direction parameter, facing, the first time.
    • Speed, and Speed by: a number parameter its speed is multiplied by, so a walk speeds up as the character does.
    • Start here: the state the animator starts in, marked Start ▶ in the graph.
  5. Add parameters: in the Parameters slot, the + beside Parameters adds a number, a switch, a trigger or a direction. Click a name to rename it; right-click it to Delete it, or Start at this value.
  6. Join states: drag from the edge of one state to another, or right-click a state › Make transition and click the other. Click the arrow, then in Properties + Condition and choose what must hold: a switch is on or is off, a trigger fired, a number > or < a value, or finished (the state's clip has played all its times). All of a transition's conditions must hold for it to be taken. An arrow from Any state can be taken from every state.
  7. Try it: the preview always plays. Set the parameters on the Parameters tab (tick moving, turn the facing dial, press Fire for a trigger) and watch the state glow in the accent colour as it changes, the clip playing below.
  8. Use it: select an entity with a Sprite, then in Properties + Component › Animator and pick the file in Animator. Press Play: the animator chooses the Sprite's clip and speed every tick. Select the entity while it plays to see its state glow, and its parameters' values on the Parameters tab.

Every change is saved at once and runs at once, in a game that's playing too. Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y over the tab undo and redo changes to the animator. If the file changes on disk (edited by hand, or by Git), the tab shows it as it is now, as a step Ctrl + Z undoes. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

In game code#

Each animator gets a Lust file of its own, which Solis writes into solis/animators/ whenever the animator changes: farmer.solanim gives solis/animators/farmer.lst. In it are a state of the graph's states (FarmerState) and a class with a method for each thing code can set or ask (FarmerAnimator). Why a file? Because then every name in the graph is something Lust checks: rename the moving switch, and every line still calling setMoving is a mistake in Problems, instead of a setting that silently does nothing.

A component holds the animator as a field with no starting value. Solis fills it in with the entity's own animator before the component's first update:

fetch "solis/animators/farmer":[FarmerAnimator, FarmerState];
fetch "solis/project":Action;
fetch "solis/input":Input;

component Farmer {
    has {
        FarmerAnimator anim;        -- filled in by Solis
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- How is the farmer moving?
        vec3 velocity = velocity();
        float speed = velocity:length();

        -- Tell the animator.
        anim:setMoving(speed > 0.1);
        anim:setSpeed(speed);
        anim:setFacing(velocity);

        -- The use button swings the hoe.
        is Input:pressed(Action.Interact)? then {
            anim:swing();
        }

        -- Stand still while using a tool.
        is anim:current() == FarmerState.UseTool? then {
            setVelocity([0, 0, 0]);
        }
    }
}

pass Farmer;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{AnimatorValue, Context, RustComponent};

// The animator's file is Lust's. Rust reaches the entity's animator
// through its host, by the graph's own names.
pub struct Farmer;

impl RustComponent for Farmer {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();

        // How is the farmer moving?
        let velocity = cx.host().velocity(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let speed = velocity.length();

        // Tell the animator.
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "moving", AnimatorValue::Switch(speed > 0.1));
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "speed", AnimatorValue::Number(speed));
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "facing", AnimatorValue::Direction(velocity));

        // The use button swings the hoe.
        if cx.host().action("Interact").pressed {
            cx.host().animator_set(me, "swing", AnimatorValue::Fire);
        }

        // Stand still while using a tool.
        if cx.host().animator_state(me).as_deref() == Some("Use tool") {
            cx.host().set_velocity(me, Vec3::ZERO);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The animator's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the entity's animator
-- through solis.Animators, by the graph's own names.
local Farmer = component("Farmer", {})

function Farmer:update(dt)
    -- How is the farmer moving?
    local velocity = solis.entity.velocity(self.me)
    local speed = math.sqrt(velocity.x * velocity.x + velocity.y * velocity.y + velocity.z * velocity.z)

    -- Tell the animator.
    solis.Animators:setSwitch(self.me, "moving", speed > 0.1)
    solis.Animators:setNumber(self.me, "speed", speed)
    solis.Animators:setDirection(self.me, "facing", velocity)

    -- The use button swings the hoe.
    if solis.Input:pressed("Interact") then
        solis.Animators:fire(self.me, "swing")
    end

    -- Stand still while using a tool.
    if solis.Animators:stateOf(self.me) == "Use tool" then
        solis.entity.setVelocity(self.me, vec3(0, 0, 0))
    end
end
A parameter orbecomes
switch movinganim:setMoving(on)
number speedanim:setSpeed(value)
direction facinganim:setFacing(direction) (on the ground: its height is left out)
trigger swinganim:swing()
its states (Idle, Use tool)FarmerState.Idle, FarmerState.UseTool
which state it's inanim:current()
jumping straight to a stateanim:jumpTo(FarmerState.Idle)
how fast it playsanim:setPlaybackSpeed(1.5)

What's set lands at the end of the tick, like a move, and the animator takes it at its next step. current() says the state as the tick started.

  • Names become Lust names: Use tool is UseTool, the file farmer is FarmerAnimator. A name that can't (it starts with a digit, or has a dash), or a parameter whose method would be one the class has already (current, jumpTo, setPlaybackSpeed), is left out, and the Console says which, so you can rename it.
  • The entity needs an Animator component using that file; the field's class says which file.

Settings#

The Animator component:

SettingWhat it does
AnimatorThe animator file (.solanim) it runs.
StateThe state it starts in; empty for the animator's own start. While playing, the state it's in.
SpeedHow fast its states play: 1 as the animator says, 2 twice as fast. It multiplies each state's own speed.

With an Animator, the animator sets the Sprite's Clip and Speed while the game runs; in the editor the sprite shows its own Clip.

Shortcuts#

These work while the pointer is over the Animator tab.

ActionShortcut
Pick a state or an arrow; add to what's pickedClick; Ctrl + click or Shift + click
Pick states with a boxDrag on empty space
Move picked statesDrag one of them
Join two statesDrag from a state's edge to another
Add a state, Make transition, Start here, DeleteRight-click empty space, a state or an arrow (Add state, Start here and Delete are on the ribbon too)
Give up an arrow started with Make transitionEsc
Delete a parameter, or start it at the value shownRight-click its name
Take away what's pickedDelete
PanMiddle-drag
Zoom round the pointerMouse wheel
Fit everything in viewF
Undo or redo a change to the animatorCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a transition is taken at once. Why: it has no conditions (its arrow says always). Fix: click the arrow and add one.
  • Problem: the sprite flickers between two states. Why: each one's transition to the other holds at the same time (moving and not moving can't both hold, but speed > 0 and speed < 1 can). Fix: make the conditions exclude each other.
  • Problem: a swing never ends. Why: its clip plays over and over, so it never finishes. Fix: make the clip play once (its Plays in the Clips tab), or leave it on a different condition.
  • Problem: a box says missing beside a clip. Why: the sprite sheet has no clip by that name (renamed in Aseprite?). Fix: pick the clip again.
  • Problem: pressing a trigger twice quickly swings once. Why: a trigger lasts one tick: one fired while already swinging is put out (it doesn't wait). That's on purpose, so presses don't pile up.
  • Problems lists an Animator with no file chosen, or whose file isn't in the project.

Related#

  • Animating sprites: the clips states play.
  • Sprites from Aseprite.
  • Save games: saves keep each animator's state and parameters.
  • Concepts: animator, state, transition, parameter, trigger.

Tile maps#

Lay out a 2D world as a grid of cells (grass, tilled earth, water) in layers under and over your sprites, with values every cell carries, such as what's planted there and whether it's watered.

When to use it#

A farm is a grid. Each square of ground is grass, tilled earth or water, and as you play it changes: the hoe tills it, a seed is planted, the can waters it, the crop grows. A tile map keeps that grid, and the running game changes it cell by cell.

A tile map stores what each cell means, not a picture:

  • Terrains (grass, tilled, water) come from a tileset, a list shared by every map in the project.
  • Layers stack: Ground, then Decoration (fences, flowers), both drawn under sprites, and Above (roofs, treetops), drawn over them so the farmer walks behind a roof.
  • Cell values are things every cell has besides its terrain. crop is a choice (wheat, corn), growth is a number, and watered is a switch.

Why meaning rather than pictures? Because the art can change without touching a single map: Solis works out which picture each cell shows from its neighbours, using the tileset's art (Tilesets and autotiling). And because "every watered crop" is a question about values, not about how things look.

Why values in the map, rather than an entity per plant? A field of a thousand crops as a thousand entities is a lot to run and save. As values, they're a few bytes each, saved with the map. A plant that needs to animate or think can still be an entity standing on its cell.

For a few things that move or think (a scarecrow that turns, a chicken), use sprites instead.

How to use it#

  1. Make a tileset: in the Library, open the folder you want it in, then New › Tileset (right-click in the Library, or + New). Solis makes tileset.tileset.lst with grass, tilled and water, and opens it in Library tools · Tileset, where terrains get their art (see Tilesets and autotiling). Choose a terrain in the Terrains slot to change its name, its code (the one character the map file writes for it) and its colour; the ribbon's Add adds one. Clicking a tileset in the Library shows its terrains in Properties too: change them there, add one with + Terrain, or take one away with ×. Every change to a tileset is an undo step of that tileset's, wherever you make it: Ctrl + Z with the pointer over Properties while it shows the tileset, or over the tileset's own tab, takes it back, so a terrain removed by mistake comes back with its tiles and rules. Dragging a colour is one step, made when you let go. The first terrain fills new maps.
  2. Make a map: New › Tile map. Solis makes map.tilemap.lst, 64 × 64 cells of the project's first tileset's first terrain. Click it in the Library to change its Tileset and its Size (in cells) in Properties.
  3. Place it: double-click the map in the Library (it goes where the viewport looks), or drag it into the viewport. Its top-left corner lands on a whole tile, and each cell is one tile across (the tile size in 2D settings). The 2D view shows it best.
  4. The Map tab of Home's bottom panel comes to the front while the map's entity is selected (select it in the Level panel), with the Home tools · Tile map tab and its ribbon. It shows four columns:
    • The map (its name, and how many cells across and down), and its Layers, top first. A click on a layer's row paints on that layer. Each has a small picture of its cells, its name (click to rename), under sprites or over sprites, an eye that shows or hides it here in the editor only (the game always shows it), and … to move it up or down or delete it. + in the column's header adds a layer on top.
    • Terrains, the tileset's, each with how many cells use it. They're the tile painter's palette: click one to paint with it.
    • Cell values. + in the column's header adds one (a switch to start). Change its name, its kind (number, switch or choice) and a choice's options (names with commas between).
    • The cell under the pointer in the viewport: each layer's terrain and each value.
  5. See the values on the map: while the map is selected, the Values list in the ribbon's Show group lays chosen values over the cells: a watered cell is tinted blue, and a number or a choice is written on its cell when you're zoomed in enough to read it. Zoomed out so far that more than 256 × 256 cells are in view, values aren't shown at all (each cell would be a speck), which keeps the editor quick over a big map. Chunks outlines the map's 32 × 32 chunks, and Walls shows what's solid.
  6. Play: each placed map is the game's own copy while it runs, so the game can change it and the file stays as it was. Select the map while playing to watch its cells in the Map tab. Save games keep the map as the game left it.

Every change in the Map tab is saved at once. Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y over the tab undo and redo them. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

Art and painting#

A terrain is drawn in its colour until its tileset gives it art: then each cell's tile is picked from its neighbours, with smooth edges (see Tilesets and autotiling). Seen from far away, a big map is drawn in its colours again, which is much quicker.

Paint a map's cells with the tile painter: while the map is selected, its brush, rectangle, line, fill and eyedropper are on the ribbon of the Home tools · Tile map tab, and the Map tab's terrain swatches are its palette (see Painting tiles). The file is plain text you can also edit by hand: each chunk of a layer is rows of codes (. grass, t tilled, a space for nothing), and cells painted with an exact tile are listed in exact blocks.

The file#

A tile map is an ordinary Lust file, farm.tilemap.lst, and its tileset is another, ground.tileset.lst. Open one in Ledger to read it: a list of the map's layers and values, then its cells in chunks of 32 × 32, each layer's rows of terrain codes (a space for an empty cell). It's safe to change by hand, keeping to the shapes Solis writes (lock values made of numbers, text in quotes, lists in [ ] and new things): Solis checks the file against those and then as Lust when it reads it, and a mistake is shown with its line. Chunks keep a change to one cell to one line, so Git shows exactly what changed. (Older maps, .soltilemap, move to Lust by themselves when the project opens: see Backups and upgrades.)

In game code#

Each tile map gets a Lust file of its own, which Solis writes into solis/maps/ whenever the map or its tileset changes: maps/farm.tilemap.lst gives solis/maps/maps/farm.lst. In it are states of the map's layers (FarmLayer), its tileset's terrains (FarmTerrain, with Empty for nothing painted) and each choice value's options (FarmCrop), and a class with a method for each thing code can ask or change (FarmMap). So watered misspelt is a mistake before the game runs, and renaming it in the Map tab points at every line still using the old name.

A component holds the map as a field with no starting value, which Solis fills in:

fetch "solis/maps/maps/farm":[FarmMap, FarmLayer, FarmTerrain, FarmCrop];

component Sprinkler {
    has {
        FarmMap farm;        -- filled in by Solis
        int x = 3;
        int y = 4;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
        bool soil = farm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y) == FarmTerrain.Soil;
        is soil && not farm:watered(x, y)? then {
            farm:setWatered(x, y, true);
            farm:setGrowth(x, y, farm:growth(x, y) + 1);
        }

        -- Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
        is farm:crop(x, y) == FarmCrop.None? then {
            farm:setCrop(x, y, FarmCrop.Parsnip);
        }
    }
}

pass Sprinkler;
end
// The map's file is Lust's. Rust reads the map through its host by its
// path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map tab's
// lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a choice by
// its place in its list.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};
use tiles::CellValue;

const FARM: &str = "maps/farm";
const GROUND: usize = 0;
const SOIL: u8 = b's';
// The farm's values, in the Map tab's order.
const WATERED: usize = 0;
const GROWTH: usize = 1;
const CROP: usize = 2;
const PARSNIP: u8 = 0;

pub struct Sprinkler {
    x: u32,
    y: u32,
}

impl RustComponent for Sprinkler {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let Some(farm) = cx.host().map(FARM) else {
            return;
        };
        let (x, y) = (self.x, self.y);

        // Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
        let soil = farm.code(GROUND, x, y) == Some(SOIL);
        let dry = farm.value(WATERED, x, y) != Some(CellValue::Switch(true));
        if soil && dry {
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, WATERED, [x, y], CellValue::Switch(true));
            let growth = match farm.value(GROWTH, x, y) {
                Some(CellValue::Number(n)) => n,
                _ => 0,
            };
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, GROWTH, [x, y], CellValue::Number(growth + 1));
        }

        // Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
        if farm.value(CROP, x, y) == Some(CellValue::Choice(None)) {
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, CROP, [x, y], CellValue::Choice(Some(PARSNIP)));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The map's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the map through solis.Maps by
-- its path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map
-- tab's lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a
-- choice by its place in its list (-1 for none).
local FARM = "maps/farm"
local GROUND = 0
local SOIL = string.byte("s")
-- The farm's values, in the Map tab's order.
local WATERED, GROWTH, CROP = 0, 1, 2
local PARSNIP = 0

local Sprinkler = component("Sprinkler", {
    { "x", "int", 3 },
    { "y", "int", 4 },
})

function Sprinkler:update(dt)
    local x, y = self.x, self.y

    -- Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
    local soil = solis.Maps:terrain(FARM, GROUND, x, y) == SOIL
    if soil and not solis.Maps:isOn(FARM, WATERED, x, y) then
        solis.Maps:setSwitch(FARM, WATERED, x, y, true)
        solis.Maps:setNumber(FARM, GROWTH, x, y, solis.Maps:number(FARM, GROWTH, x, y) + 1)
    end

    -- Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
    if solis.Maps:choice(FARM, CROP, x, y) == -1 then
        solis.Maps:setChoice(FARM, CROP, x, y, PARSNIP)
    end
end
In the Map tabbecomes
its sizefarm:width(), farm:height() (in cells)
a layer's terrain on a cellfarm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y), farm:setTerrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y, FarmTerrain.Soil)
a number value growthfarm:growth(x, y), farm:setGrowth(x, y, to)
a switch value wateredfarm:watered(x, y), farm:setWatered(x, y, on)
a choice value cropfarm:crop(x, y) == FarmCrop.Parsnip, farm:setCrop(x, y, FarmCrop.Corn)
the cell at a place in the worldfarm:cellAt(position()): a MapCell with inside (on the map?), x and y
the place at a cell's middlefarm:placeOf(x, y)
the box a map's entity coversground:mapBounds(): a MapBounds with found, low and high corners

Which cell is the player on? Ask the map with the player's place. MapCell comes from solis/tiles:

fetch "solis/maps/maps/farm":[FarmMap, FarmLayer, FarmTerrain];
fetch "solis/tiles":MapCell;

component Hoe {
    has {
        FarmMap farm;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        MapCell here = farm:cellAt(position());
        is here.inside && farm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, here.x, here.y) == FarmTerrain.Grass? then {
            farm:setTerrain(FarmLayer.Ground, here.x, here.y, FarmTerrain.Tilled);
        }
    }
}

pass Hoe;
end
// The map's file is Lust's. Rust reads the map through its host by its
// path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map tab's
// lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a choice by
// its place in its list.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

const FARM: &str = "maps/farm";
const GROUND: usize = 0;
const GRASS: u8 = b'.';
const TILLED: u8 = b't';

pub struct Hoe;

impl RustComponent for Hoe {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let at = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let (Some(farm), Some(place)) = (cx.host().map(FARM), cx.host().map_place(FARM)) else {
            return;
        };
        let ([x, y], inside) = place.cell_at(at);
        if !inside {
            return;
        }
        let cell = [x as u32, y as u32];
        if farm.code(GROUND, cell[0], cell[1]) == Some(GRASS) {
            cx.host().set_map_tile(FARM, GROUND, cell, TILLED);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The map's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the map through solis.Maps by
-- its path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map
-- tab's lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a
-- choice by its place in its list (-1 for none).
local FARM = "maps/farm"
local GROUND = 0
local GRASS, TILLED = string.byte("."), string.byte("t")

local Hoe = component("Hoe", {})

function Hoe:update(dt)
    local here = solis.Maps:cellAt(FARM, solis.entity.position(self.me))
    if here.inside and solis.Maps:terrain(FARM, GROUND, here.x, here.y) == GRASS then
        solis.Maps:setTerrain(FARM, GROUND, here.x, here.y, TILLED)
    end
end

It works wherever the map's entity is, even moved or turned. Cells are counted from the map's top left corner, x across and y down, like the Map tab; a place off the map still gets the cell it would be (handy for a tool reaching past the edge), with inside false. A 2D camera that stays inside the map is ready-made: FollowCamera2D (Characters and cameras).

  • Cells count from 0 at the map's first corner, as the Map tab shows them. A cell off the map reads as empty, 0 or off, and changing it does nothing.
  • Changes land at the end of the tick, like moves, and what code reads is the map as the tick started. They're in saves, and a solid terrain painted by code becomes a wall at once.
  • The map is the one placed by the first entity showing that file (most games have one per file).

Settings#

The Tile Map component:

SettingWhat it does
MapThe tile map file (.tilemap.lst) it shows. Its top-left corner is at the entity.

A map file's Properties:

SettingWhat it does
TilesetThe terrains its cells can be. Giving a map with an empty ground its first tileset fills the ground with that tileset's first terrain.
SizeIts width and height in cells, up to 4,096 each. Making it smaller takes away the cells past its new edges. A change that would make the map's file too big to open again isn't made (see the problems below).

A terrain's settings (right-click its swatch in the Map tab):

SettingWhat it does
SolidNothing with a 2D collider walks into its cells: fences, water, walls. A small wall mark shows on its swatch, and the Walls switch on the Tile map ribbon shows the walls it makes. See Walls and walking in 2D.

Value kinds:

KindHoldsStarts at
NumberA whole number, such as days of growth0
SwitchOn or off, such as wateredOff
ChoiceOne of its options, such as wheat or cornNone

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Undo or redo a change in the Map tab, or a painted strokeCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over the tab, or a painting tool in use)
Undo or redo a change to a tileset (its terrains, Solid)Ctrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over Properties while it shows the tileset, or over the tileset's tab)
A terrain's settingsRight-click its swatch in the Map tab
The painting toolsB, U, N, G, I (see Painting tiles)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: cells are bright pink. Why: their code isn't one of the tileset's terrains (the terrain was taken away, or its code changed), or their terrain's art is missing the tile they need. The Map tab counts unknown codes, and Problems names missing tiles. Fix: add a terrain with that code, change the cells, or fill the slot in the tileset.
  • Problem: clicking the map in the viewport selects what's behind it, or nothing. Why: clicks on a map are kept for the tile painter. Fix: select the map in the Level panel.
  • Problem: the Map tab is gone. Why: it shows only while a map is selected. Fix: select the map's entity.
  • Problem: numbers don't show on the cells. Why: cells are too small to write on, or too many are in view. Fix: zoom in.
  • Problem: a value's numbers are gone after changing its kind. Why: a value's cells start again when its kind changes. Fix: Ctrl + Z over the Map tab.
  • Problem: on a very big map, + adds no layer or value, or a value's kind won't change to number. Why: a map's layers and values together take at most 512 MB of memory. A layer, a switch or a choice takes a byte for each cell and a number four, so the biggest map (4,096 × 4,096) has room for 32 bytes a cell: 16 layers and 4 numbers, say. Fix: take away a layer or value the map doesn't need, or make the map smaller.
  • Problem: a change to a very big map isn't made, and the Console says … wasn't changed: saved like that, the map couldn't be opened again. Why: a map is kept as text, and reading text takes far more memory than the file's size, so Solis reads a map file of up to 64 MB with up to 12 million numbers, texts and symbols in it (about 2 GB of memory and 10 seconds at worst). The biggest map, 4,096 × 4,096, fits with three layers painted all over; each cell whose value isn't at its start counts too (a number in a million and a half cells is too many), and so does each exact tile. A map saved past that could never be opened again, so Solis checks every change as you make it (painting, filling, a new layer or value, a bigger size) and doesn't make one that would take the map past it. Nothing is lost: the map stays as it was, and undo still goes back through your earlier changes. Fix: split a very big world into several maps, each on its own entity, give values only to the cells that need them, and clear layers the map doesn't use; then make the change again.
  • Problem: a very big map won't open: "the map is too big to read" or "it's too big to read". Why: its file is past what Solis reads (see the problem above). Solis never saves such a file itself, so it was made by hand, by another program, or by a Solis from before this check. Fix: make it smaller in a text editor (take out a layer's Cells, or a value's cells), or go back to an earlier version of it in Git.
  • Problems lists a Tile Map with no map chosen, or whose file isn't in the project.

Related#

  • Painting tiles: the brush, rectangle, line, fill and eyedropper.
  • Tilesets and autotiling: terrains' art.
  • Sprites from Aseprite: what stands on a map.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: the tile size and the 2D view.
  • Save games: saves keep each map as the game changed it.
  • Concepts: tileset, terrain, tile map, layer, cell value, chunk.
← Previous · Chapter 42AnimatorsNext → · Chapter 44Atlas Crop: pictures cut out of a sprite sheet

Atlas Crop: pictures cut out of a sprite sheet#

Cut named pictures out of a PNG or an Aseprite sheet (a sword, a heart, a button's corner), so one sprite or a few can be used on their own, without changing the picture.

When to use it#

Artists often draw many small pictures on one sheet: every item in a game, every icon of a HUD. Atlas Crop marks each one as a crop with a name, so game code and screens can use just that part of the sheet: Picture.Sprites.Tools.Axe. The picture itself is never changed, so the artist keeps drawing on the same sheet and every crop follows.

For a sprite that plays clips, use sprites and sprite animation instead; for ground made of tiles, a tileset.

How to use it#

  1. In the Library, right-click a picture (a PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file) and choose Atlas Crop…. A Library tools · Picture tab opens after Library in the tab bar (a contextual tab: it is there only while the picture's crops are open), with the picture as its document and its crops in the Crops slot at the left. Solis makes a file beside the picture to keep the crops: sprites/tools.png gets sprites/tools.atlas.lst. ‹ Back to Library, at the right of the document's tab, goes back to the Library and leaves the crops open.
  2. Set the Grid at the top of the Crops tab to the size the pictures are drawn on (16 × 16 for most pixel art); the ribbon's Grid group says it too. Crops snap to it, so a quick drag catches a whole tile.
  3. Drag on the picture to draw a crop. It's named Crop, Crop2… at first: type a better name in Name, in the Crops tab's right-hand column, and press Rename (or Enter). A name starts with a letter and holds only letters, digits and _.
  4. Or press Every tile in the ribbon's Crop group: a crop for every grid cell with something drawn in it, named by its column and row (Tile_3_0).
  5.
