Click a crop, on the picture or in the Crops list (its size and place beside its name), to pick it: its frame turns the accent colour and thicker, while the others stay a darker grey; the ribbon's Delete, Delete crop or the Delete key over the picture removes it. Zoom in the ribbon's Grid group shows the picture at a chosen size (the wheel zooms too). Every change is saved at once, and Ctrl+Z over the tab undoes it. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.
  6. Later, double-click the .atlas.lst file in the Library to open its picture's crops again.

Game code names each crop by its picture's path and its name, from solis/project.lst: fetch "solis/project":Picture; then Picture.Sprites.Tools.Axe for sprites/tools.png's Axe. A screen shows one with image "sprites/tools.png#Axe";: the picture's path, #, and the crop's name.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
GridThe size, in the picture's pixels, crops snap to when drawn and that Every tile cuts by.
ZoomHow big the picture is shown (the ribbon's list, or the wheel).
NameThe picked crop's name, as game code uses it.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Draw a cropDrag with the left button on the picture
Pick a cropClick it
Delete the picked cropDelete, with the pointer over the picture or the Crops tab
ZoomMouse wheel over the picture
Move the pictureDrag with the middle button
Undo, redoCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y (pointer over the picture or the Crops tab)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the tab says the picture isn't in the project. Why: an atlas file belongs to the picture beside it, by its file name, and that picture was moved or renamed. Fix: move the .atlas.lst file beside the picture, or rename it to match (tools.png and tools.atlas.lst).
  • Problem: a crop isn't offered to game code. Why: its name, or a folder or picture name in its path, can't be a Lust name (the Console says which). Fix: rename it: start with a letter, and use only letters, digits and _.
  • Problem: Every tile made fewer crops than there are cells. Why: empty cells (every pixel see-through) are left out, and so are cells a crop already covers exactly. That's on purpose.

Related#

  • Sprites, Tilesets, Game screens.
  • Concepts: atlas crop.
← Previous · Chapter 43Tile mapsNext → · Chapter 45Tilesets and autotiling

Tilesets and autotiling#

Give each terrain its art from a picture of tiles. Solis picks each cell's tile from its neighbours, so the edges between grass and tilled earth, the corners of a pond and the joins of a fence come out right by themselves.

When to use it#

A tile map stores what each cell is: grass, tilled, water. Until a tileset has art, each terrain is drawn as a flat colour. That's enough to lay a farm out, but a game wants pictures, and pictures need their edges. Where tilled earth meets grass, the tile at the edge has to show both, and which tile depends on which neighbours are tilled.

Choosing those by hand, cell by cell, is slow and breaks whenever the map changes. Autotiling does it for you. You draw the tiles once and say which situation each one is for (its slot). Solis then picks the right one for every cell, on every map, as the map changes, even while the game plays.

How many tiles you need depends on the terrain's kind:

KindTilesGood for
Plain1Grass, sand: anything with no edges of its own
16-tile (dual grid)15Most ground: tilled earth, paths, snow. The fewest drawings for smooth edges and corners
47-tile47Ground with the most polished corners, such as water with inner corners
Edges16Fences, walls, roads: things that join their neighbours along their sides
Rulesas many as you useAnything else: your own patterns of the cells around

16-tile works on a dual grid: each tile is drawn half a cell off, where four cells meet, and is chosen by which of those four are the terrain. That's why 15 drawings cover every case. You still paint and the game still thinks in whole cells; only the art is shifted.

How to use it#

  1. Draw your tiles in one picture: a PNG, or an Aseprite file (handy for animated tiles), with every tile the same size in a grid. Not sure what to draw? Open the tileset, choose a terrain's kind, and press Save … template (or the ribbon's Save its template…): Solis saves a picture beside the tileset with every slot laid out at your tile size, ready to draw over.
  2. Open the tileset: double-click it in the Library. A Library tools · Tileset tab joins the tab bar after Library and comes to the front: a contextual tab, there only while the tileset is open. Its document is the tileset itself (the picture on the left, the chosen terrain's slots on the right, Try it under them), its Terrains slot at the left lists the terrains, the slot picked is at the right, and its ribbon has Terrain (Add, Remove), Kind and Picture (the tile size and the Zoom). ‹ Back to Library, at the right of the document's tab, goes back and leaves the tileset open.
  3. Choose the picture in the Terrains slot, under the terrains. Solis cuts it into tiles at the tile size shown. If the art looks cut differently, it offers the size it found: click it.
  4. Choose a terrain in the Terrains slot, and give it a kind (the ribbon's Kind list, or the tab's own). While it has no tiles, the tab guesses its kind from the picture (pick the top-left tile of its block first) and asks you to confirm. Kind at the top right changes it any time.
  5. Fill its slots on the right. Each slot shows the neighbours it's for: the terrain's colour where they're the terrain, dark where they're not.
    • Click a tile in the picture, then the slot it's for, or drag the tile onto the slot.
    • Drawn over the template? Pick the template's top-left tile and press Mark up from the template: every slot is filled from its place in one go.
    • A second tile in the same slot is a variation, so a field doesn't look tiled. Click the slot to see its tiles in Properties, with each one's Weight (how often it's picked).
  6. Try it in the patch below the slots: click cells to turn the terrain on and off and watch the edges. The patch isn't saved.
  7. Look at your map: every map using the tileset draws with the art at once, and while the game plays.

The strip at the top of the picture says where you are: ① picture, ② grid, ③ kind, ④ how many of the terrain's slots are filled.

A terrain of its own rules#

For a kind none of the others fit, choose rules and press + Rule. A rule is a small pattern of the cells around one (3 × 3 to start, up to 9 × 9) and the slot it shows. Click a cell of the pattern to change what it asks for:

MarkMeans
?Anything
=The same terrain
!Not the same terrain
_Nothing on this layer (or past the map's edge)
a terrain's codeThat terrain

The rules are tried in order (↑ and ↓ move one), and the first that matches gives the slot. The slots the rules name appear below them to fill. A cell no rule matches shows pink.

Animated tiles#

Click a slot, then in Properties set a tile's Animation:

  • tiles to the right: that many tiles of the picture, left to right from this one, each shown for so many milliseconds (water, flowers);
  • the picture's frames (an Aseprite picture): the same tile in each of its frames, each for its own time.

Settings#

In the tileset's tab (the Terrains slot, the Slot at the right and the ribbon):

SettingWhat it does
PictureThe PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file the art comes from.
Tile sizeEach tile's width and height in pixels. Usually the project's tile size (2D settings).
KindHow the chosen terrain's tiles are chosen: plain, 16-tile, 47-tile, edges or rules. Changing it takes its tiles away (Ctrl + Z brings them back).
ZoomHow big the picture is shown (the ribbon's list, or − and + under the steps).

In Properties, for a tile in a slot:

SettingWhat it does
WeightHow often it's picked among the slot's tiles: 2 is twice as often as 1, 0 never. Each cell always gets the same one.
AnimationNone, tiles to the right (with how many and how long each), or the picture's frames.

For the chosen terrain (no slot picked): its Name, Code (the character map files write for it) and Colour (drawn where it has no art), and Remove terrain.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Give a tile to a slotClick the tile in the picture, then the slot; or drag the tile onto the slot
Undo or redo a change to the tilesetCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over the tileset or its Terrains tab, or over Properties while it shows the tileset)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pink cells on a map. Why: a slot those cells need has no tile, or the cells' code isn't a terrain. Fix: the tileset's slots dash the empty ones red; Problems says which map and which slots. Fill them.
  • Problem: the edges look one tile off. Why: the template was marked up from the wrong tile. Fix: pick the template's top-left tile in the picture first; the button says where it will start. Ctrl + Z, then try again.
  • Problem: the grid lines don't match the art. Why: the tile size is different from the picture's. Fix: set it on the left, or click the size Solis found.
  • Problem: a terrain still shows its flat colour. Why: it has no tiles yet (or the tileset has no picture). Fix: fill its slots.
  • Problem: the picture won't open. Why: it isn't a PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file, or it's bigger than 4,096 pixels a side. The tab says why.
  • If a change to the tileset can't be saved, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.
  • PNG and JPEG files get a sidecar (.solmeta) like other assets, so a tileset keeps its picture when the picture is moved or renamed. Commit them with the picture.

Related#

  • Tile maps: the maps tilesets draw.
  • Sprites from Aseprite: Aseprite pictures.
  • Concepts: autotiling, kind, slot, dual grid, variation, template.
← Previous · Chapter 44Atlas Crop: pictures cut out of a sprite sheetNext → · Chapter 46Painting tiles

Painting tiles#

Paint a tile map's cells with a brush, a rectangle, a line or a fill, copy a level to paint with, and place a tile exactly as it is.

When to use it#

A tile map is a grid of terrains: grass, tilled earth, water. The tile painter is how you lay them out: paint a field of tilled earth, a pond, a path, a fence. You paint what each cell means (its terrain); the art is worked out from the neighbours by autotiling, so the edges of a pond come out smooth wherever you paint it.

Painting is for the map file, the world as the game starts. While the game runs, the map is the game's own copy, so painting is off then; game code changes cells as you play.

How to use it#

  1. Select the map's entity (in the Level panel). A Home tools · Tile map tab joins the tab bar after Home and comes to the front, with the Map tab of the bottom panel. Its ribbon holds everything for painting, so the viewport stays clear: the tools are on the ribbon rather than on the tool bar at the foot of the view because there are five of them and they are only there while a map is selected. While one is in use, no tool on the tool bar is lit; clicking one there (or pressing its key) puts the painting tool down. Bringing another tab of the bottom panel to the front (the Library, say) gives Home's own ribbon back; the Tile map tab, or the Map shelf tab, brings the painting ribbon again.
  2. Choose a tool in the ribbon's Paint group or with its key: Brush (B), Rectangle (U), Line (N), Fill (G) or Eyedropper (I). Q, W, R, S or T goes back to the transform tools. While a tool is in use, its keys show in a hint along the foot of the view.
  3. Choose what to paint: click a terrain's swatch in the Map tab's Terrains column. The outlined swatch is the one painted, and the ribbon names it beside the tools. Clicking a swatch takes the brush if no painting tool is in use.
  4. Choose the layer: click its row in the Map tab's first column, or pick it from the ribbon's Layer list (Ground to start). The row painted on is lit. Paint fences and flowers on Decoration so the ground under them stays grass.
  5. Paint in the viewport (the 2D view is easiest):
    • Brush: drag over cells to paint them. Every cell the pointer crosses is painted, however fast you drag.
    • Rectangle: drag from one corner to the other. The cells show while you drag and are painted when you let go.
    • Line: drag from one end to the other; painted when you let go.
    • Fill: click a cell. Every cell joined to it by its sides with the same terrain is painted: one field, stopping at its edges.
    • Eyedropper: drag over cells to copy them (see below). One cell picks its terrain instead.
  6. Empty cells by dragging with the right mouse button: the brush, rectangle, line and fill all take cells away instead.
  7. Undo with Ctrl + Z while a painting tool is in use (or over the Map tab). Each stroke, from pressing the button to letting go, is one step. Esc during a stroke gives it up.

Everything is saved as soon as you let go.

Picking a terrain from the map#

Alt + click a cell to paint with its terrain, like a colour picker. It also picks the cell's exact tile, if it has one.

Copying a level#

Drag over cells with the Eyedropper to copy them: a copy (some programs call it a stamp). The brush takes it, and paints the whole copy round the pointer; dragged, it repeats like a pattern, without seams. Empty cells in the copy leave the map as it is, so a copied fence keeps the grass under it.

While you hold a copy:

  • X flips it left and right, Y top and bottom, Z turns it a quarter clockwise (the ribbon's Copy group does the same: Flip X, Flip Y, Turn, and Put away);
  • the rectangle, line and fill paint with it as a pattern;
  • Esc, or clicking a terrain's swatch, puts it away.

Exact tiles#

Autotiling picks each cell's tile from its neighbours. Sometimes you want one particular tile instead: a cracked stone, a corner that breaks the rule. An exact tile is a cell that shows one tile as it is.

  1. Tick Exact on the ribbon (or hold Ctrl while painting).
  2. The Map tab shows the painted terrain's tiles under the swatches. Click the one to place. To start, it's the tile for the middle of a patch.
  3. Paint. The cell keeps that tile; its neighbours still see its terrain, so their edges still join it.

Painting the cell again without Exact makes it autotiled again. Exact tiles are art only: the game reads the terrain, never the tile.

Art or meaning#

Tab, or the ribbon's Map as list in the Show group, switches the selected map between its art and its meaning: each terrain in its flat colour, which is what the game reads. Meaning is handy for checking that a path of tiles really is all one terrain.

Settings#

The ribbon of Home tools · Tile map, while a map is selected:

GroupSettingWhat it does
PaintBrush, Rectangle, Line, Fill, EyedropperThe painting tools (B, U, N, G, I).
(in hand)The terrain, or Copy W × HWhat is painted now.
(in hand)LayerThe layer painted (a click on a layer's row in the Map tab does the same).
(in hand)ExactPlaces the tile chosen in the Map tab as it is, not the one autotiling picks. Ctrl while painting does the same for one stroke.
ShowMap asWhat the selected map shows: its art, or each terrain in its colour (Tab).
ShowValues, Chunks, WallsWhat is laid over the map: its cell values, its chunks of 32 × 32 cells, and what's solid.
CopyFlip X, Flip Y, Turn, Put awayChange or drop the copy held (X, Y, Z, Esc). Faint until you hold one.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Brush, Rectangle, Line, Fill, EyedropperB, U, N, G, I (a map selected)
PaintLeft-drag (a click for the fill)
Empty cellsRight-drag
Paint with the terrain under the pointerAlt + click
Place exact tiles for one strokeHold Ctrl while painting
Flip the copy left and right, top and bottom; turn itX, Y, Z (holding a copy)
Give up a stroke; put the copy away; leave the painting toolEsc
Art or meaningTab
Undo or redo a strokeCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y
Slide the view while paintingMiddle-drag

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: on a very big map, what you just painted disappears when you let go, and the Console says the map wasn't changed. Why: with that stroke the map's file would be too big for Solis to open again, so the stroke isn't kept; the map is as it was before it. Fix: see Tile maps for how much a map can hold and what to do.
  • Problem: the painting tools aren't on the ribbon. Why: they are on the Home tools · Tile map tab, there only while a tile map's entity is selected, and faint while the game runs. Fix: select the map in the Level panel and click the Tile map tab (or the Map shelf tab); stop the game.
  • Problem: right-dragging empties cells instead of sliding the view. Why: while a painting tool is in use, the right button empties. Fix: slide with the middle button, or press Q for Select.
  • Problem: the fill painted more than expected. Why: the fill follows every cell of the same terrain joined by its sides, on the layer painted. Fix: Ctrl + Z, then break the field with a line first.
  • Problem: painting does nothing. Why: the map has no tileset (nothing to paint with), or the layer painted is hidden. Fix: choose a tileset in the map file's Properties; check the ribbon's Layer list and the Map tab's eyes.
  • Problem: a flipped copy's exact tiles look the wrong way round. Why: exact tiles move with their cells but aren't mirrored. Fix: pick the mirrored tile from the Map tab, or leave those cells autotiled.
  • Problem: cells show pink. Why: their terrain's art is missing a tile they need (Problems names it). Fix: fill the slot in the tileset.

Related#

  • Tile maps: layers, values and the Map tab.
  • Tilesets and autotiling: how each cell's tile is picked.
  • Undo: what Ctrl + Z undoes where.
  • Concepts: tile map, terrain, layer, copy, exact tile.
← Previous · Chapter 45Tilesets and autotilingNext → · Chapter 47Walls and walking in 2D

Walls and walking in 2D#

Make terrains solid so nothing walks through fences and water, give things a 2D collider, and walk a character around a top-down map in 8 directions or 4.

When to use it#

In any top-down 2D game: a farmer who walks the farm but not through its fences, a shop counter you can't walk through, villagers who stop at walls. Solis gives you the pieces; your game decides what they mean. Solis never decides that water is solid or that NPCs walk in 4 directions: you do.

Three parts work together:

  • Solid terrains: cells nothing with a body can walk into (fences, water, rock). Set per terrain, in its tileset, so every map using the tileset agrees.
  • Collider2D: a shape on the ground for 2D physics, in pixels. Solid and still on its own (a house, a bin); ticked Character, game code walks it.
  • The TopDownController: a ready-made Lust component in the kit that walks a character with the Move action (WASD, the arrow keys, a controller's left stick).

2D physics is its own world, separate from 3D physics, and gives the same result on every PC. For 3D characters, see Characters and cameras.

How to use it#

Make terrains solid

  1. Click your tile map in the Library (or select its Tile Map entity) so the Map tab shows it.
  2. Under Terrains, right-click a terrain's swatch (say, fence) and tick Solid. A small wall mark appears on its swatch. Left-click still picks it for painting.
  3. Do the same for every terrain that should block: water, rock, walls.
  4. Press Walls at the top of the viewport (beside Chunks) to see what's solid: green rectangles over the map. Neighbouring solid cells merge into a few big rectangles, so a character sliding along a fence never catches on the seams between tiles.

Walk a character

  1. Select your player's entity (one with a Sprite, say).

  2. In Properties, choose + Component › Collider2D. Leave its shape a Circle (circles slide round corners best) and set its Radius to about a third of the sprite's width. Set Up to put the circle at its feet. A green outline shows it in the viewport.

  3. Tick Character.

  4. Fetch the kit's walker in your game code (main.lst):

    fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
end
    // The kit's components are Lust. A game in Rust brings one in from a
// main.lst of two lines beside its Rust:
//
//     fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
//     end
    -- The kit's components are Lust. A game in Lua brings one in from a
-- main.lst of two lines beside its Lua files:
--
--     fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
--     end

  5. Save, then in Properties choose + Component › TopDownController.

  6. Press Play and walk with WASD or the arrow keys. It stops at solid tiles and other colliders and slides along them.

Walk an NPC from your own code Add a TopDownController, untick Uses input, set Directions to 4 if you like, and set its wanted field from your code to where it should head ([1, 0, 0] walks right, [0, 0, 0] stops). Or call walk yourself with how far to move this tick:

component Wanderer {
    method update(float dt) {
        walk([1.5 * dt, 0, 0]);
    }
}

pass Wanderer;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Wanderer;

impl RustComponent for Wanderer {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().walk(me, Vec3::new(1.5 * dt as f32, 0.0, 0.0));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Wanderer = component("Wanderer", {})

function Wanderer:update(dt)
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, vec3(1.5 * dt, 0, 0))
end

A 2D character moves on the ground: the move's third number (height) is ignored, and it stays on its layer.

Side-on games (platformers). The second number is up and down, so walk a hero down a little every tick for gravity, and ask how its last move went:

  • grounded() is true when a floor under it stopped it going down: jump only then. A wall, or a slope steeper than about 45°, isn't ground.
  • velocity() is how fast its last tick's move really went, in metres a second: less than you asked for when something stopped it. A head bump shows as velocity().y dropping to 0 while you asked to go up.
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Hero {
    has {
        float fall = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
        fall = fall - 30 * dt;
        is grounded()? then {
            fall = 0;
            is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
                fall = 12;
            }
        }
        walk([4 * dt, fall * dt, 0]);
    }
}

pass Hero;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hero {
    fall: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Hero {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        // Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
        self.fall -= 30.0 * dt;
        if cx.host().grounded(me) {
            self.fall = 0.0;
            if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
                self.fall = 12.0;
            }
        }
        let step = Vec3::new((4.0 * dt) as f32, (self.fall * dt) as f32, 0.0);
        cx.host().walk(me, step);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Hero = component("Hero", {
    { "fall", "float", 0 },
})

function Hero:update(dt)
    -- Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
    self.fall = self.fall - 30 * dt
    if solis.entity.grounded(self.me) then
        self.fall = 0
        if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
            self.fall = 12
        end
    end
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, vec3(4 * dt, self.fall * dt, 0))
end

When an entity with a Collider2D is despawned, its collider goes with it at once, so a squashed enemy never leaves an invisible wall.

Settings#

Collider2D

SettingWhat it does
ShapeCircle (best for characters: it slips round corners) or Box (buildings, counters).
RadiusA circle's size, in pixels. A third of a 16-pixel sprite's width (about 5) is a good start.
Width, HeightA box's size, in pixels.
Across, UpWhere the shape's middle is from the entity's place, in pixels. Raise a character's circle to its feet so its head can overlap things above it, as top-down games do.
CharacterTicked: game code walks it (walk, or the TopDownController) and it slides along what's in its way. Unticked: solid and still.

Pixels become metres with the project's 2D settings (File › Project settings, pixels per unit).

TopDownController

SettingWhat it does
SpeedMetres a second at full push. 4 is a brisk walk at 16 pixels a metre.
AccelerationHow quickly it gets up to speed, in metres a second each second. High feels snappy; low feels heavy.
DecelerationHow quickly it stops when let go.
Directions8, or 4 (only the bigger of across and up counts: no diagonals, like older games).
Uses inputTicked: walks with the Move action. Unticked: walks towards wanted, set by your code.
FacingThe way it last walked (read it to choose a sprite's facing).

Terrains (right-click a swatch in the Map tab)

SettingWhat it does
SolidNothing with a Collider2D passes into its cells, on any layer. Saved in the tileset (solid = true;).

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Walk (with the TopDownController)W A S D, the arrow keys, or a controller's left stick

Change them in File › Project settings › Input (the Move action). A project with its own input actions file from before keeps its keys: add the arrows to Move there if you want them.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the character walks through a fence. Why: the fence's terrain isn't solid, or the character has no Collider2D ticked Character. Fix: right-click the fence's swatch and tick Solid; press Walls to check it shows.
  • Problem: nothing moves when I press keys. Why: the entity has no TopDownController, or its Collider2D isn't ticked Character (walk only moves characters). Fix: check both in Properties, and look in the Console for game code mistakes.
  • Problem: the character stops at a doorway it should fit through. Why: its circle is wider than the gap. Fix: make the Radius smaller, or the door wider.
  • Problem: it catches on corners. Why: a Box collider meets corners square on. Fix: use a Circle for characters.
  • Problem: the Console says 2D physics stopped and was started again. Why: 2D physics met something it couldn't work out, usually a Collider2D or a tile map whose size or place is far out of the ordinary. Rather than leave every character standing still, Solis builds 2D physics again from the entities and tile maps as they are, and the game carries on; the message names the character it was moving when it knows. If it keeps happening, it's built again at most once a second (so the game doesn't slow to a crawl), and 2D characters stand still in between. It's said once each time you press Play. Fix: look at the entity named, or at anything very big or very far away, and bring it back into range.
  • Walking into a door or a shop counter to make something happen (a trigger) comes with a later update.

Related#

  • Tile maps, Tilesets and Painting tiles
  • Input actions
  • Game code
  • Physics (3D) and Characters and cameras (3D characters)
  • Concepts: 2D
← Previous · Chapter 46Painting tilesNext → · Chapter 48Parallax layers

Parallax layers#

Make a sprite a background or foreground layer that moves with the camera at its own speed, so far hills drift slowly, leaves in front rush past, and a flat 2D level feels deep.

When to use it#

In side-on 2D games (platformers above all) and anywhere the camera travels a long way: a sky that stays put, mountains that crawl, trees that pass a little slower than the ground, and bushes or posts close to the camera that sweep past faster. It's the oldest trick for depth in 2D: things far away seem to move less when you move.

A parallax layer is an ordinary sprite with a Parallax component, so it keeps everything sprites do: clips, tint, flash, lamps and day and night.

Top-down games rarely need it: everything there is about the same distance from the camera.

How to use it#

A background

  1. Draw the layer in Aseprite: a line of hills, say, as wide as you like. For a layer that repeats, make its left and right edges meet.
  2. Drag it from the Library into the viewport, so it's a sprite. Put it where it should be in the game's first picture: around where your game's camera starts.
  3. In Properties, choose + Component › Parallax.
  4. Set Scroll across and Scroll up: 0.2 for faraway mountains, 0.5 for hills, 0.8 for trees just behind the action. Leave Repeat across ticked so the hills never run out.
  5. Press Play and move your character. The hills move slower than the ground.

Layers behind are drawn behind everything, tile maps included: the slowest first, so a 0.2 layer is behind a 0.5 one, whatever their places. The sky is usually a layer of its own with a scroll of 0, so it never moves.

A foreground

  1. Make a sprite of something close to the camera: leaves, a post, fog.
  2. Add a Parallax, tick In front, and give it a scroll above 1, such as 1.5.
  3. Press Play: it sweeps past faster than the world, over everything.

Where it's drawn. A layer is exactly where you put it while the game's camera is where it starts. As the camera moves, the layer moves at its own speed: with 0.5, half as far as the world. So the editor shows your game's first picture, layers and all. A layer can be several sprites (a row of trees with the same scrolls): they stay as far apart as you put them.

Smooth, even when slow. Through a 2D camera, each layer is drawn as a small picture of its own and slides smoothly by less than a pixel at a time, as the camera does, so a far layer crawling slowly never jumps a whole pixel at once. Up to 8 layers are drawn this way; each different set of scrolls, behind or in front, is one layer.

In the editor, layers stay where you put them (the editor's camera isn't the game's), repeated across the view, behind or in front as in the game. Clicking one behind the world selects it only where nothing else is in the way; the Level panel always finds it.

Settings#

Parallax

SettingWhat it does
Scroll acrossHow far it moves sideways with the camera. 0 stays still on the screen (the sky); 0.5 moves half as far (far hills); 1 moves with the world; 2 twice as far (close in front). From 0 to 4.
Scroll upThe same, up and down. Platformers often use the same number as across; a smaller one keeps the horizon steadier when the player jumps.
Repeat acrossDrawn again and again side by side, at its sheet's width, so it never runs out. On to start.
Repeat upDrawn again and again above and below. For skies or walls that should fill the screen whatever the height.
In frontDrawn over everything instead of behind it. Use it with a scroll above 1.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a repeated layer shows a seam where the copies meet. Why: its left and right edges don't match, or the picture has empty columns at its sides. Fix: draw it so the edges continue into each other, using the whole canvas. Copies are one canvas width apart.
  • Problem: a slow layer moves in little steps during a slow pan. Why: you have more than 8 layers (each different set of scrolls, behind or in front, is one), so they're drawn on the game's whole pixels, and a slow layer reaches the next pixel only now and then. Fix: give layers that are about as far away the same scrolls, so they share one.
  • Problem: a layer far along the level isn't where I put it. Why: layers are where you put them only while the camera is at its start; by the time the camera gets there, a slow layer has gone along with it. Fix: place layers around the camera's start, and use Repeat across for ones that must last the whole level.
  • Problem: the player bumps into nothing in front of a layer. Why: a Parallax only changes how the sprite looks; a Collider2D on the same entity stays where the entity is. Fix: keep layers as pictures only, and put colliders on entities of their own.
  • Tile maps can't be layers yet: draw backgrounds as pictures.

Related#

  • Sprites from Aseprite: making the pictures layers use.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: 2D cameras and the game's pixels.
  • Concepts: parallax, sprite.
← Previous · Chapter 47Walls and walking in 2DNext → · Chapter 49Trigger zones

Trigger zones#

A place in a level that tells your game code when something walks in or out: a door, a shop counter, a pit.

When to use it#

Whenever something should happen because of where a character is: a door that opens when the player reaches it, a shop that greets them at the counter, a pit that sends them back to the start, a room that starts its music. A trigger zone is invisible in the game. It watches a box, a circle (a sphere in 3D) or, in 2D, a shape you draw point by point, and each time a character or a moving body crosses its edge, it tells game code.

Why a zone and not a check in your own code ("is the player near the door?") every tick? The zone does the asking for you, the same way every time, and only says something when it changes: one Entered as the player steps in, one Exited as they leave, never sixty a second while they stand there. It also remembers who's inside in save games, so loading a save never says "entered" twice.

Trigger zones work the same in 2D and 3D levels: the same component, the same settings and the same events.

A zone only tells. What happens (a door opening, a fade, a teleport) is your game code's. Ready-made doors come later in stage 1, as a Door in the kit, built on trigger zones.

How to use it#

  1. On Home's ribbon, in Create, click Trigger zone (in a 3D project it's in Create › More). A new zone appears in the view, in the middle of where you're looking, and is picked.
  2. Size it: drag the small squares on its teal outline (its handles). Dragging a side moves that side and keeps the far one where it is; a circle's handle sets its radius. Sizes snap as moves do (whole pixels or tiles in 2D, the grid in 3D), and each drag is one step to undo. Or type its Size in Properties' TriggerZone card.
  3. Pick its Shape: Box, or Circle (2D) or Sphere (3D). In 2D there's Freeform too (below).
  4. Pick when it Fires: Every time something walks in or out, or Once, the first time something walks in and never again.
  5. Give it game code: in the What game code hears card, click New code for this zone…. Solis makes a code file named after the zone, with empty Entered and Exited ready to fill in, adds its component to the zone, and opens the file.
  6. Press Play and walk a character in. While playing, the card's Inside now names who is inside.

In the view, a zone is a teal outline: solid with handles when it's picked, dashed when it isn't, with its name and size beside it. Click its outline to pick it (a click inside it is left for whatever is in the zone); the Level panel lists it with a dashed square and Trigger zone. It turns and grows with its entity, like any shape: move it with the move gizmo (W), turn it with R.

A freeform shape (2D)#

A room that isn't a rectangle, a winding path, a pond's bank: pick Freeform in Shape, and drawing starts in the view.

  1. Click to place each point, going round the shape.
  2. Click the first point again, or press Enter, to close it. Esc while drawing gives up and keeps the shape it had.
  3. Later, press Tab with the zone picked (or click Edit points in its card) to change its points: drag a point to move it, Ctrl+click on an edge to add a point there, and Delete to remove the picked point. Tab or Esc finishes. Each drag or change is one step to undo.

A freeform shape may bend inward (an L, a horseshoe), but its outline may never cross itself: a change that would make it cross is refused, saying why, and the last good shape is kept. It has at most 256 points and at least 3.

A freeform shape is split into simple pieces once, when you change it, so even a big one costs the game nothing more each tick.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
ShapeBox, Circle in 2D or Sphere in 3D, and in 2D Freeform.
SizeA box's width and height (and depth in 3D), in metres; a circle's or sphere's radius. For a freeform shape, its number of points and Edit points.
NoticesWhat the zone watches for: Characters and bodies, meaning characters (a CharacterBody, or a Collider2D ticked Character) and bodies that move (a RigidBody that's dynamic or kinematic). Walls, floors and other things that never move are never "inside".
FiresEvery time: Entered whenever something walks in, Exited whenever it walks out. Once: only the first Entered (and the walker's EnteredZone), then nothing ever again, even after loading a save.
Only tagsLimits the zone to some kinds of thing: pick one or more of the project's tags with + Tag, and only what carries at least one of them counts ("only the player", "only enemies"). A chip's × takes a tag off; none chosen, the zone notices everything it can. What carries the tag is looked at as each tick starts, so something given the tag while inside is "entered" from the next tick, and something losing it "exits".
Inside nowWhile playing, who is inside the zone. While editing it says "Shown while playing".

What game code hears#

Each tick, after physics, Solis looks at who is inside each zone and compares it with the tick before:

  • The zone hears Entered(entity who) when something walks in, and Exited(entity who) when it walks out.
  • Whatever walked hears EnteredZone(entity zone) and LeftZone(entity zone).
  • A zone can be asked who's inside it now: inside(), a list of entities.
-- door.lst: a door zone that greets whoever comes in.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/zones":[Entered, Exited];

component Door {
    -- Someone walked in: say who, and how many are inside now.
    on Entered(entity who) {
        int count = #inside();
        World:say(who:name() + " came in; " + count.text() + " inside");
    }

    -- Someone walked out.
    on Exited(entity who) {
        World:say(who:name() + " left");
    }
}
pass Door;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Door;

impl RustComponent for Door {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        // The zone's events carry who walked in or out.
        let Some(Value::Entity(Some(who))) = event.values.first() else {
            return false;
        };
        let name = cx.host().name(*who).unwrap_or_default();
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // Someone walked in: say who, and how many are inside now.
            "Entered" => {
                let me = cx.me();
                let count = cx.host().inside(me).len();
                cx.host().say(&format!("{name} came in; {count} inside"));
            }
            // Someone walked out.
            "Exited" => cx.host().say(&format!("{name} left")),
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Door = component("Door", {})

-- Someone walked in: say who, and how many are inside now.
function Door:on_Entered(who)
    local count = #solis.entity.inside(self.me)
    solis.World:say(solis.entity.name(who) .. " came in; " .. count .. " inside")
end

-- Someone walked out.
function Door:on_Exited(who)
    solis.World:say(solis.entity.name(who) .. " left")
end

The one who walked in hears its own pair, which is handy for the player's own code (a "you found the shop" sign):

-- player.lst: the player notices the zones it walks through.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/zones":[EnteredZone, LeftZone];

component Player {
    -- Walked into a zone: which one.
    on EnteredZone(entity zone) {
        World:say("Now in " + zone:name());
    }

    -- Walked out of it again.
    on LeftZone(entity zone) {
        World:say("Left " + zone:name());
    }
}
pass Player;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Player;

impl RustComponent for Player {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        // These carry the zone.
        let Some(Value::Entity(Some(zone))) = event.values.first() else {
            return false;
        };
        let name = cx.host().name(*zone).unwrap_or_default();
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // Walked into a zone: which one.
            "EnteredZone" => cx.host().say(&format!("Now in {name}")),
            // Walked out of it again.
            "LeftZone" => cx.host().say(&format!("Left {name}")),
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Player = component("Player", {})

-- Walked into a zone: which one.
function Player:on_EnteredZone(zone)
    solis.World:say("Now in " .. solis.entity.name(zone))
end

-- Walked out of it again.
function Player:on_LeftZone(zone)
    solis.World:say("Left " .. solis.entity.name(zone))
end

The rules, exactly:

  • Only where things are at each tick counts. Something that goes in and out within one tick (a teleport straight through, a very fast bullet) fires nothing.
  • Several at once come in order: two walking in during the same tick arrive in the order of their IDs, the same on any computer and any number of cores.
  • Taken out while inside: something despawned inside a zone counts as leaving, so the zone hears Exited. A zone that's despawned says nothing.
  • Saved: who is inside, and whether a Once zone has fired, are kept in save games and in the game's checksum, so a loaded game carries on exactly.
  • A zone never counts itself, even if its entity is a character.

Custom code on a zone#

A zone is an entity like any other, so it can carry your own components (+ Component in Properties), in Lust, Lua or Rust. New code for this zone… is the quick way: it makes the file and adds the component in one step (one step to undo, too). See Game code for components and events.

Making one a prefab#

A zone can be made into a prefab like any entity: right-click it in the Level panel and make a prefab, and every copy has the same shape, settings and code. A "spike pit" prefab with its own Entered code, placed ten times, is ten pits that each know who fell in.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Freeform: place a point while drawingclick
Freeform: close the shapeclick the first point, or Enter
Freeform: give up drawingEsc
Edit a freeform zone's pointsTab (with the zone picked)
Move a pointdrag it
Add a point on an edgeCtrl+click
Remove the picked pointDelete
Finish editing pointsTab or Esc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: nothing is heard when the player walks in. Why: the player isn't a character or a moving body (no CharacterBody, Collider2D ticked Character, or dynamic RigidBody), or the zone has no game code. Fix: check the player's components, and use New code for this zone….
  • Problem: Entered comes once and never again. Why: Fires is Once. Fix: set it to Every time.
  • Problem: a fast teleport through a zone isn't heard. Why: only where things are at each tick counts. Fix: make the zone bigger, or check in the teleport's own code.
  • Problem: a freeform change is refused. Why: it would make the outline cross itself, or leave fewer than 3 or more than 256 points. Fix: move the point somewhere the outline stays one loop.

Related#

  • Concepts: trigger zone, event.
  • Game code: components and events.
  • Physics and Walls and walking in 2D: characters and bodies.
  • Save games: what's kept.
  • Prefabs.
← Previous · Chapter 48Parallax layersNext → · Chapter 50Tags

Tags#

Labels you give entities, such as Enemy or Collectible, so game code can find every one of a kind: "all enemies within 3 m", "the nearest collectible".

When to use it#

Whenever game code needs to find things by what they are rather than by name: a guard looking for the nearest enemy, a magnet pulling in every coin within reach, a door that opens only for the player, a turret that ignores anything flying. A tag is a label an entity carries; an entity can carry several (a bat can be both Enemy and Flying), and many entities can carry the same one.

Why tags and not names? A name belongs to one entity, and World:find("Bat 12") finds that one. A tag belongs to a kind, so code written once works for every enemy you'll ever place, copy or spawn. And because the project keeps its own list of tags, game code names each as Tag.Enemy: a misspelt tag (Tag.Enmey) is a mistake in Problems before the game runs, not a question that quietly finds nothing.

To ask "which of these have a Health?", you can already ask by component. Tags are for kinds you decide yourself, whatever components the entities have.

How to use it#

Make the project's tags#

  1. Click the File tab, then Project settings, then the Tags sub-tab.
  2. Click + New tag, type its name, and press Enter to keep it (Esc gives it up). A tag's name is what game code calls it, so it starts with a capital letter and holds only letters, digits and _: Enemy, Collectible, BigDoor. A name that can't be one says why beside it, and suggests one that can.
  3. Each tag's row says what uses it: "Used by 14 entities and 2 prefabs" (entities in all the project's levels, copies of prefabs among them).

Renaming: double-click a tag's name (or ⋯ › Rename), type the new one and press Enter. It's renamed everywhere at once: every level and prefab keeps its tags by an ID that never changes, so they all follow, and game code's name changes with it. Code still saying the old name (Tag.Enemy after renaming it Monster) becomes a mistake in Problems, pointing at each line to change.

Deleting: ⋯ › Delete. A tag nothing uses goes at once. One that's used asks first, saying what carries it (which levels' entities, which prefabs): deleting it takes it off all of them.

The tags are kept in the project's tags.lst, a small text file beside project.solis that Git can merge. If it changes on disk (a pull, an edit by hand), Solis reads it again. In the Library it's shown as Project's tags, with a gear: a double-click opens Project settings › Tags, never a code editor.

Tag entities#

  1. Pick an entity. Its tags are under its name in Properties, as chips.
  2. Click + Tag ▾: a list of the project's tags opens, with a box at the top to search it. Click one to give it, or type a name and click New tag "…" (or press Enter) to make a new tag and give it in one go.
  3. A chip's × takes that tag off.

Each change is one step to undo. With several entities picked, Properties shows the tags they all carry, and a change applies to each of them.

The Level panel shows each entity's tags faintly after its name ("Bat Enemy · Flying"), and its search finds entities by tag as well as by name: search enemy to see every enemy in the level.

Tags on prefabs#

Tags set on a prefab are on every copy of it: tag the Bat prefab Enemy, and every bat placed or spawned is an enemy. A copy may add a tag of its own or take one away: its Tags row then has the orange dot (it differs from its prefab) and ↶, which puts the prefab's tags back. As with any setting, the copy's own change wins: if the prefab's tags change later, a copy that changed its own keeps them, and the others follow.

Ask the world in game code#

Three questions, and two changes:

CallWhat it gives
hasTag(Tag.Enemy)Whether the entity carries the tag (is target:hasTag(Tag.Enemy)?).
World:within(Tag.Enemy, place, 3)Every entity carrying the tag within 3 m of place, nearest first; two at the same distance come in the order of their IDs. An empty list when there are none.
World:nearest(Tag.Enemy, place)The nearest entity carrying the tag, or nothing when none does.
addTag(Tag.Enemy), removeTag(Tag.Enemy)Give the entity the tag, or take it off.

They're answered from where everything was as the tick started, the same on every core, so a game comes out the same however many cores run it. For the same reason, a tag added or taken off lands at the end of the tick, as moves do: hasTag sees it from the next tick. Calling addTag for a tag already carried changes nothing, so it's safe every tick.

-- guard.lst: a guard that watches for enemies.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Tag;

component Guard {
    has {
        float reach = 3;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- The nearest enemy, wherever it is.
        entity closest = World:nearest(Tag.Enemy, position());
        is closest != nothing? then {
            World:say(name() + " watches " + closest:name());
        }

        -- Every enemy within reach, nearest first.
        entity array near = World:within(Tag.Enemy, position(), reach);
        int count = #near;
        is count > 0? then {
            World:say(count.text() + " enemies within reach");
        }

        -- Only those that don't fly can be caught: they stop being enemies.
        loop (entity enemy in near) {
            is not enemy:hasTag(Tag.Flying)? then {
                enemy:removeTag(Tag.Enemy);
            }
        }
    }
}
pass Guard;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Guard {
    reach: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Guard {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let place = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();

        // The nearest enemy, wherever it is.
        if let Some(closest) = cx.host().nearest("Enemy", place) {
            let name = cx.host().name(me).unwrap_or_default();
            let theirs = cx.host().name(closest).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().say(&format!("{name} watches {theirs}"));
        }

        // Every enemy within reach, nearest first.
        let near = cx.host().within("Enemy", place, self.reach);
        if !near.is_empty() {
            cx.host().say(&format!("{} enemies within reach", near.len()));
        }

        // Only those that don't fly can be caught: they stop being enemies.
        for enemy in near {
            if !cx.host().has_tag(enemy, "Flying") {
                cx.host().remove_tag(enemy, "Enemy");
            }
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Guard = component("Guard", {
    { "reach", "float", 3 },
})

function Guard:update(dt)
    local place = solis.entity.position(self.me)

    -- The nearest enemy, wherever it is.
    local closest = solis.World:nearest("Enemy", place)
    if closest then
        solis.World:say(solis.entity.name(self.me) .. " watches " .. solis.entity.name(closest))
    end

    -- Every enemy within reach, nearest first.
    local near = solis.World:within("Enemy", place, self.reach)
    if #near > 0 then
        solis.World:say(#near .. " enemies within reach")
    end

    -- Only those that don't fly can be caught: they stop being enemies.
    for _, enemy in ipairs(near) do
        if not solis.entity.hasTag(enemy, "Flying") then
            solis.entity.removeTag(enemy, "Enemy")
        end
    end
end

In Lust, Tag comes from the project's own names (fetch "solis/project":Tag;), written again whenever its tags change. In Lua and Rust a tag is its name as text ("Enemy"); a name the project hasn't is a tag nothing carries.

Distance in 2D and 3D#

In a 2D project (Project settings › General › Kind), distance is measured across the ground, whatever the layers: a bat drawn on a layer above the slug is still "within 3 m" if it's 3 m away on the map. In a 3D project, or one of Both, distance is measured in 3D: a bird 50 m up isn't within 3 m of a guard standing under it.

The questions are quick even with thousands of tagged entities: each tick, Solis sorts each tag's entities into a grid over the ground once, and a question looks only in the cells its distance reaches. 2,000 units each asking every tick cost under a millisecond.

Zones that notice only some#

A trigger zone's Only tags limits it to entities carrying at least one of the tags chosen there: a door that opens only for the Player, a pit that catches only Enemies.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Project settings › TagsThe project's tags: make, rename everywhere, delete. Kept in tags.lst.
Tags (under an entity's name)The tags it carries: chips with ×, and + Tag ▾. On a prefab's copy, the orange dot and ↶ when they differ from the prefab's.
Only tags with several zones pickedThe tags they share, by name; nothing when they differ. Pick one zone to change them.
Only tags (a trigger zone's card)The tags a zone notices; none chosen, it notices everything it can.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Rename a tag everywhereDouble-click its name in Project settings › Tags (Enter keeps it, Esc leaves it)
Keep a new tag's nameEnter (Esc gives it up)
In + Tag's box: give the first tag found, or make the tag typedEnter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says Tag.Enmey isn't a Tag. Why: the project has no tag of that name: a typo, or a tag renamed since. Fix: correct the line, or make the tag in Project settings › Tags.
  • Problem: hasTag says no just after addTag. Why: changes land at the end of the tick, so every core sees the same world during it. Fix: nothing to fix: from the next tick it says yes. Keep what you just did in a variable if the same tick needs it.
  • Problem: a name is refused. Why: game code calls a tag Tag.<name>, so it must be one Lust can name: a capital letter first, then letters, digits or _, not all capitals, and none of Lust's own words. Fix: take the suggestion beside it (big door becomes BigDoor).
  • Problem: a copy of a prefab doesn't get a tag the prefab was just given. Why: that copy changed its own tags (it has the orange dot), and a copy's own change wins. Fix: click ↶ on its Tags row to follow the prefab again.

Related#

  • Trigger zones: Only tags.
  • Prefabs: copies and their own changes.
  • Game code: components, the tick, and the project's names.
  • Settings: Project settings.
  • Concepts: tag, tick, prefab.
← Previous · Chapter 49Trigger zonesNext → · Chapter 51Data tables

Data tables#

Your game's data, such as every item with its price and description or every crop with its days to grow, in one table you edit like a spreadsheet, and game code reads by name with every spelling checked.

When to use it#

Whenever a game has many things of one kind that differ only in their numbers and words: items in a shop, enemies with their health and speed, crops, spells, levels' par times, a list of quests' titles. Without a table, those numbers end up scattered through code (is item == Item.Sword? then { price = 120; }) or copied into many components, and changing a price means hunting for it.

A data table keeps them together: one row a thing, one column a fact about it. You edit it in the Table tab, which works like a spreadsheet, and game code asks for a row by its ID: Items:row(Item.IronSword).price. Because Solis turns the table's IDs and columns into names game code checks, a misspelt row (Item.IronSwrod) or column (.prise) is a mistake in Problems before the game runs, never a price of 0 found while playing.

Tables are read-only while the game plays: they're your game's constants, its design, not something that changes as it's played. What changes (the player's gold, what's in their bag) belongs in components and game-wide objects, which are saved. That's also why a table isn't in save games: a save keeps what happened, and the table says what things are.

An inventory, a shop or a crafting system isn't built into Solis: they're games you make with tables, tags and game code. A table is the part that says what each item is.

How to use it#

Make a table#

  1. In the Library, right-click empty space or a folder and choose New table. A table called table.table.lst is made with one column, Name, and one row. Rename it like any file (right-click › Rename…) after what it holds, in the plural (items, crops, enemies): game code calls the table by that name.
  2. It opens in the Table tab, beside the level's view on Home. Later, double-click it in the Library to open it again: tables have their own icon (a little grid) and a sand-coloured mark, and the Library's Code filter shows them.

Columns and rows#

  • + Row adds a row below the one you're on, with an ID of its own (Item, Item2…). Type over it: an ID is how game code names the row, so it starts with a capital letter and holds only letters, digits and _ (IronSword, not iron sword). Solis says why one can't be, and suggests one that can.
  • + Column ▾ adds a column after the one you're on; choose what it holds:
KindHoldsGame code gets
textwords, such as a name or a descriptionstring
whole number5, -3, 120int
number0.25, 3.5float
yes or noa tick box: click it, or press Enter on itbool
choiceone of the column's own options, such as Common and Rarea state of the table's own (ItemRarity)
coloura colour, typed as #ff8800colour
sound, clip, picture, prefab, screen, level, tagone of the project's names, picked from a list as you typethat name (Picture, Sound…)
  • Right-click a heading to rename the column (its name is what game code reads, so daysToGrow rather than days to grow; the heading shows it as "Days to grow"), to type a choice's options (separated by commas; renaming one carries its cells with it), to mark a text column Translated, to change what it holds (cells whose text fits keep it), to move it left or right, or to delete it.
  • Right-click a row to add a row below, move it up or down, copy, clear, or delete it (or every row picked).
  • Each row is a names what one row is, Item for a table of items: game code's names come from it (Item, ItemRow, ItemRarity). A table read without one is named from its file (items gives Item); a new table's starts as TableRow, so set it once you've named the table.

Every change is one step to undo with Ctrl+Z over the tab, and is saved at once.

Type in cells#

Click a cell to put the cursor on it, then use the keys spreadsheets use: Enter or F2 starts typing (or just type: the first key replaces what's there), Enter keeps it and moves down, Tab keeps it and moves right, and Esc leaves the cell as it was. A double-click types too. A value that doesn't fit its column (lots in a price) isn't kept, and the Console says why.

In a choice or a name column, what fits what you've typed is listed under the cell: click one, or press Enter on a whole option.

Copy, paste and spreadsheets#

Pick a block of cells (Shift+click, a drag, or Shift with the arrows) and press Ctrl+C: it's copied as the tab-separated text spreadsheets use, so it pastes into one as cells. Ctrl+V pastes a spreadsheet's cells at the cursor, adding rows if they run past the end. Delete empties the block.

Export CSV writes the whole table beside it as a CSV file (items.csv beside items.table.lst), which any spreadsheet opens. Import CSV reads that file back: rows are matched by their ID (the first column) and columns by their name or heading, so you can edit prices in a spreadsheet and bring them back; rows and columns the table doesn't have are added. An import is one step to undo.

Look without changing#

Search shows only the rows with a cell holding what you type. Click a heading to sort the rows by it, lowest first; click again for highest first, and again for the table's own order. Both are only for looking: the table keeps its order, which is the order game code lists the rows in.

Read a table in game code#

Each table gets a Lust file of its own, which Solis writes into solis/tables/ whenever the table changes: data/items.table.lst gives solis/tables/data/items.lst. In it are a state of the rows' IDs (Item), a class for one row (ItemRow, a field a column, read-only) and the table itself (Items), which gives a row by its ID or every row in order:

-- shop.lst: a shopkeeper who knows every price.
fetch "solis/tables/data/items":[Items, Item, ItemRow, ItemRarity];
fetch "solis/world":World;

component Shopkeeper {
    has {
        int gold = 200;
    }

    -- Sells one thing, if the player has the gold.
    method sell(Item which) {
        ItemRow item = Items:row(which);
        is gold >= item.price? then {
            gold -= item.price;
            World:say("Sold: {item.name}");
        }
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Every rare item, in the table's order.
        loop (ItemRow item in Items:rows()) {
            is item.rarity == ItemRarity.Rare? then {
                World:say("{item.name}: {item.price} gold");
            }
        }
    }
}

pass Shopkeeper;
end
// Rust reads the table through its host, by the table's name and each
// row's ID and column's name as text.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Shopkeeper {
    gold: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Shopkeeper {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let tables = cx.host().tables();
        let Some(items) = tables.get("Items") else {
            return;
        };

        // One row by its ID.
        if let Some(sword) = items.row("IronSword") {
            let price = sword.whole("price").unwrap_or(0);
            if self.gold >= price {
                self.gold -= price;
            }
        }

        // Every rare item, in the table's order.
        let rare: Vec<&str> = items
            .rows()
            .filter(|row| row.text("rarity") == Some("Rare"))
            .map(|row| row.id())
            .collect();
        cx.host().say(&format!("Rare: {}", rare.join(", ")));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The table's Lust file is Lust's. Lua reaches the table through
-- solis.Items, with each row's ID as text: a misspelt one stops with
-- the nearest ID.
local Shopkeeper = component("Shopkeeper", {
    { "gold", "int", 200 },
})

function Shopkeeper:update(dt)
    -- One row by its ID.
    local sword = solis.Items:row("IronSword")
    if self.gold >= sword.price then
        self.gold = self.gold - sword.price
    end

    -- Every rare item, in the table's order.
    for _, item in ipairs(solis.Items:rows()) do
        if item.rarity == "Rare" then
            solis.World:say(item.name .. ": " .. item.price .. " gold")
        end
    end
end

Items:row(...) is quick enough to call every tick: a row is made once and kept. Items:rows() gives a new list each time, so you may change the list (not the rows). In a very big table, ask for rows by ID where you can: listing 100,000 rows makes all of them at once.

A component can keep a row's ID in a field (Item stock = Item.Apple;): Properties then offers the table's IDs as a choice.

A table saved while the game runs is read from the next tick on. A save game or a recording remembers which tables it was made with: loading or playing one back after a table changed says so once in the Console, since the game may not go the same way.

Translated on a text column does nothing yet. It marks the text the coming translations milestone will translate, so tables made now are ready for it.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Each row is aWhat one row is (Item): game code's names for the table's IDs, its row class and its choices come from it.
A column's nameWhat game code reads (row.price): a small letter first, then letters, digits and _; never id, which is the row's ID.
A column's kindWhat its cells hold, and what game code gets: see the table above.
A choice's optionsThe names a choice cell can hold, separated by commas.
TranslatedMarks a text column for translating (from the translations milestone on).

The limits: 100,000 rows, 64 columns, 2,000,000 cells in all, 1,024 options in a choice and 10,000 characters in a cell. Past one, Solis says which and suggests splitting the table.

Shortcuts#

These work inside the Table tab's grid only, once you've clicked a cell.

ActionShortcut
Type in the cell; keep what's typed and move downEnter
Type in the cellF2, or any key typed
Keep what's typed and move right; move rightTab
Move leftShift+Tab
Movethe arrow keys
Pick a blockShift + an arrow key, Shift+click, or a drag
Leave the cell as it wasEsc
Empty the cells pickedDelete
Copy, paste cellsCtrl+C, Ctrl+V
Undo, redoCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y
Sort by a columnClick its heading

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says Item.IronSwrod isn't an Item. Why: the table has no row of that ID: a typo, or a row renamed since. Fix: correct the line, or rename the row back. Renaming a row's ID doesn't change your code: Problems points at each line still using the old one.
  • Problem: a name cell shows none. Why: nothing's picked, or the file it named was deleted. Fix: type in it and pick one; game code gets an empty name from it, which matches nothing.
  • Problem: the table isn't in game code, and the Console says it can't be reached. Why: its file name can't be a Lust name (it starts with a digit), or another table or one of Solis's own objects (World, Input…) has the same name. Fix: rename the file.
  • Problem: Import CSV says there's no CSV. Why: it reads the CSV beside the table with the table's name (items.csv). Fix: export first, or save your spreadsheet under that name, as CSV in UTF-8.

Related#

  • Game code, States and Concepts: states, and the project's names.
  • Tags, for kinds of entity rather than kinds of data.
  • Save games.
← Previous · Chapter 50TagsNext → · Chapter 52Timers

Timers#

Waits your game code starts by name: "open in 2 seconds", "every 5 seconds", "each day at six". When one finishes, the component that started it hears TimerFinished.

When to use it#

Whenever something should happen later, or again and again: a door that opens two seconds after its switch is pulled, a spawner that sends a wave every five seconds, a rooster that crows each morning at six, a trap that resets after a while. A timer is a named wait: you start it, game time passes, and when it's done the component that started it is told.

Why not count seconds yourself, in a field? You can (left = left - dt;), but a timer does three things that are easy to get wrong:

  • It counts game time, exactly. A timer's seconds become whole ticks once, as it starts, and Solis counts them in whole numbers, so two seconds is always exactly 120 ticks at normal speed: no tiny rounding that builds up over a long game. It follows the game's speed (World:setGameSpeed): at half speed it takes twice as many ticks, and while the speed is 0 (paused) it doesn't count at all.
  • It's saved. A save made while a timer waits keeps it, and the loaded game finishes it on exactly the tick the saved one would have.
  • It's in order. Timers finishing in the same tick come in a fixed order (see Order), so the game comes out the same on any computer and any number of cores.

For a value that should glide to a new one over time (a door swinging open), use a tween. Timers are for when something happens; tweens for how a value moves.

How to use it#

Start a timer, and hear it finish#

Inside a component, call startTimer with the timer's name and how many seconds to wait. When the time has passed, the component gets the event TimerFinished, carrying which timer it was:

-- door.lst: a door that opens two seconds after its switch is pulled.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Timer;
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

event SwitchPulled();

component Door {
    has {
        bool open = false;
    }

    -- The switch sends this; the door waits two seconds.
    on SwitchPulled() {
        startTimer(Timer.DoorOpens, 2.0);
        World:say("The door rumbles...");
    }

    -- Two seconds of game time later.
    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        is which == Timer.DoorOpens? then {
            open = true;
            World:say("The door opens.");
        }
    }
}
pass Door, SwitchPulled;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent, Timing};

pub struct Door {
    open: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for Door {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        let me = cx.me();
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // The switch sends this; the door waits two seconds.
            "SwitchPulled" => {
                cx.host()
                    .start_timer(me, "DoorOpens", Timing::After(2.0))
                    .expect("a door's timer is its own");
                cx.host().say("The door rumbles...");
                true
            }
            // Two seconds of game time later.
            "TimerFinished" => {
                let which = match event.values.first() {
                    Some(Value::Text(name)) => name.as_str(),
                    _ => "",
                };
                if which == "DoorOpens" {
                    self.open = true;
                    cx.host().say("The door opens.");
                }
                true
            }
            _ => false,
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Door = component("Door", {
    { "open", "bool", false },
})

-- The switch sends this; the door waits two seconds.
function Door:on_SwitchPulled()
    solis.entity.startTimer(self.me, "DoorOpens", 2.0)
    solis.World:say("The door rumbles...")
end

-- Two seconds of game time later.
function Door:on_TimerFinished(which)
    if which == "DoorOpens" then
        self.open = true
        solis.World:say("The door opens.")
    end
end

Naming a timer. In Lust a timer's name is one of the game's Timer names, Timer.DoorOpens, which you bring in with fetch "solis/project":Timer;. There's no list to keep anywhere: the call that starts a timer names it. Solis reads your Lust, finds every name a startTimer, startTimerEvery or startTimerAtHour gives, and writes them into solis/project.lst as the state Timer. So a name misspelt anywhere else (stopTimer(Timer.DoorOpnes), is which == Timer.DorOpens?) is a mistake in Problems before the game runs. In Lua and Rust a timer is its name as text ("DoorOpens"): a capital letter first, then letters, digits and _.

A timer is its component's own. Two components can each have a timer called Wave, even on the same entity, and they never mix: TimerFinished goes only to the component that started the timer, and the other components on the entity don't hear it. That's also why the calls are made bare, inside the component (startTimer(...), not other:startTimer(...)): starting a timer on another entity, or in a game-wide object or a tween, is a mistake that stops with its line.

Starting a timer that's already running starts it again from the new time: the old wait is forgotten. So start a timer once, when the thing happens (the switch is pulled), not every tick: started every tick, it never finishes.

How long: the seconds are rounded to the nearest tick (a 60th of a second). 0 finishes on the next tick, never in the same one. The longest wait is about 115 days of game time.

Repeat every few seconds#

startTimerEvery finishes again and again, until you stop it:

-- spawner.lst: a wave every five seconds, until the tenth.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":[Timer, Prefab];
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

component Spawner {
    has {
        int waves = 0;
        bool started = false;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Start once, on the first tick.
        is not started? then {
            startTimerEvery(Timer.Wave, 5.0);
            started = true;
        }
    }

    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        waves = waves + 1;
        entity drone = World:spawn(Prefab.Drones.Drone, position() + [0, 0, 2]);

        -- Ten waves, then no more.
        is waves >= 10? then {
            stopTimer(Timer.Wave);
        }
    }
}
pass Spawner;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent, Timing};

pub struct Spawner {
    waves: i64,
    started: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for Spawner {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        // Start once, on the first tick.
        if !self.started {
            let me = cx.me();
            cx.host()
                .start_timer(me, "Wave", Timing::Every(5.0))
                .expect("a spawner's timer is its own");
            self.started = true;
        }
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "TimerFinished" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        self.waves += 1;
        let place = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let _drone = cx.host().spawn("drones/drone", place + glam::Vec3::Z * 2.0);

        // Ten waves, then no more.
        if self.waves >= 10 {
            cx.host().stop_timer(me, "Wave").expect("its own timer");
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Spawner = component("Spawner", {
    { "waves", "int", 0 },
    { "started", "bool", false },
})

function Spawner:update(dt)
    -- Start once, on the first tick.
    if not self.started then
        solis.entity.startTimerEvery(self.me, "Wave", 5.0)
        self.started = true
    end
end

function Spawner:on_TimerFinished(which)
    self.waves = self.waves + 1
    local place = solis.entity.position(self.me)
    local drone = solis.World:spawn("Drones.Drone", place + vec3(0, 0, 2))

    -- Ten waves, then no more.
    if self.waves >= 10 then
        solis.entity.stopTimer(self.me, "Wave")
    end
end

A repeating timer keeps its rhythm: each turn is counted from the last turn, not from when your code handled it, so it never drifts. At a game speed so fast that several turns pass in one tick, it finishes once that tick and carries on in step. The shortest repeat is one tick.

Each day at a time of day#

With day and night on the Environment, the game has a clock. startTimerAtHour finishes each day as that clock passes an hour (6.5 is half past six), until you stop it:

-- rooster.lst: crows each morning, and a bed that skips to the morning.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Timer;
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

component Rooster {
    has {
        bool started = false;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        is not started? then {
            startTimerAtHour(Timer.Dawn, 6.0);
            started = true;
        }
    }

    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        World:say("Cock-a-doodle-doo!");
    }
}

component Bed {
    -- Sleeping: the clock jumps to seven the next morning.
    method sleep() {
        World:setTimeOfDay(7.0);
    }
}
pass Rooster, Bed;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent, Timing};

pub struct Rooster {
    started: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for Rooster {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        if !self.started {
            let me = cx.me();
            cx.host()
                .start_timer(me, "Dawn", Timing::AtHour(6.0))
                .expect("a rooster's timer is its own");
            self.started = true;
        }
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "TimerFinished" {
            return false;
        }
        cx.host().say("Cock-a-doodle-doo!");
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
    // A bed calls cx.host().set_time_of_day(7.0) to skip to the morning.
}
local Rooster = component("Rooster", {
    { "started", "bool", false },
})

function Rooster:update(dt)
    if not self.started then
        solis.entity.startTimerAtHour(self.me, "Dawn", 6.0)
        self.started = true
    end
end

function Rooster:on_TimerFinished(which)
    solis.World:say("Cock-a-doodle-doo!")
end

-- A bed calls solis.World:setTimeOfDay(7.0) to skip to the morning.

When the clock jumps. Sleeping in a bed (World:setTimeOfDay(7.0) at ten at night) jumps the clock past six: the rooster crows once, on the next tick, not once for every hour skipped. Midnight works the same way: a timer at 23:30 or at 0:00 finishes as the clock goes round. Setting the clock always moves the day forward to that hour, so setting it from seven back to five is the day going on to five the next morning, which comes before six: the rooster crows when six comes.

Stop a timer, and ask about one#

CallWhat it does
startTimer(Timer.X, seconds)Finishes once, that many seconds of game time from now.
startTimerEvery(Timer.X, seconds)Finishes every that many seconds, until stopped.
startTimerAtHour(Timer.X, hour)Finishes each day as the day's clock passes that hour, until stopped.
stopTimer(Timer.X)Stops it, so it doesn't finish. One that isn't running changes nothing.
timerRunning(Timer.X)Whether it's running: is timerRunning(Timer.DoorOpens)? then { … }.
timeLeft(Timer.X)The seconds of game time left; 0 when it isn't running.
on TimerFinished(Timer which)Heard when one of this component's timers finishes.

Starting and stopping land at the end of the tick, as moves do, and timerRunning and timeLeft answer as the tick started: a timer started this tick is running from the next. In Lua they're solis.entity.startTimer(self.me, "DoorOpens", 2.0) and so on; in Rust, through the component's host: start_timer, stop_timer and timer_left (which gives None when the timer isn't running).

Order#

Timers that finish in the same tick are heard in the tick's first round of events, after the components' updates, in a fixed order: the one due earliest first, then by entity (in the order of their IDs), then by component (by name), then in the order they were started. So the same game comes out the same on one core or sixteen.

Timers, saves and new code#

  • Saves: a save game keeps every timer waiting; loaded, each finishes on the tick it would have.
  • When an entity goes: despawning an entity, or taking the component off it, ends its timers quietly: they never finish.
  • When its state changes: a timer a Lust component starts while in a state of its own (state = Mood.Stunned;) belongs to that state, and ends quietly when the component leaves it: its TimerFinished never comes. keepStarted() lets it run on. See States that start and stop.
  • New code while playing: a timer keeps running while its component is still in the code and its Lust still starts a timer of that name. Rename the timer, or take the component out, and the timers that no longer fit stop, with one note in the Console saying which.

Steps in order#

"Walk to the well, wait a second, say hello, wait two seconds, walk home": a character doing things one after another, waiting in between. Write it with one timer and a field for the step it's on. Each wait starts the timer; when it finishes, the code moves on to the next step:

-- messenger.lst: walks to the well, waits, says hello, waits, walks home.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Timer;
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

state Step = [WalkThere, WaitThere, WaitAfterHello, WalkHome, Home];

component Messenger {
    has {
        Step step = Step.WalkThere;
        vec3 well = [10, 0, 0];
        vec3 home = [0, 0, 0];
        float speed = 2;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Walking takes every tick; waiting is the timer's.
        is step == Step.WalkThere && arrived(well, dt)? then {
            step = Step.WaitThere;
            startTimer(Timer.NextStep, 1.0);
        }
        is step == Step.WalkHome && arrived(home, dt)? then {
            step = Step.Home;
        }
    }

    -- Each wait ends here, and the next step begins.
    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        is step == Step.WaitThere? then {
            World:say("Hello!");
            step = Step.WaitAfterHello;
            startTimer(Timer.NextStep, 2.0);
        } or is step == Step.WaitAfterHello? then {
            step = Step.WalkHome;
        }
    }

    -- Moves a step towards a place; true once it's there.
    method bool arrived(vec3 place, float dt) {
        vec3 way = place - position();
        float far = way:length();
        float stride = speed * dt;
        is far <= stride? then {
            moveTo(place);
            return true;
        }
