        moveTo(position() + way * (stride / far));
        return false;
    }
}
pass Messenger;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent, Timing};

#[derive(PartialEq)]
enum Step {
    WalkThere,
    WaitThere,
    WaitAfterHello,
    WalkHome,
    Home,
}

pub struct Messenger {
    step: Step,
    well: Vec3,
    home: Vec3,
    speed: f32,
}

impl Messenger {
    /// Moves a step towards a place; true once it's there.
    fn arrived(&self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, place: Vec3, dt: f64) -> bool {
        let me = cx.me();
        let now = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let way = place - now;
        let stride = self.speed * dt as f32;
        if way.length() <= stride {
            cx.host().move_to(me, place);
            return true;
        }
        cx.host().move_to(me, now + way * (stride / way.length()));
        false
    }
}

impl RustComponent for Messenger {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        // Walking takes every tick; waiting is the timer's.
        if self.step == Step::WalkThere && self.arrived(cx, self.well, dt) {
            self.step = Step::WaitThere;
            cx.host()
                .start_timer(me, "NextStep", Timing::After(1.0))
                .expect("its own timer");
        }
        if self.step == Step::WalkHome && self.arrived(cx, self.home, dt) {
            self.step = Step::Home;
        }
    }

    // Each wait ends here, and the next step begins.
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "TimerFinished" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        if self.step == Step::WaitThere {
            cx.host().say("Hello!");
            self.step = Step::WaitAfterHello;
            cx.host()
                .start_timer(me, "NextStep", Timing::After(2.0))
                .expect("its own timer");
        } else if self.step == Step::WaitAfterHello {
            self.step = Step::WalkHome;
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Messenger = component("Messenger", {
    { "step", "string", "WalkThere" },
    { "well", "vec3", vec3(10, 0, 0) },
    { "home", "vec3", vec3(0, 0, 0) },
    { "speed", "float", 2 },
})

-- Moves a step towards a place; true once it's there.
function Messenger:arrived(place, dt)
    local now = solis.entity.position(self.me)
    local way = place - now
    local far = math.sqrt(way.x * way.x + way.y * way.y + way.z * way.z)
    local stride = self.speed * dt
    if far <= stride then
        solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, place)
        return true
    end
    solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, now + way * (stride / far))
    return false
end

function Messenger:update(dt)
    -- Walking takes every tick; waiting is the timer's.
    if self.step == "WalkThere" and self:arrived(self.well, dt) then
        self.step = "WaitThere"
        solis.entity.startTimer(self.me, "NextStep", 1.0)
    end
    if self.step == "WalkHome" and self:arrived(self.home, dt) then
        self.step = "Home"
    end
end

-- Each wait ends here, and the next step begins.
function Messenger:on_TimerFinished(which)
    if self.step == "WaitThere" then
        solis.World:say("Hello!")
        self.step = "WaitAfterHello"
        solis.entity.startTimer(self.me, "NextStep", 2.0)
    elseif self.step == "WaitAfterHello" then
        self.step = "WalkHome"
    end
end

Why a field and not "wait 1 second" in the middle of the code? Because the step is a field, it's saved: a save made while the messenger waits at the well loads with it still waiting there, and saying hello a second later. Code paused halfway through a method can't be saved, so Solis has no wait for game code.

Later, Lust will let you write the waits where they happen, as blocks run later: after 1.0 { World:say("Hello!"); }. That will make steps in order much shorter. Such a block may use only the component's own fields, so it can be saved just like this one.

Settings#

Timers have no settings of their own: they're started and stopped by game code. A time-of-day timer uses the Environment's Day and night clock (A day lasts, Starts at), as Sky, fog and exposure describes.

Shortcuts#

Timers have no shortcuts.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a timer never finishes. Why: it's started again every tick (startTimer in update with nothing around it), so each start pushes it back. Fix: start it once, when the thing happens, or check timerRunning first.
  • Problem: Problems says Timer.DoorOpnes isn't a Timer. Why: no startTimer in the game's Lust names it: a typo, or the timer was renamed. Fix: use the name the start call gives, or start the timer under that name.
  • Problem: Problems says a timer's name isn't a Timer, though it's set in a variable first (Timer next = Timer.Later;). Why: only a start call names a timer. Fix: start it by name somewhere (startTimer(Timer.Later, …)), even if other code chooses which to start.
  • Problem: a timer stopped when the code changed while playing. Why: its name, or its component, is gone from the new code; the Console says which. Fix: start it again, under its new name.
  • Problem: a timer stopped, and its TimerFinished never came, though nothing stopped it. Why: it was started while its component was in a state of its own, and the state changed. Fix: start it after setting the new state, or call keepStarted() after starting it (States that start and stop).
  • Problem: timerRunning says no just after startTimer. Why: starts land at the end of the tick, so every core sees the same timers during it. Fix: nothing to fix: from the next tick it says yes.
  • Problem: startTimer stops with "a timer belongs to the component that starts it". Why: it was called on another entity, or in a game-wide object or a tween. Fix: send that entity an event, and let its own component start its timer.

Related#

  • Game code: components, events, the tick, tweens and game-wide objects.
  • States that start and stop: timers that end with their state.
  • Save games: what a save keeps.
  • Sky, fog and exposure: the day and night clock.
  • Concepts: timer, tick, event, state.

States that start and stop#

A component's own state, such as Calm or Stunned, ends what it started while in it: its timers, tweens and looping sounds stop by themselves when the state changes, and the component hears the change.

When to use it#

Whenever a character, a door or a machine is in one of a few modes, and each mode starts things of its own. A stunned character flashes, plays a dizzy sound on a loop and starts a timer to recover. When the stun ends (because the timer finished, or because something knocked it out of the stun early), the flash, the sound and the timer must all stop. Written by hand, that means remembering to stop each one wherever the stun can end, and a forgotten one shows up as a character still flashing, or recovering from a stun it already left.

A Lust component's own state does that bookkeeping for you: what it starts while in an option ends when it leaves that option. It's the same rule Lust already has for objects a class makes in its state (things made in a state end with it), carried over to what the engine runs: timers, tweens and looping sounds.

This is a Lust component's own state, the one written state = Mood.Calm; in its has. A field that holds a state (Mood mood = Mood.Calm;) is an ordinary value: changing it ends nothing. Lua and Rust components have no state of their own (see In Lua and Rust).

How to use it#

Enter a state in the code that sets it#

There's nothing new to learn to enter a state: the code that sets state = Mood.Stunned; does the entering work right there, on the next lines. Whatever it starts (a timer, a tween, a sound) belongs to Stunned, because that's the component's state at the moment it starts:

-- hero.lst: stunned by a hit, recovering a second and a half later.
fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":[Timer, Sound];
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

state Mood = [Calm, Stunned];
event Hit(float damage);
event MoodChanged(Mood from, Mood to);

component Hero {
    has {
        state = Mood.Calm;
        float flash = 0;
    }

    -- A hit stuns: everything started here belongs to Stunned.
    on Hit(float damage) {
        state = Mood.Stunned;
        startTimer(Timer.Recover, 1.5);
        tween flash to 1 over 1.5;
        playSound(Sound.Sfx.Dizzy);
    }

    -- The stun is over: setting the state ends the rest.
    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        is which == Timer.Recover? then {
            state = Mood.Calm;
        }
    }

    -- Leaving work in one place, whoever changed the state.
    on MoodChanged(Mood from, Mood to) {
        is from == Mood.Stunned? then {
            flash = 0;
            World:say("Back on my feet.");
        }
    }
}
pass Hero, Hit, MoodChanged;
end
// A Rust component has no state of its own, so nothing ends by itself:
// keep the mode in a field, and stop what it started yourself.
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent, SoundAt, Timing};

#[derive(PartialEq)]
enum Mood {
    Calm,
    Stunned,
}

pub struct Hero {
    mood: Mood,
}

impl Hero {
    /// Leaves the stun: stops what it started.
    fn recover(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>) {
        let me = cx.me();
        self.mood = Mood::Calm;
        cx.host().stop_timer(me, "Recover").expect("its own timer");
        cx.host().stop_sounds_on(me);
        cx.host().say("Back on my feet.");
    }
}

impl RustComponent for Hero {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        let me = cx.me();
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // A hit stuns.
            "Hit" => {
                self.mood = Mood::Stunned;
                cx.host()
                    .start_timer(me, "Recover", Timing::After(1.5))
                    .expect("its own timer");
                cx.host().play_sound("sfx/dizzy", SoundAt::On(me));
                true
            }
            // The stun is over.
            "TimerFinished" => {
                if self.mood == Mood::Stunned {
                    self.recover(cx);
                }
                true
            }
            _ => false,
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- A Lua component has no state of its own, so nothing ends by itself:
-- keep the mode in a field, and stop what it started yourself.
local Hero = component("Hero", {
    { "mood", "string", "Calm" },
})

-- Leaves the stun: stops what it started.
function Hero:recover()
    self.mood = "Calm"
    solis.entity.stopTimer(self.me, "Recover")
    solis.entity.stopSounds(self.me)
    solis.World:say("Back on my feet.")
end

-- A hit stuns.
function Hero:on_Hit(damage)
    self.mood = "Stunned"
    solis.entity.startTimer(self.me, "Recover", 1.5)
    solis.entity.playSound(self.me, "Sfx.Dizzy")
end

-- The stun is over.
function Hero:on_TimerFinished(which)
    if self.mood == "Stunned" then
        self:recover()
    end
end

Here the stun ends when Recover finishes. But if something else changes the state first (a second hit that knocks the hero out, say, state = Mood.KnockedOut;), the stun's timer, its flash and its dizzy loop all stop at that moment, with nothing more to write.

What ends with the state, and what doesn't#

While a component is in an option of its own state, these belong to that option and end when it leaves it:

Started in the stateWhen the state changes
A timer (startTimer, startTimerEvery, startTimerAtHour)It stops, and TimerFinished never comes. Even one that was due this very tick isn't heard once the state has changed.
A tween (tween flash to 1 over 1.5;)It stops where it is: the value keeps what it had reached, and its done block doesn't run.
A sound set to Loop (Sound events), played with playSound or Audio:playIt fades out. A sound that plays once finishes as usual.

And these don't:

  • Spawned entities stay. A smoke puff spawned while stunned is an entity of its own, and goes on after the stun ends. Despawn it yourself if it should go.
  • What's started outside the component's methods belongs to no state: in a tween's done block, or in a game-wide object.
  • What a component without a state of its own starts ends only as it always has.

The moment that counts is the call: a timer belongs to the option the component is in when the timer starts, the value its code has just set. Starting things and then setting the state means they belong to the state before.

Options inside options#

A state's options can hold options of their own, and each counts separately, as in Lust:

-- fighter.lst: a stance inside combat.
fetch "solis/project":[Timer, Sound];

state Mood = [Calm, Combat [Melee, Ranged]];

component Fighter {
    has {
        state = Mood.Calm;
    }

    method enterCombat() {
        state = Mood.Combat;
        playSound(Sound.Music.Battle);
    }

    method closeIn() {
        state = Mood.Combat.Melee;
        startTimerEvery(Timer.Swing, 0.8);
    }

    method backOff() {
        state = Mood.Combat.Ranged;
    }

    method calmDown() {
        state = Mood.Calm;
    }
}
pass Fighter;
end
// Rust components have no state of their own, so options inside
// options are Lust's: in Rust, stop each thing when its mode ends.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Fighter;

impl RustComponent for Fighter {
    fn update(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {}

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- Lua components have no state of their own, so options inside
-- options are Lust's: in Lua, stop each thing when its mode ends.
local Fighter = component("Fighter", {
    { "mood", "string", "Calm" },
})
  • backOff() (from Combat.Melee to Combat.Ranged): the swings started in Melee stop; the battle music started in Combat goes on, since Ranged is still inside Combat.
  • Moving out to Combat itself (from Combat.Melee) ends nothing: Melee is inside it.
  • calmDown() (leaving Combat altogether): what began in Combat and in either stance ends.

Keep something going: keepStarted()#

Sometimes a thing started in a state should outlive it: a door's slow swing that should finish even after the door is locked, or battle music that should play on into the victory. Call keepStarted() after starting it: what the component has started in its state so far no longer belongs to the state, and carries on when it changes. Things started after the call belong to the state as usual:

-- gate.lst: the gate keeps swinging after it's locked; the alarm doesn't.
fetch "solis/project":[Timer, Sound];
fetch "solis/timers":TimerFinished;

state Gate = [Shut, Opening, Locked];

component Guard {
    has {
        state = Gate.Shut;
        float swing = 0;
    }

    method open() {
        state = Gate.Opening;
        tween swing to 90 over 3.0;
        keepStarted();

        -- Started after keepStarted(): ends with Opening.
        playSound(Sound.Alarm);
        startTimer(Timer.Lock, 1.0);
    }

    on TimerFinished(Timer which) {
        state = Gate.Locked;
    }
}
pass Guard;
end
// Rust components have no state of their own, so what they start never
// ends with one: keep_started() keeps nothing, and is there so the three
// languages share the same calls.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Guard;

impl RustComponent for Guard {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().keep_started(me).expect("its own");
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- Lua components have no state of their own, so what they start never
-- ends with one: keepStarted keeps nothing, and is there so the three
-- languages share the same calls.
local Guard = component("Guard", {})

function Guard:update(dt)
    solis.entity.keepStarted(self.me)
end

Like timers, keepStarted() is called bare, inside the component: it keeps what this component started. Called on another entity, or in a game-wide object or a tween, it stops with its line.

Hear the state change#

To hear its own state change, a component's game declares an event for the state, named after it with Changed on the end and carrying the option before and the option now:

state Mood = [Calm, Stunned];
event MoodChanged(Mood from, Mood to);

Then every component whose own state is a Mood hears MoodChanged when its state changes, however it changed: in its own update, in a handler, or in a tween's done block. It's the place for leaving work (put the sword away, stop glowing), kept in one handler instead of copied wherever the state can change (see on MoodChanged in the first example).

  • When: the change is noticed as the tick ends, after everything in it has landed, and heard in the next tick's first round of events: after the timers' TimerFinished, in order of entity, then component name.
  • Once a tick: if the state changes several times in one tick, the event says the first from and the last to. If it ends the tick where it began (stunned and back), nothing is heard.
  • Only the component whose state changed hears it, not the others on its entity.
  • What ends, ends first. The timers, tweens and loops of the options it left have already stopped by the time the event arrives.
  • Declared the wrong way (event MoodChanged(int from);), it's a mistake in Problems before the game runs, saying how to declare it.

Why one event per state, and not one StateChanged for all? In Lust an event carries the same kinds everywhere in the game, so one event can't carry a Mood for the hero and a Gate for the guard. Naming it after its state lets each carry its own, checked before the game runs.

Saves, and new code while playing#

  • Saves: a save game keeps which state each timer belongs to, and a change waiting to be heard. Loaded, the game hears exactly what the saved one would have (never a change twice), and its timers still end when their state changes. Tweens aren't kept in saves yet, whatever their state.
  • Loading or editing values while playing sets a component's state without "changing" it: nothing ends, and nothing is heard.
  • New code while playing keeps each component's state where it can. Tweens stop with new code, as they always have.

In Lua and Rust#

Lua and Rust components have no state of their own: a Lua component's fields are plain values Solis doesn't see change, and a Rust component's are its own. So what they start belongs to no state, and ends only when they stop it, or when the entity goes. They have keepStarted too (solis.entity.keepStarted(self.me), cx.host().keep_started(me)), which keeps nothing for them: it's there so the three languages share the same calls. Their examples above show the same game written by hand, stopping each thing where the mode ends.

Settings#

States have no settings of their own: they're written in game code.

Shortcuts#

States have no shortcuts.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a timer stopped before it finished, and TimerFinished never came. Why: the component's state changed after it started, so it ended with it. Fix: start it after setting the new state, or call keepStarted() after starting it.
  • Problem: nothing stops when the state changes. Why: the "state" is a field (Mood mood = Mood.Calm;), not the component's own state. Fix: write it state = Mood.Calm; in the has, and set it with state = …;.
  • Problem: MoodChanged never comes. Why: the game doesn't declare it, or the state changed and changed back in the same tick. Fix: declare event MoodChanged(Mood from, Mood to); beside the state.
  • Problem: a looping sound kept playing after the state changed. Why: it was started before the state was set, so it belongs to the state before, or keepStarted() came after it. Fix: set the state first, then start the sound.
  • Problem: a tween's value stopped halfway. Why: the state changed while it ran, so it stopped where it was. Fix: set the value yourself in the leaving work (on MoodChanged), or keep the tween with keepStarted().

Related#

  • Timers: waits that end with their state.
  • Game code: components, events, tweens and the tick.
  • Sound events: which sounds loop.
  • Save games: what a save keeps.
  • Concepts: state, timer, tween, event.
← Previous · Chapter 52TimersNext → · Chapter 54Characters and cameras

Characters and cameras#

A character that walks, sprints, jumps and climbs, and three cameras (third person, first person and RTS), ready-made, so you can walk around a level before writing any code.

When to use it#

Almost every game has someone to move around and a camera to see them with. Getting these right is fiddly: a character has to climb steps, slide along walls instead of sticking to them, not float off the top of a slope, and ride a moving platform; a camera behind it mustn't end up inside a wall. Solis has them ready:

  • CharacterBody (a built-in component) does the hard part: it moves a standing capsule as far as it can go, the way game characters move. It's what moveCharacter moves.
  • CharacterController (a ready-made component in Lust) reads the player's input and tells the CharacterBody where to go.
  • ThirdPersonCamera, FirstPersonCamera and RtsCamera (ready-made, in Lust) put the camera behind the character, in its eyes, or high above a map. FollowCamera2D follows the player in a 2D game.

They're written in Lust and their files are in your project's solis/kit/ folder, so you can read exactly what they do and copy them to make your own. Use them as they are to get going; change a copy when your game needs something different.

For a thing that's pushed around by physics (a ball, a crate) use a RigidBody instead: a character isn't moved by physics, it moves itself and pushes physics things out of its way.

How to use it#

Try the playground first. Playground on the launcher's Learn (Make it in a folder…), or a New project started from Playground, makes a new project with a level to walk around in: steps, a gentle ramp and one too steep to climb, crates to push, a moving platform to ride, and a character with the third-person camera. Press Play, click the Game panel, and walk with W A S D, look with the mouse, jump with Space, sprint with Shift. F6 saves the game and F7 loads it. Esc gives the editor the mouse back.

It has sounds too (Sound events): footsteps as the character walks (faster when it runs, made by the playground's Footsteps code), music, a radio on a crate whose chatter makes the music dip as you come near (the Mixer's Voice ducking Music), and a cave with a drip, where every step echoes (a reverb zone). The sounds are Solis's own, free to use for anything.

A character in your own level

  1. Add an entity for the character (Home › Empty, which adds an empty one, or a model of a person) with its feet where it should stand.

  2. In Properties, choose + Component › CharacterBody. A green capsule shows its shape when it's selected. Its feet are at the entity's origin.

  3. Make sure there's ground under it: an entity with a Collider, see Physics.

  4. In main.lst, fetch the ready-made components:

    fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
end
    // The kit's components are Lust. A game in Rust brings them in from a
// main.lst of three lines beside its Rust:
//
//     fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
//     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
//     end
    -- The kit's components are Lust. A game in Lua brings them in from a
-- main.lst of three lines beside its Lua files:
--
--     fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
--     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
--     end

    (For a 2D game, fetch FollowCamera2D and the kit's TopDownController instead: see Tile maps.)

  5. Add CharacterController to the character. Set its camera to the camera entity (next step).

  6. On the entity with the Camera component, add ThirdPersonCamera and set its target to the character.

  7. Press Play and click the Game panel.

The other cameras

  • FirstPersonCamera: set its body to the character. It sits at the eyes and turns the character with it, so untick the CharacterController's facesWhereItWalks (it would turn the other way).
  • RtsCamera: needs no character. It looks down on the map from above, as strategy games do.
  • FollowCamera2D, for a 2D game (a camera whose View is 2D: 2D: pixel-perfect): set its target to the player, and its bounds to the entity showing your tile map. It has no keys: it just follows.
    • The player can walk a little way from the middle (the deadZone, in metres across and up) before the camera moves, so small steps don't shake the picture.
    • Then it catches up smoothly in about smoothing seconds, easing in and stopping without going past (0 follows at once). Why: a camera glued to the player jerks with every step; a little slack and easing feels calm, as in farming and adventure games.
    • With bounds set, it never shows past the map's edges: near the edge the player walks towards the side of the screen instead. A map smaller than the view stays in the middle.
    • The picture stays crisp: Solis keeps the camera on whole pixels as it draws, whatever the camera does.
RTS cameraKeyboard and mouseGamepad
Move over the maparrow keysleft stick
Drag the maphold the middle mouse button and move the mouse
TurnAlt + left or right arrowright stick
Zoommouse wheel, Page Up and Page Downright and left triggers

These are the ready-made actions Pan, Drag, Turn and Zoom, so you can rebind them in File › Project settings › Input. A project made before these cameras existed doesn't have them yet: the Input page offers to add them.

Moving a character from your own code

walk(wanted) moves the component's character by wanted metres (target:walk(wanted) moves another), as far as it can: it climbs steps and slopes, slides along walls, pushes crates and rides moving platforms, and stops where it can't go. Two characters standing in one another (spawned on one spot, say) are pushed apart gently as they walk, rather than stuck together. It happens at the end of the tick, after physics has had game code's other changes. Call it once a tick with speed times dt, plus your own falling. Always multiply by dt: it's the tick's length at the game's speed, so the character slows down and stops with World:setGameSpeed like everything else. A walk without dt ignores the game's speed.

fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Hopper {
    has {
        float fall = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        vec3 move = Input:axis(Action.Move);
        vec3 step = [move.x, move.y, 0];
        is grounded()? then {
            fall = 0;
            is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
                fall = 5;
            }
        } or {
            fall = fall - 20 * dt;
        }
        walk(step * 4 * dt + [0, 0, fall * dt]);
    }
}

pass Hopper;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hopper {
    fall: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Hopper {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let dt = dt as f32;
        let wanted = cx.host().action("Move").axis;
        let step = Vec3::new(wanted.x, wanted.y, 0.0);
        if cx.host().grounded(me) {
            self.fall = 0.0;
            if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
                self.fall = 5.0;
            }
        } else {
            self.fall -= 20.0 * dt;
        }
        cx.host().walk(me, step * 4.0 * dt + Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, self.fall * dt));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Hopper = component("Hopper", {
    { "fall", "float", 0 },
})

function Hopper:update(dt)
    local move = solis.Input:axis("Move")
    local step = vec3(move.x, move.y, 0)
    if solis.entity.grounded(self.me) then
        self.fall = 0
        if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
            self.fall = 5
        end
    else
        self.fall = self.fall - 20 * dt
    end
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, step * 4 * dt + vec3(0, 0, self.fall * dt))
end

Why your own falling? Because how a character falls and jumps is part of how a game feels (floaty or snappy), so it's yours to choose. On the ground it stops falling (fall = 0): the CharacterBody keeps it to the ground going down steps and slopes (its Keeps to the ground setting).

In Lua the move is a vec3(x, y, z) (a table works too, but only with its parts named: { x = 1, y = 0, z = 0 }).

Settings#

CharacterBody (built-in)

SettingWhat it does
HeightFeet to head, metres. 1.8 suits a person.
RadiusHalf its width. 0.35 m suits a person; wider characters can't fit through narrow gaps.
Step heightThe tallest step it walks up without jumping. 0.35 m climbs stairs but not a table.
Steepest slopeThe steepest slope it walks up, in degrees; it slides down steeper ones. 45° is usual.
Keeps to the groundHow far down it stays on the ground walking down steps and slopes, instead of flying off them. 0 never.
MassHow hard it pushes crates it walks into.

CharacterController (ready-made)

SettingWhat it does
cameraThe camera following it: forward is the way that camera looks. Nothing: forward is the way the character faces.
walkSpeed, sprintSpeedMetres a second, walking and with Sprint held.
jumpHeightHow high a jump goes, metres.
gravityHow fast it falls. 20 feels snappier than real life's 9.81, as most games do.
facesWhereItWalksIt turns to face where it's walking (third person). Untick for first person.
turnSpeedHow fast it turns to face where it walks, degrees a second.

ThirdPersonCamera (ready-made)

SettingWhat it does
targetThe character it follows.
distanceHow far behind it stays, metres. A wall in between pulls it closer.
heightHow high above the character's feet it looks: about the head.
wheelZoomsTick it to let the mouse wheel (Zoom) change the distance, between closest and farthest. Off, the distance stays fixed.
lowest, highestHow far down and up the player can look, degrees.

FirstPersonCamera (ready-made): body (the character), eyes (how high its eyes are), turnsBody, lowest and highest.

RtsCamera (ready-made): focus (the point on the map it looks at), height, lowest and highest (how far it zooms), tilt (degrees it looks down), panSpeed and turnSpeed.

FollowCamera2D (ready-made): target (who it follows), bounds (an entity with a tile map it stays inside; empty: no edges), deadZone (how far, in metres across and up, the target can move from the middle before it follows; 1 and 0.75 to start), smoothing (about how many seconds it takes to catch up; 0.2 to start, 0 for at once), and speed (how fast it's moving now; you don't need to set it).

The fields at the bottom of each (fall, yaw, pitch) are how it's moving right now: how fast it's falling, and which way it's looking. While playing, Properties shows them changing. They're fields so a save game keeps them; you don't need to set them.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
WalkW A S D (left stick)
LookMouse (right stick)
JumpSpace (A)
SprintShift (left stick click)
Save and load, in the playgroundF6 and F7

All of these are the game's only while it has the mouse and keys (click the Game panel); see Input. The kit's actions (Move, Look, Jump, Sprint, Zoom, Pan, Turn, Drag) are always named in game code, so the kit works in a project that hasn't made them all; one your project hasn't made in File › Project settings › Input is never pressed.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the character doesn't move. Why: the game doesn't have the keys, or there's no ground under it (it fell). Fix: click the Game panel; give the floor a Collider.
  • Problem: W walks the wrong way. Why: the CharacterController's camera isn't set, so forward is the way the character faces. Fix: set it to the camera.
  • Problem: the character can't get up a step. Why: the step is taller than its Step height. Fix: raise Step height, or make the step lower.
  • Problem: it slides down a ramp it should walk up. Why: the ramp is steeper than Steepest slope. Fix: raise it, or make the ramp gentler.
  • Problem: my changes to solis/kit/character.lst disappeared. Why: Solis writes the solis/ folder again whenever the project opens, so it always matches this version of Solis. Fix: copy the file outside solis/ (say, player.lst), rename the component inside (component MyController), and fetch that instead.
  • Problem: the game slows down with a big crowd of characters. Why: each character's move looks around it for walls, steps and slopes, about 10 to 15 microseconds each. Solis works them out on every core at once, so a few hundred cost little, but thousands add up. Fix: for a huge horde, move the far-away ones yourself with moveTo and give a CharacterBody only to those near the player.
  • Problem: the first-person view spins when I walk. Why: both the camera and the controller are turning the character. Fix: untick the CharacterController's facesWhereItWalks.

Related#

  • Physics: colliders, rigid bodies, pushing things
  • Input: the actions, and rebinding them
  • Save games
  • Game code
  • Concepts: character controller, ready-made components
← Previous · Chapter 53States that start and stopNext → · Chapter 55Save games

Save games#

Save the whole game and load it back exactly as it was: every entity, every component's values, the lasers in flight, physics, sprites' clips, animators' states, tile maps as the game changed them, the timers waiting (and the state each ends with), a change of state waiting to be heard, the clock, the time of day and the random numbers.

When to use it#

Whenever a player should be able to stop and carry on later: a quick-save key, a save point, a checkpoint before a boss. Solis saves everything for you, so you don't write any code to list what to keep, and nothing gets forgotten. A loaded game carries on exactly as the saved one would have: the same crate falls the same way, the same random numbers come up.

It's also a debugging tool: save just before something goes wrong, and you can load and watch it again and again.

How to use it#

From game code (in Lust, fetch "solis/world":Saves; then Saves:saveTo("quick"); in Lua, solis.Saves:saveTo("quick"); in Rust, cx.host().save_game("quick", false), with true to load):

fetch "solis/world":Saves;
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component QuickSave {
    method update(float dt) {
        is Input:pressed(Action.QuickSave)? then {
            Saves:saveTo("quick");
        }
        is Input:pressed(Action.QuickLoad)? then {
            Saves:loadFrom("quick");
        }
    }
}

pass QuickSave;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct QuickSave;

impl RustComponent for QuickSave {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        // The slot's name, then whether to load it (true) or save it (false).
        if cx.host().action("QuickSave").pressed {
            cx.host().save_game("quick", false);
        }
        if cx.host().action("QuickLoad").pressed {
            cx.host().save_game("quick", true);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local QuickSave = component("QuickSave", {})

function QuickSave:update(dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("QuickSave") then
        solis.Saves:saveTo("quick")
    end
    if solis.Input:pressed("QuickLoad") then
        solis.Saves:loadFrom("quick")
    end
end

Add the QuickSave and QuickLoad actions in File › Project settings › Input and bind them to keys of your choice (Input).

  • A slot is a save's name: letters, digits, _ and - (quick, slot_1, before-boss), but not a name Windows keeps for a device (CON, NUL, PRN, AUX, COM1, LPT1 and so on). Saving to a slot that has a save replaces it. A project keeps at most 100 saves, and 2 GB of them together; past that, game code can replace one but not add more (the Console says so).
  • Both happen at the end of the tick, after every component's update, like moves (what game code sees). A load replaces the whole game, so nothing else runs in that frame after it.
  • Asking for the same slot again in one tick saves once (a save is the whole game, so a Saves:saveTo in every unit's update would otherwise make thousands at a time). At most four slots are saved or loaded in one tick.
  • Loading doesn't run the game's starts again (the code outside components, and its fields' starting values): what they did already happened in the saved game.
  • Saves:saveTo, Saves:loadFrom and Input:rebind work from update and events, not while a component starts (the Console says so if you try).
  • A Saves:loadFrom from game code leaves the game the mouse and keys, so the player carries on at once; Debug › Load save gives them back to the editor.
  • Game-wide objects (a clock, the money: Game code) are kept with every field a component's could have, and loading gives them back. An object or field the code no longer has is left out, and the Console says which.
  • Physics is kept as each body's place and motion. Saving starts physics afresh from those, which a loaded game does too, so the loaded game carries on exactly as the saved one does (a stack of crates may settle by a hair as you save).

From the editor: Debug › Load save picks a save from the project's saves folder and plays from it, whether or not the game is running. Stop still puts the level back as it was before you pressed Play: a save is a moment in a game, not a change to your level. If you edit the level after loading, Stop offers to keep those edits as usual, and Keep makes them on your level from before Play, never on the save's (a change to an entity only the save had can't be kept; see Play mode).

Saves survive updates (Backups and upgrades): a save made by an earlier Solis loads in a later one, upgraded as it's read. A save is never refused just for being older, so a game's update never wipes its players' progress. The very first saves (format 1, from before the Phase 6 review) kept physics in a form Solis no longer reads, so things that were moving start at rest where they were, and the Console says so. A save is still refused when it was made by a newer Solis.

Your game's own versions: when your game changes in a way old saves don't fit (a new map, say), that's for your game to decide, not Solis. Keep a version number in a component's has block (int saveVersion = 3;), and check it in code after a load: carry on, put things right, or tell the player.

Where saves live: in the project's saves folder, one .solsave file per slot, beside project.solis. New projects keep this folder out of Git, since saves are your test plays, not part of the game. An exported game keeps players' saves in their own saved-games folder instead (Exporting for playtesting).

Why the game must come out the same everywhere#

A save, a recording and (later) a game played online all rest on one promise: the same game, given the same input, comes out exactly the same, tick by tick, on any PC and with any number of cores (determinism). A loaded save only carries on as the saved game would have if every sum works out to the very same bits; a recording only replays if it does on the PC replaying it; two players online only stay in step if their PCs agree, since they send each other only their input.

The game state is what has to agree: where everything is, physics, every component's values, tile maps, animators, zones, timers, the random numbers. What's only shown (sounds, light, the sky, screens, shakes) doesn't, and needn't.

Solis keeps its own side of the promise:

  • game code reads the world as the tick started and its changes land in a fixed order, so the number of cores never changes the result (what game code sees);
  • physics is built to give the same answer on every PC (Physics);
  • game code's maths (Maths:sin, Maths:exp, Maths:power and the rest in Lust; math.sin, math.exp, math.pow and the rest in Lua) is worked out by Solis's own maths, the same to the last bit everywhere, never by the computer's system library, which rounds the last digit differently on Windows and on Linux;
  • every tick, the game's checksum sums up its whole state, so a replay that stops matching says at which tick;
  • Solis checks itself: every change to Solis plays a recorded game, with physics, 2D and 3D, spawns, tile maps, animators, zones, timers, speed changes and game code in all three languages, on Linux and on Windows, on one core and on four, and compares every tick. A sum that works out differently on another PC is caught before it reaches your game.

Your side, in game code:

  • Roll random numbers with the game's own: World:random(), World:randomRange and World:randomInt; in Rust cx.host().random(), and in Lua math.random follows it too (Random numbers). They follow the game's seed, so a save or a replay rolls the same numbers. Lust's own Random (Random[1, 6], Random:chance) doesn't follow it yet, so avoid it in anything the game keeps.
  • Never keep real time in game state: World:frameTime() is how long the frame took on this PC, which differs every time. Use the dt your update is given.
  • In Lua, raise to a power with math.pow(a, b), not a ^ b: the ^ sign is worked out by the computer's own library, which can round differently on another PC (a whole power of two, such as 2 ^ 3, is exact anywhere). In Lust, Maths:power is always exact.
  • A tween's done block (tween … { … }) can run in a different order, against another tween's ending in the same tick, with another number of cores. Until Solis puts them in a fixed order, keep what a done block does to the component's own fields, or glide the value yourself in update.

Settings#

Save games have no settings: everything is saved.

Shortcuts#

None of its own. A game chooses its own save and load keys through input actions.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the Console says the game wasn't saved because save games are kept in a project. Why: saves are files in a project's folder. Fix: open or make a project on the launcher.
  • Problem: "the saves folder is a link to somewhere else". Why: Solis only writes saves into a real folder in the project, so a project you downloaded can't send them elsewhere on your computer. Fix: delete the saves link (or move the real folder into the project).
  • Problem: "Couldn't load quick: it was saved by the project …". Why: a save belongs to the project that made it. Fix: load it in that project.
  • Problem: "Couldn't load …: it's damaged". Why: the file was cut short or changed (a save carries a checksum, so a damaged one is refused rather than half loaded). Fix: save again.
  • Problem: a value in my component isn't the same after loading. Why: a save keeps every field in a component's has block, but not other variables the code keeps for itself. Fix: put anything that must survive a load in has.
  • Problem: the Console says a component's saved values were left out. Why: the game's code has no component by that name any more (it was renamed or removed since the save). The rest of the save loads. Fix: nothing, if it was removed on purpose; if it was renamed, its values start fresh.
  • Problem: "Couldn't load …: it was made by a newer Solis". Why: someone saved it with a newer build. Fix: update Solis.
  • Problem: "The game wasn't saved: the tile map on … has grown too big to be loaded again". Why: a save keeps each tile map as the game has changed it, and a map is read back within the same limits as a map file: 64 MB and 12 million numbers, texts and symbols, which a number in a million and a half cells is past. A save that couldn't be loaded would be the player's progress lost, so it isn't written; the save in that slot before stays. Fix: keep values only on the cells that need them, or split the world into several maps.
  • Problem: "The game wasn't saved: it would be … MB". Why: a save can be at most 256 MB to load back, and this game is bigger. Fix: fewer entities or physics bodies.
  • Problem: loading ended my recording. Why: a recording plays back from Play, so it can't carry on across a load. What was recorded up to the load is saved in the recordings folder. Fix: record again from Play to record past it.
  • Problem: loading says "The project's data tables have changed since … was saved". Why: a save doesn't keep your data tables (they're the game's design, not its progress), only which ones it was made with; you've changed one since, so prices or numbers the game reads may differ from when it was saved. A recording played back says the same. Fix: nothing, if the change is meant; the save loads either way.
  • Problem: replaying a recording didn't change my saves. Why: a replay makes the same saves the recorded play did (so it plays out the same), but doesn't write them over your saves.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Input
  • Play mode
  • Checking a project: recordings a project keeps, played back before an update
  • Concepts: save game, determinism, checksum
← Previous · Chapter 54Characters and camerasNext → · Chapter 56Exporting for playtesting

Exporting for playtesting#

Makes a folder holding your game, ready to zip and send to a friend, who plays it without the editor.

When to use it#

When you want someone else to try your game: a friend, a tester, or yourself on another computer. They get a folder with a program named after your game. Double-clicking it starts the game straight away, filling its window, with no launcher, no editor and nothing to install.

It's a playtest build, made in seconds, because the game's Lust and Lua code runs as it does when you press Play. A finished release with an installer comes later (the Build tab shows its place: Targets, Build, Installer and Your Rust code are unfinished parts). Until then, a game's own Rust code isn't built into an export.

How to use it#

  1. Open your project, and save the level your game starts in.
  2. Click Build in the tab bar (or search for Export for playtesting…; Home's ribbon no longer has a Build button). The Build tab is Export for playtesting as a page, with the Console in the bottom panel under it. The same settings are also in File › Project settings › Build.
  3. Check the settings (see the table below). They start from your project's name and the open level, and next time from what you chose last. The name, level and window are remembered with the project. The folder is remembered by Solis on this computer, so a project you got from someone else never decides where its export goes.
  4. Click Export at the end of the Export row (the big Export on the Build tab's ribbon does the same). The card beside the settings and the Console say where it went. Click Open folder on the card, or on the Build tab's ribbon, to see it.
  5. Zip that folder (in Windows Explorer, right-click it, then Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder) and send the zip.

Your friend unzips it (all of it, somewhere they can write, such as their Documents) and double-clicks <Game>.exe inside. Double-clicking it inside the zip doesn't work: Windows takes only the program out, without the game beside it.

What's in the folder, and why:

FileWhat it is
<Game>.exeThe program, named after your game. It's the same program as the editor: finding playtest.txt beside itself, it plays instead.
playtest.txtThe game's name, the level it starts in, and its first window.
game/Your project's files: code, levels, sprites, sounds, screens. The editor's own things stay out: its cache, saves, recordings, backups and Git's history.

Where the player's things go: everything that's the player's goes in their own folder, Saved Games/<Game> on Windows (next to other games' saves):

  • saves/: the game's save games;
  • settings.txt: the player's settings (text size, UI size, fullscreen, window size), kept from one start to the next;
  • log.txt: warnings and mistakes the game reported, like the Console's (past 1 MB it starts again, keeping the one before as log.old.txt);
  • crash log.txt: written if the program stops unexpectedly. It says what happened and the last things the game said. Ask your playtesters to send it to you.

Quitting: give your pause menu a Quit button that calls Window:quit() (see Game code). The game closes at the end of that tick. While you play in the editor, play stops instead, and the Console says the exported game would close. The window's close button always works too.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Game's nameThe program's name (Farm.exe), the window's title, and the player's saves folder (Saved Games/Farm). Characters Windows can't use in file names are taken out. Keep it the same between builds, so saves carry over.
Starts inThe level the game opens in.
Into the folderWhere the export goes. Solis suggests a new dated folder each time, beside your last export (in Documents the first time), so older builds stay. A folder that already has files in it isn't used, and nor is one inside your project. If the suggested folder has files in already (a second export the same day), the export goes in a numbered folder beside it, ending (2), then (3); the page and the Console say which. A folder you typed or chose with … is used exactly as given, or refused. Solis doesn't look inside any folder until you click Export.
WindowWindowed or Fullscreen, and the window's size, when the game first starts. After that, the player's own choice (in your game's menu, or with Alt+Enter) is kept.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Switch the exported game between fullscreen and a windowAlt+Enter

In an exported game, every key is the game's, Esc included.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the game says "The game can't start: its code has mistakes." Why: the exported code doesn't compile. Fix: fix the mistakes in the Problems panel, then export again.
  • A game needs no code of its own. A level made only of the editor's own components (sprites, physics, animators, sounds) exports and plays as it does when you press Play. The files Solis writes in its solis folder, which describe the engine to game code, don't count as your code.
  • Problem: "already has files in it". Why: exports never mix with, or replace, anything, and a folder you chose yourself is never swapped for another. Fix: choose a new folder, or empty that one.
  • Problem: after updating Solis, the page suggests a folder in Documents again, not beside your last export. Why: where a game went used to be written in the project's own folder. A project can come from someone else, so that file could point your export at a folder of their choosing, even one on another computer. Solis now remembers it itself, on this computer, and no longer reads it from the project. Fix: choose your folder once more; it's remembered from then on.
  • Problem: you exported to a folder on another computer (\\server\share\…), and next time the page suggests Documents. Why: only a folder on this computer's own drives is suggested again, so opening the page never reaches for another computer. Fix: type or choose the network folder each time.
  • Problem: the game says "The game's files can't be read", or "The game stopped". Why: the game folder is missing or damaged, or it's somewhere the game can't write (the first start writes a cache into game/). Fix: unzip the whole export again, somewhere like Documents. The message names the log with more.
  • Problem: the export is big. Why: it holds the program and every file in the project (all the Library shows), used or not. Fix: move files the game doesn't use out of the project's folder.
  • Problem: Windows warns about the program when your friend opens it. Why: it isn't signed, as programs from big companies are. Fix: they choose More info › Run anyway. Send builds only to people who trust you.
  • Problem: saves from an older build are gone. Why: the game's name changed, so the saves folder did too. Fix: keep the name the same.
  • Problem: Rust components of your own don't run. Why: building a game's own Rust code comes with the full export (Your Rust code on the Build tab's ribbon, not built yet). Fix: use Lust or Lua for now.

Related#

  • Screens: the player's settings and a pause menu.
  • The UI sample: a pause menu with Quit, ready to export.
  • Save games.
  • Concepts: player setting, playtest.

Your first game: the turret sample#

A small game to read, play and change: a turret shoots at a drone, and the drone's health, armour and sparks react. It's written in all three of Solis's languages, which talk to each other through events.

When to use it#

Right after reading Game code, or instead of it if you learn best from a working example. Everything in it is ordinary game code you can change while it runs.

How to use it#

  1. On the launcher's Learn, click Make it in a folder… under Turret sample and pick an empty folder (or start a New project from Turret sample). Solis makes a project there called Turret sample, opens it, and opens its level.
  2. Press Play. The sample has no models yet, so its story is told in the Console (later phases give it models). Watch the Console: every half second the turret fires. The drone's armour dents three times ("Sparks fly from Drone: 2 armour plates left"), and after eight hits the drone is destroyed and drops to the ground.
  3. While it plays, click the Game panel and press P (or Start on a controller): the game stops and a pause menu shows (the Pauser component on the Game entity, and ui/pauseMenu.lst). Resume carries on; Quit leaves it stopped with a note. See Game screens.
  4. Press Stop, then open the code from the Library's Code tab.

What's in it#

The turret (Lust, in main.lst) has a target (the drone, set in Properties), ammo, damage and a cooldown. Each tick, update counts the cooldown down. When it reaches zero, it fires: send Hit(this, damage) to target;.

In the sample each component is written in one language: the turret and Health in Lust, Armour in Rust, Sparks in Lua. The switch above each example shows it in all three, so you can read the whole sample in the language you know.

event Hit(entity by, float damage);

component Turret {
    has {
        entity target = nothing;
        int ammo = 12;
        float damage = 2.5;
        float cooldown = 0.5;
        float reload = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        reload = reload - dt;
        is reload <= 0 && ammo > 0? then {
            send Hit(this, damage) to target;
            ammo = ammo - 1;
            reload = cooldown;
        }
    }
}

pass Turret;
end
use reflect::{EntityId, Value};
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Turret {
    target: Option<EntityId>,
    ammo: i64,
    damage: f64,
    cooldown: f64,
    reload: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Turret {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        self.reload -= dt;
        if self.reload <= 0.0 && self.ammo > 0 {
            let me = cx.me();
            let hit = vec![Value::Entity(Some(me)), Value::Float(self.damage)];
            cx.send(self.target, "Hit", hit);
            self.ammo -= 1;
            self.reload = self.cooldown;
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Turret = component("Turret", {
    { "target", "entity" },
    { "ammo", "int", 12 },
    { "damage", "float", 2.5 },
    { "cooldown", "float", 0.5 },
    { "reload", "float", 0 },
})

function Turret:update(dt)
    self.reload = self.reload - dt
    if self.reload <= 0 and self.ammo > 0 then
        solis.send(self.target, "Hit", self.me, self.damage)
        self.ammo = self.ammo - 1
        self.reload = self.cooldown
    end
end

The drone carries three components, one in each language. Each reacts to the events it cares about:

ComponentLanguageReacts toDoes
HealthLust (main.lst)HitTakes the damage; at 0 it sends Destroyed to the drone.
ArmourRust (armour.rs)HitDents a plate, and sends Dented with the plates left.
SparksLua (sparks.lua)Dented, DestroyedSays so in the Console; when destroyed, drops the drone to the ground.

The drone's armour (in the sample, Rust: armour.rs) dents a plate at each hit and says how many are left:

event Hit(entity by, float damage);
event Dented(int platesLeft);

component Armour {
    has {
        int plates = 3;
    }

    on Hit(entity by, float damage) {
        is plates > 0? then {
            plates = plates - 1;
            send Dented(plates) to this;
        }
    }
}

pass Armour;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Armour {
    plates: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Armour {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Hit" || self.plates == 0 {
            return false;
        }
        self.plates -= 1;
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.send(Some(me), "Dented", vec![Value::Int(self.plates)]);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(), and the RustKind that registers it: see armour.rs.
}
local Armour = component("Armour", {
    { "plates", "int", 3 },
})

function Armour:on_Hit(by, damage)
    if self.plates > 0 then
        self.plates = self.plates - 1
        solis.send(self.me, "Dented", self.plates)
    end
end

And its sparks (in the sample, Lua: sparks.lua) react to each dent:

fetch "solis/world":World;

event Dented(int platesLeft);

component Sparks {
    has {
        int shown = 0;
    }

    on Dented(int platesLeft) {
        shown = shown + 1;
        World:say("Sparks fly from " + name() + ": " + platesLeft.text() + " armour plates left.");
    }
}

pass Sparks;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Sparks {
    shown: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Sparks {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Dented" {
            return false;
        }
        self.shown += 1;
        let plates = match event.values.first() {
            Some(Value::Int(left)) => *left,
            _ => 0,
        };
        let me = cx.me();
        let name = cx.host().name(me).unwrap_or_default();
        cx.host().say(&format!("Sparks fly from {name}: {plates} armour plates left."));
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Sparks = component("Sparks", {
    { "shown", "int", 0 },
})

function Sparks:on_Dented(platesLeft)
    self.shown = self.shown + 1
    solis.World:say("Sparks fly from " .. solis.entity.name(self.me) .. ": " .. platesLeft .. " armour plates left.")
end

The events are declared once, in Lust (event Hit(entity by, float damage);). Lust checks its own sends before the game runs, so a wrongly-sent event in Lust is a mistake in Problems. When Lua or Rust sends one with the wrong values, it isn't sent, and the Console names the component that sent it.

Things to try#

  • While it plays, change the turret's damage to 10 in Properties: the drone goes down in two hits.
  • While it plays, change reload = cooldown; in main.lst to reload = cooldown / 5; and save. The turret fires five times faster at once, keeping the ammo it has left. (Changing a starting value instead, such as cooldown = 0.5, doesn't change a turret that's already running: running components keep their values. Set it in Properties for that.)
  • In sparks.lua, change what it says and save while it plays: the next dent says the new words.
  • Give the drone more armour: select it and set Plates to 10.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I changed armour.rs and nothing changed. Why: Solis can't build a game's own Rust yet (that comes with the full export, which isn't built yet). Until then, the Armour built into Solis runs, and the Console says your changes don't. Fix: try changes in the Lust and Lua instead.
  • Problem: "Couldn't make the sample game". Why: the folder is already a project, or already has a file where the sample's would go (such as main.lst); Solis never replaces your files. Fix: choose an empty folder.

Related#

  • Game code: components, events and changing code while it runs, in detail
  • Play mode
  • Concepts: component, event, tick
← Previous · Chapter 56Exporting for playtestingNext → · Chapter 58The Console

The Console#

Messages from the editor and the engine, and a command line for doing things by typing.

When to use it#

  • To see what's happening: the Console reports the editor starting, the graphics card in use, models imported and reloaded, files saved, and anything that went wrong. Warnings and errors from the libraries Solis is built on (the graphics layer, for example) show here too, named after the library.
  • To do things by typing: some jobs are quicker typed than clicked, such as selecting every entity called "Lamp", or setting the exact position of ten things at once. Everything a command changes is an ordinary undo step, the same as doing it with the mouse.

How to use it#

Reading messages

  1. Each message shows its time, how serious it is as a word in its colour (INFO, WARN in amber, ERROR in red, with the row faintly tinted), and the text. A long message is cut short: click it to read it in full in a strip below the list (with Copy, to paste it somewhere), and click it again or Close to put the strip away.
  2. The bottom panel's bar, while the Console's tab is in front, has its filter: Info, Warnings and Errors, each with how many there are. Click one to hide those messages, and again to show them. The Console's tab counts its warnings and errors too, even while the panel is folded, and the folded line shows the newest warning or error faintly.
  3. Type in Search the log to show only messages containing that text (capitals don't matter).
  4. Clear (the bin) empties the Console; Copy copies the messages shown.

Typing commands

  1. Press ' (on a Norwegian keyboard, the key with ' and * next to Æ) to jump to the command line at the bottom of the Console: the Console's tab comes to the front of the bottom panel, opened if it was folded. You can also click in it. The command line is the Console's own, so it shows only while the Console's tab is in front.
  2. Type a command, such as select Crate, and press Enter. The Console repeats it after a ›, then answers: what it found, or, if something's wrong, why (in red).
  3. The command line keeps the keyboard, ready for the next command. Press Esc or click elsewhere to leave it.
  4. Up and Down bring back earlier commands. Solis remembers the last 100, even after it's closed.
  5. Tab finishes what you're typing: a command's name, an entity's name after select, or a component's setting after get and set. If several fit, they're listed at the right of the command line, after a Tab key; type a little more and press Tab again.

Names never care about capitals. A name with spaces goes in quotes: select "Point light 1".

Commands#

CommandWhat it does
helpLists every command. help set says how one is used.
clearEmpties the Console.
select Crate LampSelects every entity with those names (or IDs). select all selects everything, select none nothing.
find harLists the entities whose names contain "har", with their IDs.
framePoints the camera at the selection, like F.
new Harbour wallAdds an empty entity where the camera looks, named as you say, and selects it.
deleteDeletes the selection and everything under it.
duplicateDuplicates the selection, like Ctrl + D.
get TransformShows a component's settings on the selected entity. get Light.color shows one. While the game plays, it shows them as the game has them now.
values HeroShows every component of the entity called Hero (or, with no name, the selected one) as it is now. While the game plays, that's as game code has changed it: the score, the hero's health, where things are. Properties shows the same for the selected entity.
set Transform.position 0 0 2Changes a setting on every selected entity that has that component, as one undo step. While the game plays, the running game takes the value as well, whatever it had made of it: set Score.points 0 starts the score again, even though the level held 0 all along (it's get that shows the game's value). Stop then lists it with your other changes.
undo, redoLike Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y.
saveSaves the level, like Ctrl + S.
look unlitChooses the viewport's look: standard, stylized or unlit.
tool rotateChooses a tool: select, move, rotate, scale or transform.
play, pause, step, stopLike the buttons at the top (step runs one tick while paused): see Play mode.
statsCounts the entities, models, lights and triangles, and says how fast the editor is drawing.
seed, seed 42, seed newThe seed the running game started with (where its random numbers come from), and the one in use if game code or a load changed it since. With a number, every Play starts from that seed, so a play can be repeated; seed new gives each Play a new one again.
ui test, ui test keep, ui test whole, ui test offWhile playing, shows a sample HUD over the Game panel (a day box with the date and time, money, an energy bar with its label and a hotbar), laid out by a scale rule: grow with the screen, keep its size, or whole steps for pixel art. Make the panel bigger or smaller to see each part stay pinned to its corner. Game UI you make yourself is a screen.
checksumWhile playing, the game's checksums at this tick: two plays that agree at the same tick are in exactly the same state.

Values for set:

  • Numbers: set Light.strength 250. A unit after the number is fine (2m).
  • Three numbers (positions, scales): 0 0 2 or 0,0,2. Two for a game code's vec2: 3 4.5.
  • Rotations: three angles in degrees, around X, Y and Z, as Properties shows them: set Transform.rotation 0 0 90.
  • Colours: #ff8800 (as in a paint program), or three numbers from 0 to 1. A game code's colour can be see-through: #ff880080, or a fourth number for how solid it is (get shows it the same way).
  • Choices: one of the choices Properties offers, such as set Light.kind spot.
  • On or off: on, off, yes, no, true, false.
  • Models and entities can't be typed yet; choose them in Properties.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Jump to the command line' (not while typing in another field)
Run the commandEnter
Earlier and later commandsUp, Down
Finish a nameTab
Leave the command lineEsc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing ' types a ' instead of jumping to the command line. Why: another text field (a search box, a name) has the keyboard. Fix: press Esc or click the viewport first.
  • Problem: "nothing is called …". Why: no entity has exactly that name. Fix: find with part of the name lists the real names; Tab finishes them for you.
  • Problem: set says "nothing selected has a Light". Why: set only changes entities that have that component; it never adds one. Fix: select the right entities, or add the component in Properties first.
  • Problem: "No sound: couldn't open the sound card …". Why: Solis found no sound card it could use (none plugged in, or another program holding it). Fix: nothing is broken, and everything else works. Plug in speakers or a headset: Solis tries again every 30 seconds and says "Sound is on." when it finds one.
  • The Console keeps the newest 2,000 messages. Messages from other libraries that repeat every frame are shown once.
  • Mistakes in the level itself (a missing model, say) are listed in the Problems panel, beside the Console.

Related#

  • Problems
  • Undo and redo
  • Entities and components
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Interface tour
  • Concepts: command, console

Problems#

A list of the mistakes found in your game's code (with the file and line) and in the open level (naming the entity each is on).

When to use it#

When something in the level doesn't look right, or the Problems tab shows a number beside its name. Problems are things Solis can't fix by itself, usually because files changed outside it: a model deleted in Explorer, a level merged by Git, a component from a newer version of your game's code. The level still opens and saves: nothing is lost, but something needs your attention.

How to use it#

  1. Click the Problems tab (beside the Console). The number on the tab says how many there are; with none, the tab has no number.
  2. Mistakes in the game's code come first, each with its file, line and column: click one to open the file in your code editor. Then come the level's, each naming its entity and what's wrong with it. Point at a line to read it all.
  3. Click a level line to select its entity. The Level panel unfolds to show it, and Properties shows its settings, ready to fix.
  4. Fix it, and the line goes away by itself: Solis looks again whenever the level or the project changes.

What it finds#

ProblemWhy it happensWhat to do
main.lst, line 6:15: …A mistake in the game's code: a misspelt name, text where a number should be, a missing }. The line and column (how far along the line) say where.Click it to open the file, fix it and save.
The game's code starts at main.lst …There are Lust files but no main.lst at the Library's top (the project's folder).Make main.lst there and fetch the other files from it.
X's model isn't in the projectThe model's file was deleted, or never committed to Git (with its .solmeta file).Put the file back (or commit it), or choose another model in Properties, or delete the entity.
X's Model has no model chosenA Model component was added but never given a model.Choose one in Properties, or remove the component.
X's sprite sheet isn't in the project / X's Sprite has no sprite sheet chosenThe sprite's Aseprite file was deleted or never committed, or no sheet was chosen.Put the file back, or choose a sheet in Properties.
X rests between pixelsIn a 2D game, a sprite was placed at a spot that isn't a whole pixel (snapping off, or a typed place). The game draws it on the nearest pixel, so it may seem to jump a pixel as it moves.Move it with snapping to pixels on, or type a whole number of pixels.
X has a … component that isn't knownThe level was saved by a newer Solis, or names a component from game code that isn't built yet. The component is kept exactly as it was, so saving loses nothing.Usually nothing: it comes back to life when the code that defines it is there. Remove it if it's left over.
X is a copy of a prefab that isn't in the projectThe prefab's file was deleted or not committed.Put the file back, or unpack the copy to keep it as ordinary entities.
X's parent isn't in the levelUsually a Git merge that kept a child but not its parent.Drag it onto another entity in the Level panel, or onto empty space to make it stand alone.
X is inside itselfEntities are under each other in a loop, so none of them is anywhere in the tree. Level files with such a loop are put right as they open (see the tips below), so this is rare. Until it's fixed, each stands alone, in the editor and the game alike.Drag it onto another entity in the Level panel, or onto empty space to make it stand alone.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: opening a level, the Console says X was inside itself: its parents led back to it. It's now at the top level. Why: the file put entities inside each other in a loop, which no tree can be. It's usually a Git merge that combined two moves: one put A under B while the other put B under A. Solis moves one entity of the loop to the top level and leaves the rest under it; with many loops it names the first five and counts the rest. Fix: drag it to where it belongs in the Level panel and save. The file itself isn't changed until you save.
  • Problem: models show as missing for a moment after opening a project. Why: Solis is still listing the project's files. Fix: nothing; they disappear as soon as the Library is ready.
  • Problem: a code mistake stays after I fixed it. Why: Solis checks again when a code file in the project is saved. Fix: make sure you saved the file inside the project's folder, not a copy elsewhere.

Related#

  • Game code
  • The Console
  • Projects and the Library
  • Saving levels
  • Concepts: entity, component, prefab
← Previous · Chapter 58The ConsoleNext → · Chapter 60The Profiler

The Profiler#

Shows where each frame's time goes, so you can see what makes a game or the editor slow.

When to use it#

A game feels slow, or you want to know how much more it can take: more units, more lights, more code. A frame is one picture on screen; at 60 frames a second each one has about 16.7 milliseconds (ms, thousandths of a second). The Profiler shows how those milliseconds are spent, on the CPU (the computer's processor, which runs game code and the editor) and the GPU (the graphics card, which draws). Fix the biggest part first.

How to use it#

  1. Click Debug in the tab bar: the Profiler is in the centre (the Game is a tab beside it), with the Console and Problems in the bottom panel under it. Its left slot, Running, isn't built yet.
  2. Press Play, or move around the viewport: the Profiler measures every frame the editor draws. When nothing moves, Solis doesn't draw (the viewport says Idle), so nothing new is measured.
  3. The frame-time graph along the top shows the last 240 frames, a bar each, newest on the right. The dashed lines are 60 and 30 frames a second: a bar above a line is a frame too slow for it, and bars over 60 frames a second's budget are lighter. Click a bar to pick that frame: it turns the accent colour, and the line at the top right says its number and time.
  4. The timeline under it shows the frame picked (or the newest): the CPU's parts laid end to end along a ruler of milliseconds, and under them the GPU's. A part long enough has its name on it. The lanes for threads aren't built yet.
  5. Statistics on the right are averaged over the last 60 frames: the CPU's and the GPU's time a frame (each with a bar, its share of 60 frames a second's 16.7 ms), draw calls, triangles, model copies in view, what was sent to the graphics card, entities and game components running.
  6. CPU and GPU on the ribbon hide or show those lanes and figures.

What the parts mean#

PartWhat it is
Game codeYour Lust, Lua and Rust components: their updates, events, and taking in changes made while playing.
WorldThe game's world: stepping its clock, working out where things are, taking in the level's changes.
Preparing to drawWorking out what each view shows: which models where, the lights.
Drawing (CPU)Handing that to the graphics card.
SoundThe game's sounds: choosing which are heard, placing them, the buses.
EditorEverything else: the panels, the mouse and keys, the interface.
GPU: shadows, models, the last passThe graphics card's own time: the sun's shadows, the models and sky, then exposure and colour. Measured only on cards that offer it; the Profiler says when yours doesn't.
Projectiles drawnHow many lasers and other projectiles the Game tab drew. Shown when there are some.
The countsModel copies in view, copies casting shadows into it, triangles, draw calls (one per model part, however many copies), and how much was sent to the graphics card. Copies out of view aren't drawn at all (culling), and copies that didn't move aren't sent again, so a still scene sends next to nothing.

The CPU and the GPU work at the same time, each on its own frame, so the slower of the two sets the frame rate, not their sum.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Pick a frame to look atClick its bar in the graph

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Game code is the biggest part. Why: many components, or one doing a lot each tick. Fix: do less each tick (check things every few ticks, not every one), or move the busiest code to Rust.
  • Problem: the GPU's times say they aren't measured. Why: your graphics card or its driver doesn't offer timestamps. Fix: the CPU's numbers still work; update the graphics driver, which often adds them.
  • Problem: Preparing to draw goes up when I turn the camera towards the crowd. Why: only what's in view is drawn, so looking at more draws more. Fix: nothing to fix; it's the view that counts, not the size of the level.
  • Problem: the numbers jump while nothing changes. Why: other programs share the computer. Fix: read Statistics' averages, not single bars.

Related#

  • Play mode
  • Game code
  • Concepts: frame, CPU, GPU, frames a second
← Previous · Chapter 59ProblemsNext → · Chapter 61The benchmark: how much can this computer play?

The benchmark: how much can this computer play?#

Two fleets of ships flying loops and firing lasers, in three sizes, so you can see what your computer keeps at 60 frames a second.

When to use it#

  • Before you plan a big game: see how many units and projectiles your computer (and your players' computers) can take.
  • After changing your graphics card, driver or settings: compare the numbers.
  • When something feels slow: if the benchmark is fine, the slowness is in your own game, and the Profiler shows where.

How to use it#

  1. On the launcher's Learn, click Make it in a folder… under Benchmark and choose an empty folder (or start a New project from Benchmark). Solis makes a new project there and opens it on target.sollevel.
  2. Press Play. The ships appear over the first few frames (500 a tick, so no frame stalls), then fly and fire.
  3. Open the Profiler (beside the Console) to see the frame's time, and where it goes.
  4. Press Stop, open another level from the Library, and play that.
LevelShipsLasers in flightWhat it shows
target.sollevel2,000about 20,000Solis's target: should hold 60 frames a second.
stress.sollevel10,000about 100,000Far past it: should stay playable (30 frames a second or better) without stutter.
ceiling.sollevel1,000, then moreten per shipAdds 1,000 ships every few seconds while it holds 60 frames a second, then says in the Console where it ended: "This computer keeps 60 frames a second up to about 14,000 ships and 140,000 lasers."

The ceiling run measures for two seconds after each step settles, so it takes a minute or two. Keep the window in front while it runs; the frame rate of a window in the background says little.

What's in it#

Everything is ordinary Solis, so you can read and change it:

  • ships/fighter.glb: a ship model Solis made (about 2,000 triangles, with levels of detail), and ships/fighter.solassembly, an prefab of it with the Ship component.
  • main.lst: the game code. Ship flies its loop and fires a laser six times a second; Fleets makes the ships with World:spawn; Ceiling is the ceiling run, reading frameTime().
  • The three levels: the sun and sky, a camera, and one entity whose component makes the fleets. Change Ships on it in Properties to try your own number.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the frame rate is stuck at 60 even with few ships. Why: your screen shows 60 pictures a second, and Solis waits for it. Fix: nothing to fix: 60 is the goal. Ships past that are what the ceiling run finds.
  • Problem: the ceiling run's number changes between runs. Why: other programs share the computer. Fix: close what you can and run it twice; the higher number is closer to what the computer can do.
  • Problem: the first frames after Play are slow. Why: the ships are being made, 500 a tick. Fix: watch the numbers once all are made.

Related#

  • The Profiler
  • Game code: World:spawn, World:fire and World:frameTime
  • Levels of detail
  • Concepts: frame, frames a second, CPU and GPU

Editing#

All but Ctrl + Space don't work while you're typing in a field: there, Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y undo the typing instead. See Undo and redo.

Where the pointer rests decides what a key acts on, so one press never does two things. With the pointer over a tab that edits a file of its own (Clips and Frames, Animator, Tileset, Atlas Crop, the UI editor's Canvas and Elements), the keys are that tab's alone: undo and redo, Delete, Ctrl + D and Esc act on what the tab shows, as its table above says, and never on the level as well. The level's other keys (the tools' and the tile painter's keys, F, F2, Ctrl + A, and X, Y, Z and L) wait until the pointer is back over the viewport or another panel. Over the Map tab, undo and redo are the map's, and every other key is still the level's; the same goes for Properties while it shows a tileset's terrains, where undo and redo are that tileset's. On the UI tab, Properties shows the screen's settings, so over it the keys are the screen's, as over Elements: Delete removes the picked piece, never an entity. On a tab that doesn't show the level (Library, Audio, Debug, Build), the level's keys, undo and redo among them, rest too, since what they would change isn't on screen: a Delete over the Mixer never deletes an entity you can't see. They still work over the Level list and Properties wherever those are, and over the Library (its browser on either tab, or Home's folder trees), F2 renames the file picked there and Delete deletes what's picked. New, open and save, the search and Ctrl + Space work wherever the pointer is.

The search list#

Space, or a click on Search or run a command in the tab bar, opens it (the box shows the key at its right end); see the Interface tour. These keys are the ones Solis has always had: the design the editor's look follows shows other keys in its pictures, and Solis keeps its own (decision 0103↗).

ActionShortcut

Over the Frames tab, Space plays and stops the clip instead, so point somewhere else first.

The list shows each thing's shortcut beside it, so it is also the quickest place to look a key up. It finds the things without a button on the ribbon too, such as New level, Open level… and Save level as… (on the level's tab: its + and a right-click), Reset layout (File › Preferences), Close project (File), and showing or hiding the viewport's corner controls (the Show ▾ pill).

The frame: slots, groups and the bottom panel#

Every tab has the same frame (left slot, centre, right slot, and the bottom panel under the centre), filled with its own panels; the layout chosen in File › Preferences › Layout moves the slots. These size it, and each tab remembers what you did, for each layout (or one set for every tab, with Each tab keeps its own panel sizes off). No keys were added for any of it: everything is a drag or a click.
